questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding Dronabinol are true? 1. It is used in AIDS-related weight loss 2. It acts on the CB1 receptor 3. It is used in chronic pain management 4. It is excreted unchanged in faeces
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 2

• Target: CB1 receptors (primarily CNS)
• Action: Inhibits neurotransmitter release (via ↓ cAMP, ↓ Ca²⁺ influx)
• Modulates:

• Appetite
• Nausea
• Pain perception (limited clinical role)

Dronabinol is a synthetic THC used for AIDS-related anorexia/cachexia and chemotherapy-induced nausea. It acts mainly via central CB1 cannabinoid receptors to stimulate appetite. It is not a standard drug for chronic pain management. The drug undergoes hepatic metabolism rather than being excreted unchanged in feces.

| Feature | CB1 | CB2

| ------- | --- | ---

| Location | CNS (brain) | Immune cells

| Function | Appetite, mood, nausea | Immune modulation

| Target of Dronabinol | ✔ Yes | ❌ No

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The term “beaten bronze appearance” describes a characteristic textural change seen in certain corneal disorders. This appearance is associated with abnormalities in which corneal layer?
questions.explanation: The "beaten bronze" (or "beaten silver") appearance is a classic clinical description used in ophthalmology to describe the characteristic textural change seen on the corneal endothelial layer. This appearance is most famously associated with Fuchs' endothelial corneal dystrophy, although it can also be seen in cases of posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy. The endothelium is the innermost layer of the cornea, responsible for pumping water out to keep the cornea clear. In these disorders, the endothelial cells become irregular, sparse, and may develop small outgrowths called guttae. Under the slit-lamp microscope using specular reflection, these guttae give the endothelium an irregular, dimpled appearance resembling hammered or beaten metal. The stroma (Option B), sub-epithelial layer (Option C), and epithelial layer (Option D) are not associated with this specific descriptor. As the disease progresses, the failing endothelium leads to corneal edema, causing blurred vision and eventually painful blisters (bullae) on the corneal surface, a condition known as bullous keratopathy
questions.learning: The "beaten bronze" (or "beaten silver") appearance is a classic clinical description used in ophthalmology to describe the characteristic textural change seen on the corneal endothelial layer.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old P2L2 woman presents with complaints of a mass descending through the vagina and wishes to retain her fertility. She underwent an abdominal sling procedure with mesh placement. Which is the correct site of attachment of the mesh?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sacral Promontory

In abdominal sling procedures such as sacral colpopexy, which is used to treat pelvic organ prolapse while preserving fertility, the mesh is typically attached to the sacral promontory. This site provides strong support for the prolapsed vaginal apex and allows for a durable suspension without significant compromise to the patient's fertility.

Various surgeries were performed for the management of uterovaginal prolapse:

• Anterior colporrhaphy: This is done for cystocele or cystourethrocele.
• Posterior colporrhaphy/ colpoperineorrhaphy: This is done for posterior defects like rectocele or rectal defects with perineal laxity.
• Le Forte's repair: This is preferred only in elderly women with advanced prolapse, or those unfit for surgery. Women wanting an active sexual life are poor candidates for this procedure as it creates an adhesive area in the midline.
• Abdominal sling surgeries: Young women desirous of retaining menstrual and reproductive functions are ideal candidates. These surgeries use tapes as slings to prevent organ descent. These include:

• Abdominal wall cervicopexy (modified by Purandare and Mathre) - sling attached to cervix posteriorly near uterosacral ligaments.
• Shirodkar's sling surgery - the sling fixes the cervix to the lumbosacral fascia.
• Khanna's sling surgery - sling fixed to the anterior superior iliac spine, strengthening the Mackenrodt's ligament.

• Fothergill surgery (Manchester operation): An anterior colporrhaphy is combined with amputation of the cervix. The Mackenrodt ligaments are then sutured in front of the cervix followed by a colpoperineorrhaphy. It is suitable for women <40 years desiring reproductive function, but fertility may be reduced.
• Ward-Mayo surgery: This is a combination of vaginal hysterectomy + pelvic floor repair. It is done in women >40 years, not desiring reproductive function.
• Moschowitz surgery: This is performed for enterocele repair where the pouch of Douglas is obliterated.

Management of Vault prolapse:

• If the patient is fit for abdominal surgery: Transabdominal sacral colpopexy, i.e., suspending the vault to the sacral promontory extraperitoneally. It is best suited for younger women since coital difficulty following vaginal surgery is avoided
• If the patient is not fit for abdominal surgery: Right Transvaginal sacrospinous colpopexy. It is usually preferred in obese and elderly women, who are not fit for abdominal surgery.
• Colpocleisis is permissible if sexual activity is not desired
questions.learning: Sacral Promontory — In abdominal sling procedures such as sacral colpopexy, which is used to treat pelvic organ prolapse while preserving fertility, the mesh is typically attached to the sacral promontory.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Feed forward control system is employed during the regulation of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Temperature

Feed forward control system is employed during regulation of temperature.

Feed forward control

There is a control system in our body when no stimulus is required but still the system anticipates and makes corrective changes.

Such a system is called Feed forward or Anticipatory or Adaptive Control.

Examples include

• Temperature control – Thermoregulatory responses are initiated by hypothalamus BEFORE the changes in environmental temperature have succeeded in changing the body’s core body temperature
• Cephalic phase of gastric secretion- Just thinking about food increases gastric acid production
• Thinking about exercise itself increases heart rate & respiratory rate
• Role of cerebellum in motor coordination

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Komal, a 2-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with a high fever, cough, red eyes, and rash. Parents say that the rash started on the forehead and behind the ears, then subsequently spread to the neck and body. On examination, a confluent maculopapular rash is noted as shown below. Which of the following is false regarding this child's condition?
options: The period of infectivity is 3 days before and 5 days after the appearance of rash
The most common cause of death is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The most common cause of death is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of measles. The most common cause of death is pneumonia (Hecht's giant cell pneumonia).

Measles (rubeola) is caused by RNA paramyxovirus. The infection is spread via droplets, with a secondary attack rate ≥of 90%. The patients are infectious from 3 days before to 5 days after the appearance of the rash. The rash appears on the 4th day of the fever. It starts from the retro auricular region. Koplik spots and Warthin–Finkeldey giant cells are pathognomonic.

Measles can lead to subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) as a late complication.

Measles can be prevented by administering live attenuated, Edmonston–Zagreb strain or combined MMR given at 9 months of age.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the standard glucose load given for identifying diabetes in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 75 g

For IADPSG criteria, an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is done in the fasting state using 75 g of glucose, and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is diagnosed if any one of the following cut-offs is met i.e.

* Fasting: >92 mg/dl

* 1 hour: >180 mg/dl

* 2 hour: >153 mg/dl

Earlier, a two-step approach was being used to diagnose GDM. In this, the first step (screening) is a 50-gram one-hour glucose challenge test (GCT). The patients having a positive result of >140mg/dl, are candidates for the OGTT. A 100-gram, three-hour oral glucose tolerance test (GTT), is the diagnostic test for gestational diabetes mellitus. GDM is diagnosed if two or more values are positive.

Diabetes in Pregnancy Societies of India(DIPSI) recommends a 1-step procedure with 75 g oral glucose without regard to the time of the last meal. A venous plasma glucose value at 2 hours >140 mg/dL is diagnosed as GDM.

Some complications of GDM include:

* Maternal

* Hypertension, preeclampsia

* Hydramnios

* Increased operative interventions

* Future development of diabetes mellitus

* Fetal and neonatal

* Fetal macrosomia

* Congenital anomalies

* Metabolic abnormalities such as hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and neonatal hypoglycemia.

* Respiratory distress syndrome

* Subsequent childhood and adolescent obesity

Screening is usually done at 24-28 weeks of gestation. Early diagnosis and treatment are important to prevent complications.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with a high fever, altered sensorium, headache, neck rigidity, and seizures. He was diagnosed with HSV encephalitis. Which of the following tests can be used to confirm the diagnosis?
options: CSF culture on chick embryo lines
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CSF PCR for viral DNA

HSV-DNA demonstration in CSF by PCR is the investigation of choice for HSV encephalitis.

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis is defined as inflammation of brain parenchyma caused by the herpes virus, and it typically presents as an acute febrile illness.

Patients typically present with acute onset of fever, altered levels of consciousness, personality changes, and evidence of either focal or diffuse neurologic signs and symptoms, especially in the temporal lobe. Focal or generalized seizures occur in many patients with HSV encephalitis. Other most commonly encountered focal findings include aphasia, ataxia, upper motor neuron or lower motor neuron type lesions, and cranial nerve deficits.

HSV-DNA demonstration in CSF by PCR is the investigation of choice for HSV encephalitis. Other investigations that can help include CSF examination, CSF culture, serological studies, MRI, CT, EEG, and brain biopsy.

The T2-weighted MRI of the brain will show hyperintensity in the temporal lobe in most of the patients. Bilateral involvement of the temporal lobe is more common in HSV encephalitis.

The image below is a coronal T2-weighted MR image showing a high signal intensity in the temporal lobes in a patient with HSV encephalitis.

Management includes supportive therapy (monitoring of intracranial pressure, fluid restriction, avoidance of hypotonic IV fluids), anticonvulsants for seizures, and intravenous acyclovir is beneficial in the treatment of HSV encephalitis.

Other options:

Option A: IgM antibodies in CSF - Serological tests to detect antibodies are used for primary herpes infections.

Option B: Tzanck smear of CSF - A positive smear shows multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and ground glass appearance. It is a rapid, inexpensive, and fairly sensitive diagnostic test. The Tzanck smear is typically used to diagnose cutaneous herpes infections, such as herpes simplex or varicella-zoster virus. It is not an appropriate diagnostic test for HSV encephalitis, as it does not provide definitive confirmation of the presence of HSV in the CSF.

Option D: CSF culture in chick embryos - It is not a sensitive test used for the diagnosis of HSV encephalitis. Negative CSF viral cultures have no value in ruling out HSV encephalitis. Although this method can be used to isolate HSV, it is not as sensitive or specific as PCR for viral DNA and it can take a longer time to obtain results.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A young boy suffers trauma to his right eye and develops monocular diplopia. What is the most likely cause for his symptom?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Iridodialysis

The most likely cause for the boy's symptom is iridodialysis.

Iridodialysis refers to the detachment of the iris root from the ciliary body and is associated with a D-shaped pupil. A black biconvex area is seen at the periphery at the site of detachment.

Causes of Uniocular Diplopia:

* Refractive errors

* Dry eye syndrome

* Corneal abnormalities

* Cataracts

* Retinal disorders

Causes of Binocular Diplopia:

* Strabismus

* Cranial nerve palsy

* Graves' disease

* Trauma or injury

* Multiple sclerosis

* Myasthenia gravis

Other options:

* Festooned pupil - It is seen in posterior synechiae with the adhesion of the pupillary margin to the lens capsule.

* Iris bombe refers to the forward bowing of the iris seen in closed-angle glaucoma with irido-lenticular contact and in seclusio pupillae with 360-degree posterior synechiae. Drainage of aqueous is blocked due to the irido-lenticular apposition and pressure of the accumulated aqueous causes the iris to bow forward.

* Iridodonesis refers to a tremulous iris caused by a lack of support. It is seen in pseudophakia after cataract surgery and in lens dislocation.
questions.learning: Iridodialysis — The most likely cause for the boy's symptom is iridodialysis. Iridodialysis refers to the detachment of the iris root from the ciliary body and is associated with a D-shaped pupil.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Calcitonin levels are increased in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyperparathyroidism

Calcitonin levels are increased in hyperparathyroidism.

Due to elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels in hyperparathyroidism, there is osteoclast activation. This leads to increased calcium levels in plasma. As a response to this, there is an increase in the level of calcitonin to regulate the high calcium levels.

Calcitonin is secreted by the parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid gland. Its principal effects are to lower serum calcium and phosphate by its action on bone and kidney. In bone, calcitonin inhibits osteoclasts and reduces bone resorption. In the kidney, it inhibits the reabsorption of both calcium and phosphate.

Other options

Option A: In hyperthyroidism, the direct effect of thyroid hormones can lead to bone resorption and mild hypercalcemia. However, hyperparathyroidism is a better answer.

Options B and D: Hypoparathyroidism and Cushing’s syndrome will have low serum calcium and hence, will not have increased calcitonin levels.
questions.learning: Hyperparathyroidism Calcitonin levels are increased in hyperparathyroidism. Due to elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels in hyperparathyroidism, there is osteoclast activation.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient comes with a history of asthma and sinusitis. On looking into his medical records, you notice this has been attributed to Samter's triad. Which drug should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspirin

In a patient with Samter's triad, aspirin should be avoided as he will have aspirin intolerance.

Samter's triad is also known as aspirin-induced asthma or aspirin-sensitive asthma. It consists of:

• Nasal polyposis
• Bronchial asthma
• Aspirin intolerance

Patients with Samter's triad will have persistent nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, anosmia, nasal polyps, and recurrent chronic rhinosinusitis. Asthma and aspirin intolerance develop later.

Acute asthma attacks usually occur 3 hours after intake of aspirin or NSAIDs. Severe rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection, facial flushing, and periorbital edema are also seen. Aspirin-induced hypersensitivity reactions also may occur.

Patients should avoid aspirin and NSAIDs that inhibit COX-1. Treatment may involve aspirin desensitization and endoscopic sinus surgery.
questions.learning: Aspirin — In a patient with Samter's triad, aspirin should be avoided as he will have aspirin intolerance. Samter's triad is also known as aspirin-induced asthma or aspirin-sensitive asthma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Submerged portion of iceberg shows which disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mild cases of Influenza

The iceberg phenomenon illustrates that the clinically apparent cases of a disease represent only a small visible portion, while a much larger submerged portion consists of subclinical, mild, or inapparent cases.

• Submerged portion includes:

• Subclinical infections
• Mild or atypical cases
• Undiagnosed cases
• Carriers (where applicable)

Measles, tetanus, rabies (+/- rubella) are exceptions to this theory and do not show the submerged cases and all cases are clinically apparent.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was brought by her mother to the outpatient department with an abdominal swelling. She has mild discomfort but no other symptoms of pain or vomiting. On examination, the swelling is fluctuant, soft in consistency, and moves freely in a plane perpendicular to the attachment of mesentery. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chylolymphatic cyst

The given clinical scenario is typical of the mesenteric cyst with a positive Tillaux sign. The most common type of cyst is chylolymphatic cyst.

In chylolymphatic cyst there is congenitally misplaced lymphatic tissue which has no efferent communication with the lymphatic system.The thin wall of the cyst, is composed of connective tissue, lined by flat endothelium, and is filled with clear lymph or chyle.

Mesenteric cyst:

* Cysts may occur in the mesentery of the small intestine or the colon and can be of different types:

* Chylolymphatic

* Enterogenous

* Urogenital remnant

* Dermoid.

* Most commonly presents as painless abdominal swelling with the following characteristic physical signs,

* Fluctuant swelling near the umbilicus

* Swelling moves freely in a plane at right angles to the attachment of the mesentery (Tillaux’s sign)

* Presence of zone of resonance around the cyst

* Investigations- USG and CT scan demonstrate the type of cyst.

* Treatment of choice is enucleation with or without resection of the bowel.
questions.learning: Chylolymphatic cyst — The given clinical scenario is typical of the mesenteric cyst with a positive Tillaux sign. The most common type of cyst is chylolymphatic cyst.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Niacin is synthesized from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tryptophan

The precursor for niacin is tryptophan and is coded by UGA in the mitochondria.

Tryptophan can be converted into niacin (vitamin B3). Approximately 60 mg of tryptophan is equivalent to 1 mg of dietary niacin (NADH & NAD+).

Tryptophan also produces serotonin and melatonin.

Clinical correlation: Deficiency of the enzyme kynureninase or Vit B6 results in niacin deficiency and pellagra-like symptoms and xanthurenic aciduria.
questions.learning: Tryptophan — The precursor for niacin is tryptophan and is coded by UGA in the mitochondria. Tryptophan can be converted into niacin (vitamin B3).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 70-year-old man with a long-standing medical history is on multiple medications. He has developed excessive bilateral breast tissue enlargement. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Goserelin

Gynecomastia (benign enlargement of male breast tissue) occurs due to an imbalance between estrogen and androgen activity, often caused by medications that reduce androgen levels or increase estrogenic effects.

Goserelin is a GnRH agonist used in conditions such as prostate cancer. With continuous administration, it suppresses LH and FSH secretion, leading to decreased testosterone production. The resulting relative increase in estrogen effect can cause gynecomastia and breast tenderness.

Why not other options:

• Tamoxifen – a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that is actually used to treat gynecomastia.
• Terbinafine – antifungal; gynecomastia is not a typical adverse effect.
• Procainamide-Anti-arrythmic-Not associated with gynecomastia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Anti-citrullinated peptide antibody is useful in diagnosis of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rheumatoid arthritis

Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (Anti-CCP or ACPA) antibodies are highly specific serological markers for Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). They may be detected years before the onset of symptoms and are associated with more aggressive, erosive disease and a poorer prognosis.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Sjögren’s syndrome: Characteristically associated with Anti-Ro (SSA) and Anti-La (SSB) antibodies.
• C. Scleroderma: Associated with Anti-centromere antibodies (limited cutaneous disease) and Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) antibodies (diffuse disease).
• D. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): Characteristically associated with ANA, Anti-dsDNA, and Anti-Smith (Sm) antibodies.
questions.learning: Rheumatoid arthritis Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (Anti-CCP or ACPA) antibodies are highly specific serological markers for Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: An IT employee who has recently taken up the job is feeling guilty, hopeless and not able to concentrate on work. His symptoms started 3 years back when he started college. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dysthymia

The above scenario is consistent with the diagnosis of dysthymia.

Dysthymia / Persistent Depressive Disorder:

•

DSM V Criteria for diagnosis of dysthymia: Depressed mood for most of the day as indicated by either subjective account or observation by others, for at least 2 years. In children and adolescents - at least 1 year.

Presence of two (or more) of the following while being depressed.

• Poor appetite or overeating
• Insomnia or hypersomnia
• Low energy or fatigue
• Low self-esteem
• Poor concentration and/or difficulty making decisions
• Feelings of hopelessness

Early-onset, beginning in childhood or adolescence and in most cases by the age of 20 years. More common in unmarried and young persons with low income.

Cyclothymia:

• A milder form of bipolar disorder which is chronic in nature.
• Characterized by episodic mood swings of hypomania and mild depression.

Adjustment disorder:

• It is an abnormal and excessive reaction to an identifiable life stressor.
• It is a temporary condition
• Eg: Feeling sad or hopeless in an exaggerated manner after a stressful life event. Inability to cope with stressful situations.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with weakness of the distal leg muscles and diminished deep tendon reflexes, without any sensory complaints such as tingling or numbness. Examination reveals muscle wasting below the knee. A similar clinical history is reported in his elder brother. Based on these findings, what is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease is a group of inherited motor and sensory neuropathies. The clinical presentation of a young adult with progressive distal muscle weakness, absent reflexes, and characteristic distal atrophy ("inverted champagne bottle" legs) is classic. The fact that the patient's brother has a similar history points to a genetic etiology, most commonly autosomal dominant (CMT1A). Refsum’s disease (Option B) also features neuropathy but is accompanied by retinitis pigmentosa and ichthyosis. Neuropathy in Sjogren's syndrome (Option C) and Rheumatoid arthritis (Option D) is typically acquired, not familial, and usually involves significant sensory symptoms like pain or paresthesias. CMT predominantly affects the long axons of the peripheral nerves. Patients often develop high foot arches (pes cavus) and hammertoes. Diagnosis is confirmed by nerve conduction studies showing slow velocities and genetic testing. Management is largely supportive, including orthotics and physical therapy to maintain mobility and prevent complications from foot deformities

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: According to Weigert Meyer's rule of duplication of the ureter, the lower pole ureter in the urinary bladder is:
options: Lateral and cephalad to the upper pole ureter
Lateral and caudal to the upper pole ureter
Medial and cephalad to the upper pole ureter
Medial and caudal to the upper pole ureter
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lateral and cephalad to the upper pole ureter

The lower pole ureter is lateral and cephalad to the upper pole ureter.

According to Weigert Meyer's rule of congenital complete duplication of the ureter,

* The ureter draining the upper segment of the kidney inserts in the bladder inferior and medial to the ureter draining the lower segment of the kidney (Weigert–Meyer rule). The lower moiety of the completely duplicated system is generally normal.

* The upper ureter is considered ectopic and the lower ureter is considered orthotopic.

* Ectopic ureters are more prone to obstruction.

* Orthotopic ureters are more prone to reflux due to perpendicular entry into bladder musculature rather than oblique entry.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient undergoing anticancer therapy is found to have neutropenia on blood examination, increasing the risk of infection. Which drug is most effective for managing this complication?
questions.explanation: Neutropenia is a common and dangerous side effect of cytotoxic chemotherapy, leaving patients vulnerable to life-threatening infections. To manage neutropenia and stimulate the production of white blood cells, the drug of choice is Filgrastim. Filgrastim is a recombinant human Granulocyte Colony-Stimulating Factor (G-CSF). It works by binding to specific receptors on hematopoietic progenitor cells in the bone marrow, stimulating their proliferation and differentiation into functional neutrophils. Romiplostim (Option A) is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist used to increase platelet counts in ITP. Oprelvekin (Option B) is a recombinant IL-11 also used to stimulate platelets. Epoetin alfa (Option D) is recombinant erythropoietin used to stimulate red blood cell production to treat anemia. In clinical practice, prophylactic Filgrastim is often given to patients receiving high-risk chemotherapy to reduce the duration of neutropenia and the incidence of febrile neutropenia episodes. Understanding these specific growth factors is essential for managing the hematological toxicities associated with modern cancer treatment
questions.learning: Neutropenia is a common and dangerous side effect of cytotoxic chemotherapy, leaving patients vulnerable to life-threatening infections. To manage neutropenia and stimulate the production of white blood cells, the drug of choice is Filgrastim.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presents with non-blanching rashes over the legs and buttocks, joint pain, abdominal pain with vomiting, and blood in the stools. Investigations reveal a normal platelet count, while urinalysis shows marked hematuria (+++) with mild proteinuria (+). Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of a palpable (non-blanching) purpuric rash on the buttocks and lower limbs, arthralgia (joint pain), and gastrointestinal symptoms (abdominal pain, bloody stool) in a young child is pathognomonic for Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP). HSP is an IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis. A critical diagnostic clue provided is the normal platelet count, which distinguishes the purpura of HSP from thrombocytopenic conditions like ITP (Option C). The presence of hematuria and proteinuria confirms the associated renal involvement, known as HSP nephritis. SLE (Option A) and PAN (Option D) can cause vasculitis but are much rarer in children and typically present with a different constellation of multi-organ findings and laboratory markers (like ANA or ANCA). Therefore, the classic clinical tetrad of rash, joints, gut, and kidney in a pediatric patient definitively identifies HSP
questions.learning: The combination of a palpable (non-blanching) purpuric rash on the buttocks and lower limbs, arthralgia (joint pain), and gastrointestinal symptoms (abdominal pain, bloody stool) in a young child is pathognomonic for Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a class of 100 students, 80% are immunized against measles. Despite this, 12 students develop the disease. What is the secondary attack rate in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The secondary attack rate (SAR) measures the spread of a disease among susceptible individuals following exposure to a primary case. It is calculated as the number of secondary cases divided by the total number of susceptible individuals, multiplied by 100. In this scenario, out of 100 students, 80% are immunized, meaning 80 students are protected and 20% (20 students) are susceptible. Given that 12 students were affected (secondary cases), the calculation is , which equals 60%. Option B (80%) refers to the immunization coverage rather than the attack rate. Option C (70%) and Option D (50%) are mathematically incorrect based on the provided data. SAR is a critical epidemiological tool used to assess the infectivity of a pathogen and the effectiveness of control measures like vaccines in a community setting. Thus, 60% accurately represents the transmission rate among the vulnerable population in this class
questions.learning: The secondary attack rate (SAR) measures the spread of a disease among susceptible individuals following exposure to a primary case. It is calculated as the number of secondary cases divided by the total number of susceptible individuals, multiplied by 100.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following are correctly matched? 1. First arch – Maxillary artery 2. Second arch – Hyoid or stapedial artery 3. Third arch – Common carotid artery and distal internal carotid artery 4. Sixth arch – Arch of the aorta 5. Fourth arch – Right proximal subclavian artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, and 5

First arch forms the maxillary artery, second arch gives hyoid and stapedial arteries, and the right fourth arch forms the proximal right subclavian artery.

The third arch forms the common carotid and proximal internal carotid artery (not distal), while the sixth arch forms pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus, not the aortic arch.

The third arch gives the common carotid and the proximal internal carotid — not the distal ICA.

• Third aortic arch artery → common carotid artery + proximal (first part of) internal carotid artery
• Distal internal carotid artery → derived from the dorsal aorta cranial to the third arch (the persisting cranial portion of the ipsilateral dorsal aorta)

Other sources worth pairing:

• External carotid → sprouts from the third arch / common carotid, not from the 1st arch proper.
• Distal right subclavian → right 7th intersegmental artery + right dorsal aorta.
• Left subclavian → left 7th intersegmental artery entirely (no arch contribution).

Why this asymmetry matters clinically

The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks the right subclavian (4th arch) because the right 5th and 6th arches regress distally. The left RLN hooks the ligamentum arteriosum (left 6th arch), which stays put — hence the left nerve's long thoracic descent and its vulnerability in aortic arch pathology.

Aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) = failure of the right 4th arch, with the right 7th intersegmental artery persisting off the descending aorta → dysphagia lusoria and a non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve (critical in thyroid surgery).

| Arch | Derivative(s)

| ---- | -------------

| 1st | Maxillary artery (mostly regresses); part of external carotid

| 2nd | Stapedial + hyoid arteries (largely regress)

| 3rd | Common carotid + proximal internal carotid

| 4th | Left: arch of aorta (between left CCA and left subclavian) Right: proximal right subclavian artery

| 5th | Never forms / regresses completely (no derivative)

| 6th | Left: left pulmonary artery + ductus arteriosus Right: right pulmonary artery (distal part regresses — no ductus)
questions.learning: 1, 2, and 5 First arch forms the maxillary artery, second arch gives hyoid and stapedial arteries, and the right fourth arch forms the proximal right subclavian artery.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a normal distribution curve, what proportion of the data lies within one standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explanation: A normal (Gaussian) distribution is a symmetrical, bell-shaped curve commonly used in statistics and biostatistics. According to the empirical rule (68–95–99.7 rule), about 68% of observations lie within one standard deviation (±1σ) of the mean. 1. 1. Option B (34%) represents the area on one side of the mean within one standard deviation. 2. 2. Option D (95%) corresponds to values within two standard deviations (±2σ). 3. 3. Option C (99% or more precisely 99.7%) represents values within three standard deviations (±3σ). Therefore, the correct answer is 68%
questions.learning: A normal (Gaussian) distribution is a symmetrical, bell-shaped curve commonly used in statistics and biostatistics. According to the empirical rule (68–95–99.7 rule), about 68% of observations lie within one standard deviation (±1σ) of the mean.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with weight loss, fever, and a painless swelling of the jaw. Histopathological examination of the biopsy shows the features depicted in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of a rapidly growing painless jaw swelling, weight loss, and fever in a young child is highly characteristic of the endemic (African) form of Burkitt Lymphoma. The provided biopsy image confirms this with the classic "starry sky" appearance—this pattern is created by sheets of medium-sized, dark-staining B-lymphocytes (the "sky") with interspersed pale, "tingible-body" macrophages containing cellular debris (the "stars"). Kikuchi disease (Option A) and Infectious mononucleosis (Option B) typically involve painful lymphadenopathy and show different histological patterns . Hodgkin's lymphoma (Option C) is characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells, not a starry-sky pattern. Burkitt lymphoma is associated with the Epstein-Barr Virus and involves a translocation of the c-myc gene on chromosome 8. It is one of the fastest-growing human tumors, requiring immediate aggressive chemotherapy. The pathognomonic histology and jaw location make Burkitt lymphoma the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical combination of a rapidly growing painless jaw swelling, weight loss, and fever in a young child is highly characteristic of the endemic (African) form of Burkitt Lymphoma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following has the highest oxygen concentration in fetal circulation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inferior vena cava

Inferior vena cava has the highest oxygen concentration in fetal circulation.

The blood gets oxygenated in the placenta and this passes to the umbilical vein. From the umbilical vein, 50% of the blood enters the hepatic circulation and 50% bypasses the liver to enter the inferior vena cava. From here, the blood enters the heart via the right atrium. The right atrium also receives deoxygenated blood from the superior vena cava. This mixed blood is distributed to the body via aorta.

Therefore, inferior vena cava has the highest concentration of oxygen in the fetal circulation.
questions.learning: Inferior vena cava Inferior vena cava has the highest oxygen concentration in fetal circulation. The blood gets oxygenated in the placenta and this passes to the umbilical vein.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Procidentia as a degree of uterovaginal prolapse is characterised by descent of:
options: Uterine cervix outside vagina but uterine body inside vagina
Uterine body with fundus outside vagina with eversion of entire vagina
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Uterine body with fundus outside vagina with eversion of entire vagina

Procidentia is complete (third-degree) uterovaginal prolapse, in which the entire uterus, including the fundus, protrudes outside the vaginal introitus, accompanied by complete eversion of the vagina.

Why not the other options?

• A. Uterus into vagina: Describes first-degree prolapse.
• B. Uterine cervix outside vagina but uterine body inside vagina: Describes second-degree prolapse.
• C. Uterine cervix below ischial spine: Not the definition of procidentia.
questions.learning: Uterine body with fundus outside vagina with eversion of entire vagina Procidentia is complete (third-degree) uterovaginal prolapse, in which the entire uterus, including the fundus, protrudes outside the vaginal introitus, accompanied by complete eversion…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which enzyme serves as the rate-limiting step in the heme synthesis pathway?
questions.explanation: The synthesis of heme is a complex pathway occurring partly in the mitochondria and partly in the cytosol. The rate-limiting and primary regulatory step of the entire pathway is the first step: the condensation of succinyl-CoA and glycine to form delta-aminolevulinic acid. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthase. This enzyme requires pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B6) as a cofactor and is inhibited by the end-product, heme (feedback inhibition). HMB synthase (Option A) is the enzyme deficient in acute intermittent porphyria. ALA dehydratase (Option B) and Ferrochelatase (Option D) are enzymes later in the pathway that are highly sensitive to lead inhibition but are not the primary rate-limiting steps under normal physiological conditions. Proper regulation of ALA synthase is essential to ensure that heme production matches the body's requirements for hemoglobin and other hemoproteins while preventing the accumulation of toxic porphyrin intermediates
questions.learning: The synthesis of heme is a complex pathway occurring partly in the mitochondria and partly in the cytosol. The rate-limiting and primary regulatory step of the entire pathway is the first step: the condensation of succinyl-CoA and glycine to form…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient after a road traffic accident presented with pain abdomen. The resident examines the child and found that vitals were stable and tenderness was present in the left lumbar region. Which is the best investigation of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Contrast enhanced CT scan

The given clinical vignette with abdominal pain and tenderness in the left lumbar region following a road traffic accident is suggestive of blunt renal trauma. The investigation of choice is CECT in a hemodynamically stable patient.

Blunt trauma is the main cause of renal injuries and is generally self-limiting. Radiological investigations are indicated when there is gross haematuria, shock in combination with microscopic haematuria, pediatric renal trauma, and penetrating injuries.

CECT is the investigation of choice. It assesses the extent of the injury, showing laceration, extravasation, surrounding hemorrhage, and vessel injury. It also shows non-renal injuries and effectively stages renal pedicle injuries. Arterial occlusion will manifest as rim enhancement of the normal renal contour.

Blunt trauma is mostly treated conservatively. Most of the penetrating injuries require surgical renal exploration.

Absolute indications for surgical intervention in renal trauma are:

• Massive hemorrhage
• Renal pedicle avulsion (grade 5 injury)
• Expanding, pulsatile, or uncontained retroperitoneal hematoma

Relative indications are:

• Large laceration of the renal pelvis or avulsion of the ureteropelvic junction
• Bowel or pancreatic injuries
• Persistent urinary leakage, postinjury urinoma, or perinephric abscess
• Complete renal artery thrombosis of both kidneys
• Renal hypertension

Other options:

Option D: Exploratory laparotomy is recommended in unstable patients and those with penetrating renal injuries.
questions.learning: Contrast enhanced CT scan — The given clinical vignette with abdominal pain and tenderness in the left lumbar region following a road traffic accident is suggestive of blunt renal trauma.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following are advantages of endotracheal intubation, in a child requiring pediatric advanced life support? I. Inspiratory time can be controlled II. Positive end-expiratory pressure can be provided III. Peak expiratory pressure can be controlled IV. Reduced risk of aspiration of gastric contents Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

In Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS), endotracheal intubation (ETI) provides a definitive airway for children requiring advanced airway management. It ensures effective oxygenation and ventilation, protects the airway from aspiration, and allows precise control of ventilatory parameters.

Why is B correct?

• I. Inspiratory time can be controlled. ✔

• Correct.
• Mechanical ventilation through an endotracheal tube allows precise control of inspiratory time, tidal volume, respiratory rate, and FiO₂.

• II. Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) can be provided. ✔

• Correct.
• PEEP helps prevent alveolar collapse, improves functional residual capacity, and enhances oxygenation.

• III. Peak expiratory pressure can be controlled. ✘

• Incorrect.
• Ventilators control peak inspiratory pressure (PIP), not peak expiratory pressure.

• IV. Reduced risk of aspiration of gastric contents. ✔

• Correct.

A cuffed (or appropriately fitted uncuffed in infants) endotracheal tube provides airway protection and reduces the risk of aspiration.
questions.learning: I, II and IV — In Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS), endotracheal intubation (ETI) provides a definitive airway for children requiring advanced airway management.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct about mesenteric cysts?
options: It occurs most commonly in children less than 18 years of age.
It is more common in males as compared to females.
It presents most commonly as a painless abdominal swelling.
Percutaneous aspiration with injection of sclerosant is the preferred treatment option.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It presents most commonly as a painless abdominal swelling.

A mesenteric cyst is a rare benign intra-abdominal cyst arising from the mesentery of the small or large intestine, most commonly from the small bowel mesentery. It usually presents as a slow-growing, painless abdominal swelling and is treated by complete surgical excision to prevent recurrence and complications.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. It occurs most commonly in children less than 18 years of age: Mesenteric cysts can occur at any age. Although they are seen in children, most cases are diagnosed in adults (4th–5th decade).
• B. It is more common in males as compared to females: There is no significant male predominance; many studies report an equal or slight female predominance.
• D. Percutaneous aspiration with injection of sclerosant is the preferred treatment option: Aspiration has a high recurrence rate and risk of infection. Complete surgical excision (laparoscopic or open) is the treatment of choice.
questions.learning: It presents most commonly as a painless abdominal swelling. A mesenteric cyst is a rare benign intra-abdominal cyst arising from the mesentery of the small or large intestine, most commonly from the small bowel mesentery.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The following image indicates:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Occulomotor palsy

The given image is suggestive of oculomotor nerve palsy.

The central image shows the primary position of gaze where the patient's left eye is deviated down and out with ptosis of the left eyelid. From the eye movements in other positions, it can be seen that adduction and elevation are absent and depression is reduced in the left eye. All of these findings are indicative of oculomotor nerve palsy.

3rd Cranial nerve(oculomotor nerve) palsy presents with:

• Ptosis due to weakness of levator palpebrae superioris muscle (LPS)
• Abduction and depression in the primary position (down and out) due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus(6th nerve supply) and superior oblique muscles(4th nerve supply)
• Dilated pupil and defective accommodation due to parasympathetic palsy (involvement of Edinger Westphal parasympathetic supply)
• Limited adduction, elevation and depression due to ipsilateral paralysis of medial rectus, inferior oblique and inferior rectus .

Option A: Trochlear(4th cranial) nerve palsy presents with superior oblique muscle paralysis.

Clinical findings of trochlear nerve palsy include:

•  Hypertropia (elevation) in the primary position
• Extorsion that is greatest in abduction
• Compensatory head posture with contralateral face turn and head tilt with chin slightly depressed. This position is assumed to avoid Diplopia.
• Limitation of depression
• Normal abduction and elevation.

The below given image depicts 4th cranial nerve palsy.

Option B: Lateral rectus palsy is seen in cases of isolated Abducens nerve palsy. These patients present with esotropia/convergent squint in primary position with limitation of abduction on the side of the lesion. This is due to unopposed action of the medial rectus muscle in the affected eye.

There is also a compensatory head turn towards the side of the lesion to reduce the symptom of Diplopia. The adduction is normal in lateral rectus palsy.

Option C: Internuclear opthalmoplegia occurs following an injury to the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). A unilateral lesion to the MLF leads to the failure of adduction in the ipsilateral eye with a normal abduction of the contralateral eye.

The below given image depicts the pathogenesis of Inter nuclear opthalmoplegia in detail.
questions.learning: Occulomotor palsy — The given image is suggestive of oculomotor nerve palsy. The central image shows the primary position of gaze where the patient's left eye is deviated down and out with ptosis of the left eyelid.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. The radiological image shows the following findings. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Orbital blowout fracture

The given CT image shows the characteristic "hanging drop sign" indicating a blowout fracture of the orbital wall.

Hanging drop/tear-drop sign is characteristic of an orbital "blow-out" fracture, which represents the orbital contents herniating through the floor of the orbit into the maxillary antrum.

Blow-out orbital fractures are caused by trauma to the orbit by a large, rounded object, e.g cricket ball, a human fist, etc. This force can cause the displacement of the eyeball backwards and an increase in intraorbital pressure. This leads to fracturing at the weakest point of the orbital wall (orbital floor and sometimes medial wall). Clinical signs are periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis and subconjunctival haemorrhage (later stages).

Definitive treatment is by surgical repair 10-14 days after injury with initial supportive management with analgesics and antibiotic

Indications for surgery in a "blow-out" fracture are as follows:

* Diplopia not resolving significantly in the early days after trauma

* A fracture with a large herniation of tissues into the antrum

* Incarceration of tissues in the fracture, resulting in globe retraction and increased applanation tension on attempted upward gaze

* Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

The most useful projection for detecting an orbital floor fracture is the Water’s view.

Other options:

Option B: Zygomatic fracture Involves zygomatic bone (cheekbone), producing “flattened cheek” and step deformity at the infraorbital rim.

Option C:  Maxillary fracture Involves alveolar process / maxillary sinus walls. Here, the fracture is confined to the orbital floor.

Option D: Le-fort 1 fracture is a horizontal fracture of the maxilla, separating the upper alveolar part (upper teeth + palate) from the rest of the face.

Pearl PF1981: Le-Fort's classification of Maxillary Fracture

Le-Fort I is a transverse fracture of the maxilla

* Fracture line passes through the lower part of nasal septum, maxillary antra and the pterygoid plates

* It separates palate from the rest of the face leading to floating teeth or palate

* Also called Guerin’s fracture.

Le-Fort II is a pyramidal fracture

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, lacrimal bone, floor of the orbit, upper part of the maxillary sinus and pterygoid plates

* X-ray or CT appears like hanging maxilla

* It is associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

Le-Fort III is craniofacial dysjunction i.e., facial skeleton completely disconnected from its cranial attachment

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, ethmo-frontal junction, superior orbital fissure, lateral wall of the orbit, fronto-zygomatic and temporo-zygomatic sutures and the upper part of pterygoid plates

* It is also associated with CSF rhinorrhea.
questions.learning: Orbital blowout fracture — The given CT image shows the characteristic "hanging drop sign" indicating a blowout fracture of the orbital wall. Hanging drop/tear-drop sign is characteristic of an orbital "blow-out" fracture, which represents the orbital…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Osborn waves in ECG show prolonged repolarization with a distinctive convex elevation of the J point. These waves are associated with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Systemic hypothermia

Osborn (J) waves are positive deflections at the J point on ECG and are classically associated with systemic hypothermia (typically when core temperature is <32°C). They result from delayed ventricular repolarization and become more prominent as body temperature decreases.

Why not the other options?

• B. Acute pericarditis: Causes diffuse concave ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression, not Osborn waves.
• C. Acute myocarditis: May show nonspecific ST-T changes, arrhythmias, or conduction defects, but not characteristic Osborn waves.
• D. Brugada syndrome: Shows coved ST-segment elevation in V1–V3 with RBBB-like pattern, distinct from Osborn waves.
questions.learning: Systemic hypothermia Osborn (J) waves are positive deflections at the J point on ECG and are classically associated with systemic hypothermia (typically when core temperature is <32°C).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old male patient presented to the hospital with palpitations. On examination, a diastolic murmur is heard in the left third intercostal space and pistol shot sound is heard over the femoral arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aortic regurgitation

The presence of a diastolic murmur along with the pistol shot sound over the femoral is most likely to be due to aortic regurgitation.

Due to aortic regurgitation, there is a backflow of the blood from the aorta to the ventricle, during the diastole. This increases the end-diastolic (EDV) volume in the left ventricle and at the same time decreases the diastolic blood pressure (DBP).

Increased EDV leads to an increase in stroke volume and systolic blood pressure (SBP). The patient develops wide pulse pressure due to increased SBP and decreased DBP. The clinical manifestations in AR is mainly due to the wide pulse pressure.

As the regurgitation worsens, the ventricle undergo dilatation and eccentric hypertrophy to eject the additional amount of regurgitant blood. Eventually, these adaptive measures fail and left ventricular failure develops.

Pearl PF1019: Different signs in Aortic Regurgitation

Sign

Description

De Musset's sign

Head nodding with each heartbeat

Collapsing/Water Hammer/Corrigan pulse

It is a bounding pulse with rapid upstroke  and descent

Lighthouse sign

Alternate flushing & blanching of the forehead

Landolfi’s sign

Alternating constriction and dilation of pupil

Becker’s sign

Retinal artery pulsations

Quincke’s pulse

Alternate flushing and paling of the skin at the root of the nail while pressure is applied to the tip of the nail

Rosenbach’s sign
Pulsation of liver

Gerhardt’s sign
Pulsation over spleen, detected in the   presence of splenomegaly

Traube’s sign

A pistol shot sound over femoral arteries

Durozeiz’s sign

To-and-fro murmur over the femoral artery when is lightly compressed with a stethoscope

Hill’s sign

The systolic blood pressure of the lower limb exceeds that of the upper limb at least by 20mm Hg

Muller’s sign

Systolic pulsation of uvula
questions.learning: Aortic regurgitation — The presence of a diastolic murmur along with the pistol shot sound over the femoral is most likely to be due to aortic regurgitation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are probable sites for Ectopic pancreas? 1. Submucosa of the stomach and duodenum 2. Liver 3. Small bowel mesentery 4. Splenic hilum Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Ectopic (heterotopic) pancreas is pancreatic tissue located outside the normal pancreas without any anatomical or vascular continuity. It is most commonly found in the upper gastrointestinal tract but may occur at several other sites.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Submucosa of the stomach and duodenum ✔️: Correct. Most common site (also jejunum).
• 2. Liver ✔️: Correct. Rare but reported site.
• 3. Small bowel mesentery ✔️: Correct. Rare site.
• 4. Splenic hilum ❌: Incorrect. Not a recognized site of ectopic pancreas.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Ectopic (heterotopic) pancreas is pancreatic tissue located outside the normal pancreas without any anatomical or vascular continuity. It is most commonly found in the upper gastrointestinal tract but may occur at several other sites.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of atypical depression?
options: Reactive mood response to positive stimulus
Responds better to TCAs than MAO-I and SSRI
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Responds better to TCAs than MAO-I and SSRI

Patients with atypical features do respond effectively to treatment with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs).

Mood reactivity, increased sleep, weight gain, and leaden paralysis (heaviness of body) are features of atypical depression.

Mood reactivity is the capacity to be cheered up when presented with positive events.

Leaden paralysis is the heavy, leaden feelings in arms or legs.
questions.learning: Responds better to TCAs than MAO-I and SSRI Patients with atypical features do respond effectively to treatment with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text:
Which of the following are a part of the limbic system?

1. Amygdala
2. Hippocampus
3. Thalamus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3

The amygdala, hippocampus, and thalamus are all a part of the limbic system.

The limbic system refers to the interconnected neuronal circuit in the basal part of the brain that controls emotional behavior and other vegetative functions such as body temperature, the osmolality of the body fluids, and the drives to eat and drink and to control body weight.

The limbic system includes the following:

• Subcallosal gyrus
• Cingulate gyrus
• Parahippocampal gyrus
• Hippocampal formation
• Amygdaloid nucleus
• Mammillary bodies
• Anterior thalamic nucleus
• Hypothalamus

The connecting pathways for this system comprise the alveus, the fimbria, the fornix, the mammillothalamic tract, and the stria terminalis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following denotes an "infant at risk"?
options: Infant of mother who has not taken folic acid during pregnancy
Infant with history of premature birth at <32 weeks gestation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Infant with history of premature birth at <32 weeks gestation

An infant with a history of premature birth at <32 weeks gestation will be considered a high-risk infant according to AIIMS protocols on Neonatology.

The inclusion criteria for high-risk neonates according to AIIMS protocol are:

1. Birth weight <1500 grams
2. Gestation age <32 weeks
3. Infants with a birth weight of ≥ 1500gm or gestation age ≥ 32 weeks with any of the following risk factors:

• Intrauterine growth centile <3rd centile
• Meningitis
• Received mechanical ventilation for 48 hours or more
• Hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy stage 2 or higher
• Major malformation
• Inborn error of metabolism/ chromosomal or genetic disorders/ intrauterine infections
• Symptomatic hypoglycemia
• Symptomatic polycythemia
• Retrovirus positive mother
• Hyperbilirubinemia requiring exchange transfusion OR Rh isoimmunization/cholestasis
• Abnormal neurological examination at discharge/ seizures
• Major morbidities such as chronic lung diseases, IVH grade III or more and periventricular leukomalacia

Note: Although Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine mentions infants of working mothers (Option A) as high-risk infants, premature infant with < 32 weeks gestation is chosen over it, as AIIMS protocols are used as the preferred reference for AIIMS exams.
questions.learning: Infant with history of premature birth at <32 weeks gestation An infant with a history of premature birth at <32 weeks gestation will be considered a high-risk infant according to AIIMS protocols on Neonatology.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient underwent cystoscopy, which showed multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder. The histopathology image is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Malakoplakia

The cystoscopy findings of multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder and histopathology image showing Michaelis–Gutmann bodies are consistent with the diagnosis of malakoplakia.

Malakoplakia is a rare inflammatory reaction seen in chronic cystitis. It is caused due to acquired defects in phagocyte function, chronic bacterial infection by Escherichia coli or Proteus species, and immunosuppression (renal transplant patients).

The term malakoplakia means soft plaques. Grossly, malakoplakia appears as soft, yellow, slightly raised mucosal plaques.

Microscopically, they are composed of large, foamy macrophages mixed with occasional multinucleate giant cells and lymphocytes. The macrophages in malakoplakia have abundant granular cytoplasm due to phagosomes stuffed with undigested bacterial products and intracellular deposition of calcium and iron within enlarged lysosomes form laminated basophilic concretions. These are known as Michaelis–Gutmann bodies, pathognomonic of malakoplakia (shown below).

The image given below shows the Von Kossa stain demonstrating calcium and iron-containing Michaelis-Gutman bodies (MG bodies) in malakoplakia.

Note: Xanthogranulomatous cystitis is morphologically and probably pathogenetically similar to malakoplakia, but it lacks Michaelis–Gutmann bodies.

Other options:

Option A: Interstitial cystitis, also known as chronic pelvic pain syndrome, is a disorder of the urinary bladder that presents with urinary tract symptoms of more than six weeks duration of unknown etiology. Grossly, it is associated with chronic mucosal ulcers called Hunner's ulcers. Microscopically, there is a non-specific increase in mast cells in the submucosa. Biopsy should be done in all cases to rule out carcinoma in situ.

The cystoscopy image shows Hunner's ulcer, seen in interstitial cystitis.

Option C: Polypoid cystitis is an inflammatory lesion resulting from irritation of the bladder mucosa, most commonly due to indwelling catheters. The urothelium is thrown into broad bulbous polypoid projections due to marked submucosal edema. They must be differentiated from papillary urothelial carcinoma.

The given image below shows polypoid cystitis showing broad polypoid growth, prominent blood vessels, and metaplastic urothelium in H&E stain.

Option D: Acute cystitis is characterized by an inflammation of the urinary bladder following infection, most commonly by Escherichia coli, Proteus, Klebsiella, and Enterobacter. It is more commonly seen in women due to the short urethra. Microscopically, there is hyperemia and neutrophilic infiltration of the mucosa.
questions.learning: Malakoplakia — The cystoscopy findings of multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder and histopathology image showing Michaelis–Gutmann bodies are consistent with the diagnosis of malakoplakia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old mentally challenged pregnant female was brought to the hospital for MTP. Consent in this case will be given by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Legal guardian

A legal guardian provides consent in the case of a mentally ill patient.

Consent of parent/legal guardian is needed if the age of the patient is <18 years or if the patient is mentally ill.
questions.learning: Legal guardian — A legal guardian provides consent in the case of a mentally ill patient. Consent of parent/legal guardian is needed if the age of the patient is <18 years or if the patient is mentally ill.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following are incorrectly paired?
options: CCK - I cells, Duodenum and jejunum
Motilin - M cells, Duodenum and Jejunum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Motilin - M cells, Duodenum and Jejunum

Motilin is secreted by the Mo cells(not M cells) in the stomach, small intestine, and colon

Motilin is a gastrointestinal hormones that is secreted by enterochromaffin cells and Mo cells in the stomach, small intestine, and colon. It mediates its action via G-protein-coupled receptors on enteric neurons in the duodenum and colon. It produces contraction of smooth muscle in the stomach and intestines in the period between meals.

M cells are microfold cells are located in the epithelium covering mucosa-associated lymphoid tissues of the small intestine such as the Peyer's patches (PPs). Their function is to transport luminal antigens to the underlying lymphoid follicles to initiate an immune response.

Gastrin is secreted by G cells of the antrum, duodenum, and jejunum. It stimulates gastric acid secretion and mucosal growth.

Secretin is secreted by the S cells of the duodenum. Its primary function is to promote the secretion of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice by the ductal cells of the pancreas and duodenum. This secretion is poor in enzymes.

Cholecystokinin (CCK) is secreted by I cells of the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. It stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, pancreatic bicarbonate secretion, gallbladder contraction, and growth of the exocrine pancreas. It also inhibits gastric emptying.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: According to KDIGO staging of chronic kidney disease (CKD), what is the GFR range for stage 3b?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 30–44 mL/min/1.73m²

KDIGO classifies CKD stage 3b as an eGFR of 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m².

Stage 3 is subdivided into 3a (45–59) and 3b (30–44) due to differing risks of progression and complications.

Higher values represent earlier stages, while 15–30 corresponds to stage 4.

GFR ranges for CKD staging:

• Stage 1: >90 mL/min/1.73m²
• Stage 2: 60–89 mL/min/1.73m²
• Stage 3a: 45–59 mL/min/1.73m²
• Stage 3b: 30–44 mL/min/1.73m²
• Stage 4: 15–29 mL/min/1.73m²
• Stage 5: <15 mL/min/1.73m²

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the Orthotolidine test used to determine?
options: Free and combined chlorine in water
questions.explanation: The Orthotolidine (OT) test is a standard colorimetric method used in public health to monitor the effectiveness of water chlorination. When the OT reagent is added to chlorinated water, it reacts with chlorine to produce a yellow color; the intensity of the color is then compared against standard discs to quantify the chlorine levels. Specifically, a reading taken after 5 seconds estimates the "free residual chlorine," while a reading after 5 minutes estimates the "total chlorine" (free plus combined). Nitrates (Option A) and Nitrites (Option B) are typically measured using the Griess test or specialized sensors. Ammonia (Option D) is often determined using the Nesslerization method or the phenate method. While the OT test is simple and fast, it has been largely superseded by the DPD (N,N-diethyl-p-phenylenediamine) test in modern settings because OT can give false positives in the presence of iron, manganese, or nitrites. Nonetheless, OT remains a classic test for ensuring water safety

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the condition in the image shown below:
questions.explanation: The X-ray demonstrates a “triple bubble sign”, which consists of three air-filled shadows representing the stomach, duodenum, and proximal jejunum. This indicates an obstruction distal to the duodenum, specifically at the level of the jejunum, confirming jejunal atresia. Jejunal atresia is a congenital intestinal obstruction, commonly caused by an intrauterine vascular accident. It leads to dilatation of proximal bowel segments. Another associated feature may be the “apple peel” appearance, where the distal bowel coils around a vascular pedicle. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Duodenal atresia: Shows a double bubble sign (only stomach and duodenum), not triple bubble. (C) Small bowel obstruction: Typically shows multiple air-fluid levels (step-ladder pattern), not a fixed triple bubble. (D) Ileal atresia: Shows a multiple bubble pattern due to distal obstruction, not just three bubbles. Thus, the presence of a triple bubble sign confirms jejunal atresia

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Increased LH: FSH ratio is seen in
questions.explanation: An increased LH:FSH ratio (typically greater than 2:1 or 3:1) is a classic biochemical finding in Polycystic Ovarian Disease (PCOD) or Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). This hormonal imbalance occurs because increased GnRH pulse frequency leads to preferential LH secretion, which stimulates the ovarian theca cells to produce excessive androgens. In premature menopause (Option A) and Turner's syndrome (Option D), both LH and FSH are significantly elevated due to primary ovarian failure, but FSH is characteristically higher than LH. Sheehan syndrome (Option B) involves panhypopituitarism, leading to low levels of both gonadotropins. While the LH:FSH ratio is no longer part of the formal Rotterdam diagnostic criteria for PCOS, it remains a valuable clinical marker that supports the diagnosis in patients presenting with oligo-ovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic morphology on ultrasound. This shift in gonadotropin balance is fundamental to the pathophysiology of the condition
questions.learning: An increased LH:FSH ratio (typically greater than 2:1 or 3:1) is a classic biochemical finding in Polycystic Ovarian Disease (PCOD) or Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A diabetic woman is admitted with complaints of vomiting. She gives a history of consuming food from outside. On evaluation, her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg. Her arterial blood gas (ABG) report shows the following findings. What is the cause of her ABG findings?

pH - 7.52

HCO3 - 30 meq/L

PaCO2- 20 mmHg

Na - 123 mEq/L.

K - 3.2 mEq/L

Cl - 67 mEq/L
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Persistent vomiting

This patient has hypovolemic, hypochloremic, hypokalemic, hyponatremic metabolic alkalosis with respiratory alkalosis. This is most probably due to persistent vomiting.

Inference from the given question stem:

Step 1: pH in this patient is 7.52 which is alkalemia.

Step 2: Bicarbonate level in this patient is 30 mEq/L which is increased. This signifies the presence of an excess of base. Hence, this is metabolic alkalosis.

Step 3: PaCO2 level in this patient is 20 mmHg, which is less than normal. This signifies respiratory alkalosis.

Step 4: Electrolyte imbalance -

• Na - 123 mEq/L signifies hyponatremia
• K - 3.2 mEq/L signifies hypokalemia
• Cl - 67 mEq/L signifies hypochloremia

Step 5: Volume depletion - Blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg signifies hypovolemia due to persistent vomiting.

Vomiting leads to loss of Hcl (acid) from the stomach resulting in metabolic alkalosis and hypochloremia. This causes failure of secretion of HCO3- into the small intestine and HCO3- is added into the extracellular fluid.

Increased level of HCO3- will be excreted in the urine making the urine alkaline with increased potassium and sodium excretion in the urine. This leads to hypokalemia and hyponatremia.

Other options:

Option A: Diabetic ketoacidosis is associated with high anion gap metabolic acidosis along with hyponatremia and hypochloremia. It may initially present with hyperkalemia.

Option C: Septic shock is characterized by high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Option D: Renal tubular acidosis is characterized by hyperchloremic, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.
questions.learning: Persistent vomiting — This patient has hypovolemic, hypochloremic, hypokalemic, hyponatremic metabolic alkalosis with respiratory alkalosis. This is most probably due to persistent vomiting.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient is undergoing modified radical neck dissection (MRND) for laryngeal malignancy. While ligating the internal jugular vein, his etCO2 dropped from 40 mmHg to 14 mmHg, and the patient developed hypotension along with cardiac arrhythmia. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Venous air embolism

A drastic fall in etCO2 with hypotension during neck surgery is most likely due to venous air embolism (VAE).

In modified radical neck dissection (MRND), a head-up position is given to provide a bloodless surgical field. VAE into severed vessels is likely to occur when the surgical site is above the right atrium and venous pressure at the incision site is below the atmospheric pressure. Pulmonary artery pressure will rise and etCO2 will fall after a venous air embolism.

In sympathetic overactivity and carotid body stimulation, blood pressure will rise.

In vagal stimulation, a drastic drop in etCO2 is unlikely.
questions.learning: Venous air embolism — A drastic fall in etCO2 with hypotension during neck surgery is most likely due to venous air embolism (VAE). In modified radical neck dissection (MRND), a head-up position is given to provide a bloodless surgical field.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP) image of the child is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ureterocele

The image shown above depicts the "cobra head" sign on excretion urography in a patient with a bilateral ureterocele.

A ureterocele is the cystic enlargement of the intramural ureter. It is common in females. Clinical presentation: Children with a ureterocele usually present with infection. Adults present with renal stones.

Diagnosis: IVU shows a classical cobra head sign or ‘adder head’ sign or 'spring onion sign'. It refers to a dilated, contrast-filled distal ureter, surrounded by a thin rim of ureteric wall and bladder mucosa. On ultrasonography, it can be seen as a fluid-filled cystic mass in the bladder. Cystoscopy shows a bulging, translucent swelling involving the ureteric orifice where there is urinary stasis.

Treatment: Surgical excision with re-implantation of the ureter is the treatment of choice for a simple ureterocele.

Other Options:

Option B: Due abnormal ascent of the metanephros during embryological development leads to an ectopic kidney, increasing the risk of infection, hydronephrosis, etc.

Option C: Duplication of Ureter: Also known as Duplex Kidney, this is due to the incomplete fusion of the upper and lower poles of the kidney. The drooping lily sign is seen on Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP).

Option D: Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of severe obstructive uropathy in children. Diagnosis is most commonly made antenatally with ultrasound (Keyhole sign is seen). Clinically, a poor urinary stream, dribbling, and palpable bladder (due to diverticula) can be present. The investigation of choice is micturating cystourethrography.

Pearl PF1667: IVU signs and associated conditions

Medullary sponge kidney

* Bouquet of flowers/ paintbrush appearance

* It refers to the cystic dilatation of the distal collecting tubules

Duplex kidney

* Drooping lily sign

* It refers to the inferolateral displacement of the lower pole due to an obstructed upper pole in a duplicated collecting system

Horseshoe kidney

* Handshake sign - due to the position of the lower poles closer to the spine, and the lower calyces closer to each other

* Flower vase sign - due to medially rotated calyces

Retroperitoneal fibrosis

* Maiden waist deformity

* It refers to the medially drawn ureters caused by fibrosis at the lumbosacral junction

Retrocaval ureter

* Fish hook / Reverse J deformity

* Right ureter hooks behind the IVC as it passes posterior to it

Ureterocele

* Cobra/ Adder head appearance

* It refers to the dilation of the distal ureter

Transitional cell carcinoma of the ureter

* Goblet sign

* It is due to the focal dilation of the ureter by an intraluminal mass

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a correct match for ABCD according to paediatrics advanced life support?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dehydration

According to paediatrics advanced life support (PALS), the incorrectly matched one is D-dehydration.

The American Heart Association, in its Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) curriculum, supports the structured format of the airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure- ABCDE for primary assessment.

Airway- The primary survey's first and most important portion is the patient’s airway. A simple chin-lift or jaw thrust manoeuvre re-aligns the airway. An artificial airway that is appropriate for the patient’s situation like oropharyngeal airways (OPA), and nasopharyngeal airways (NPA) can be used.

Breathing-Assessment of breathing includes respiratory rate, effort, abnormal sounds, and pulse oximetry. Central cyanosis is a sign of severe hypoxia and indicates an emergent need for oxygen supplementation and respiratory support.

Circulation- Cardiovascular function is assessed by evaluation of skin colour and temperature, heart rate, heart rhythm, pulses, and capillary refill time.

Disability- This refers to a child’s neurologic function in terms of the level of consciousness. An assessment of light reflex and use of either of the standard scores used in paediatrics. Any child with a depressed level of consciousness should be immediately assessed for abnormalities in cardiorespiratory status.

Exposure- Exposure is the final component after the child has been stabilized. This includes exposing the child to assess for previously unidentified injuries by performing a focused physical exam, and assessing for burns, bruising, bleeding, joint laxity, and fractures.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young adult presents with a deformed nose after falling from a ladder. The CT scan shows a displaced nasal fracture. What is the ideal time to reduce the fracture in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5-7 days following injury

The ideal time for reduction of fracture of the nasal bone is 5-7 days following injury, once the edema from the injury has subsided.

The presence of edema interferes with the accurate reduction of the fracture. In most cases, the deformity is due to edema. So, ice packs and head elevation are advised initially after injury. After 3-5 days, the edema would subside and the underlying deformity will be apparent on clinical assessment.

After 2 weeks it is difficult to reduce since the process of callus formation and the bony and fibrous union would have started.
questions.learning: 5-7 days following injury The ideal time for reduction of fracture of the nasal bone is 5-7 days following injury, once the edema from the injury has subsided.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female, married for the past 5 years, presents with complaints of inability to conceive despite regular intercourse. Physical examination is unremarkable. Semen analysis of the husband revealed no abnormalities. Hysterosalpingography reveals the following picture. The anomaly shown in the image below falls under which category of the american fertility society classification of mullerian duct anomalies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Class II

The image shows a hysterosalpingogram of a unicornuate uterus, which falls under Class II of Mullerian duct anomalies

In the unicornuate uterus, the formation of the uterus and fallopian tube occurs entirely from one Mullerian duct due to developmental arrest of other Mullerian ducts. On Hysterosalpingography, the endometrial cavity usually appears fusiform shape tapering at the apex and draining into a single Fallopian tube. The uterus generally appears shifted off the midline.

The AFS (American Fertility Society) classification of Mullerian duct anomalies is as follows:

* Class I—Mullerian agenesis or hypoplasia.

* Class II—Unicornuate uterus, with absent or defective development of one Mullerian duct.

* Class III—Uterus didelphys

* Class IV—Bicornuate uterus

* Class V—Septate uterus

* Class VI—Arcuate uterus

Infertility is defined as lack of conception despite 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse in women aged < 35 years old and despite 6 months of regular unprotected intercourse in women aged > 35 years old.
