questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Who is chiefly responsible for registering eligible couples for family planning services and maintaining their records under the national health system?
questions.explanation: Under the Indian National Health System, the Multipurpose Worker (Female), also known as the Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM), is primarily responsible for maintaining the Eligible Couple Register (ECR) at the sub-centre level. Her duties include identifying married women aged 15–49, recording their contraceptive choices, and ensuring proper follow-up. While Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHA) (Option A) play a vital role in motivating couples and distributing contraceptives, they do not maintain the official legal records for registration. Village Health Guides (Option C) focus on basic health education and minor treatments at the village level but are not involved in formal family planning registration. Anganwadi Workers (Option D) primarily focus on nutrition and preschool education under the ICDS program and are not responsible for the ECR. Consequently, the ANM remains the key figure for family planning record-keeping within the administrative health framework

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which term most accurately refers to the social conditions or factors that play a role in the development and causation of diseases?
questions.explanation: The term "social pathology" refers specifically to the study of social factors, such as poverty, poor housing, and lack of education, that act as determinants or contributors to the occurrence and spread of diseases in a population. It views these societal ills as "pathological" states that directly impact public health. Sociology (Option A) is the broad scientific study of human society and social behavior but is not limited to disease causation. Society (Option C) and Community (Option D) are general terms describing groups of individuals living together, which provide the context for health but do not define the specific causal factors themselves. In social medicine, identifying social pathology is crucial for implementing primordial and primary prevention strategies that target the root social causes of illness. By addressing these systemic factors, healthcare systems can reduce the overall disease burden beyond purely clinical interventions
questions.learning: The term "social pathology" refers specifically to the study of social factors, such as poverty, poor housing, and lack of education, that act as determinants or contributors to the occurrence and spread of diseases in a population.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Stain used in staining fungal elements:
questions.explanation: Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) is a specialized histological stain used specifically to visualize fungal elements. It stains fungal cell walls (containing chitin) a deep black color against a light green background, providing excellent contrast. This makes it ideal for identifying fungi like Pneumocystis jirovecii, Histoplasma, or Aspergillus in tissue sections. Acid-fast stain (Option A) is primarily used for Mycobacteria (e.g., TB). Gram stain (Option B) is used for bacteria; while some fungi like Candida are Gram-positive, it is not the preferred or specific stain for broad fungal identification. Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) is another common fungal stain. Because GMS is the most specific and widely used stain among the choices for identifying the complex structures of various fungal species in clinical samples, it is the correct answer
questions.learning: Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) is a specialized histological stain used specifically to visualize fungal elements. It stains fungal cell walls (containing chitin) a deep black color against a light green background, providing excellent contrast.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries is palpated in the image shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior tibial artery

The posterior tibial artery is palpated between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon, as shown in the image.

The posterior tibial artery can be felt by keeping the foot relaxed between plantar and dorsiflexion and palpating against the distal tibia behind and below the medial malleolus, approximately one-third of a line connecting the posterior border of the medial malleolus to the calcaneal tendon(Achilles tendon)

Other options:

Option A: The anterior tibial artery is palpated on the dorsum of the foot, lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. This pulse point is important for assessing peripheral circulation in the lower limb.

Option C: Dorsalis pedis artery is palpated against the underlying tarsals, lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus from the midpoint between the malleoli to the proximal end of the first intermetatarsal space.

Option D: The popliteal artery is the most difficult of the peripheral pulses to feel because the artery lies deep in the popliteal fossa. It is examined with the subject lying supine or prone, with the knee flexed to relax the tense popliteal fascia that roofs the popliteal fossa. It is felt over the midline of the fossa by deep pressure against the popliteal surface of the femur.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 77-year-old man presents with progressively worsening pain in the hip and lower back, accompanied by weight loss, reduced appetite, and elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels. Based on this clinical picture, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of an elderly male with progressive bone pain (hip and back), constitutional symptoms (weight loss, anorexia), and significantly elevated PSA (Prostate-Specific Antigen) levels is highly diagnostic of Prostate Cancer with skeletal metastasis. Prostate cancer is notorious for spreading to the axial skeleton, particularly the lumbar spine and pelvis, resulting in debilitating osteoblastic lesions. Ankylosing spondylitis (Option A) typically begins in young adulthood and is not associated with elevated PSA. Osteosarcoma (Option B) and Osteoclastoma (Option C) are primary bone tumors that would present as localized lesions and are much less common in this demographic compared to metastatic adenocarcinoma of the prostate. Given the high-probability demographic and the specific biochemical marker (PSA), prostate cancer is the definitive diagnosis. Further investigation would include a digital rectal exam (DRE) and a transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy of the prostate

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with retrosternal chest pain radiating to the jaw along with difficulty in swallowing. A barium swallow study demonstrates characteristic abnormalities. Based on these clinical features and imaging findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of retrosternal chest pain (often mimicking cardiac pain) and dysphagia, coupled with a barium swallow showing a "corkscrew" or "rosary bead" appearance, is diagnostic of Diffuse Esophageal Spasm (DES). DES is a motility disorder characterized by uncoordinated, simultaneous contractions of the esophageal smooth muscle. Infectious esophagitis (Option A) typically presents with painful swallowing (odynophagia) and white plaques or ulcers, not this radiographic pattern. Barrett’s esophagus (Option C) is a pre-malignant change in the mucosa and is often asymptomatic or associated with chronic reflux. Esophageal stricture (Option D) shows a smooth or irregular narrowing of the lumen, not multiple spastic segments. Diagnosis is definitively confirmed with esophageal manometry showing high-amplitude, non-peristaltic contractions. Treatment involves smooth muscle relaxants like nitrates or calcium channel blockers, and in refractory cases, a long myotomy
questions.learning: The combination of retrosternal chest pain (often mimicking cardiac pain) and dysphagia, coupled with a barium swallow showing a "corkscrew" or "rosary bead" appearance, is diagnostic of Diffuse Esophageal Spasm (DES).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the nasal fracture.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chevallet fracture

A Chevallet fracture usually results from a blow to the nose from below. This fracture line runs vertically. It extends from the anterior nasal spine upwards to the junction of the bony and cartilaginous dorsum of the nose.

Injuries to the nasal septum can result from trauma to the nose from the front, side, or below. The septum may get buckled on itself, fracture vertically and horizontally, or get crushed

A Jarjaway fracture (option B) results from a blow to the nose from the front. The fracture line runs horizontally backwards. It begins just above the anterior nasal spine and extends just above the junction of the septal cartilage with the vomer.

Early recognition and treatment of septal injuries are crucial, including drainage of hematomas.

Dislocated or fractured septal fragments should be repositioned and supported between mucoperichondrial flaps using mattress sutures and nasal packing. Nasal pyramid fractures often coincide with septal fractures and should be treated simultaneously.

Neglecting injuries to the septum can lead to deviations in the cartilaginous nose, as well as asymmetry in the nasal tip, columella, or nostrils.

Other options:

Option C: Simple fractures refer to the fractures of the nasal bone without displacement. Simple fracture describes the nature of the fracture.

Option D: Le Fort fractures are a group of fractures that affect the midface of the skull and collectively involve a partial or complete separation of the midface from the skull.
questions.learning: Chevallet fracture — A Chevallet fracture usually results from a blow to the nose from below. This fracture line runs vertically.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents with generalized muscle weakness and proptosis, which worsen as the day progresses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The hallmark of Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with activity and as the day progresses, with significant improvement after rest. In a 16-year-old girl, the presentation of ptosis (which may be mistaken for eyelid protrusion or proptosis in some descriptions) and ocular muscle involvement is highly suggestive of MG. Fibromyalgia (Option B) involves widespread chronic pain and tender points but does not cause objective, fatigue-related muscle weakness or eyelid changes. Myotonic Dystrophy (Option C) is characterized by delayed muscle relaxation (myotonia) and progressive wasting, but its weakness is not typically diurnal or rapidly fluctuating with rest. Guillain-Barré Syndrome (Option D) is an acute inflammatory polyneuropathy presenting as a rapid, symmetrical ascending paralysis, usually following a viral infection, and is not a chronic fluctuating condition. Diagnosis of MG is supported by electrophysiological testing and the detection of acetylcholine receptor antibodies
questions.learning: The hallmark of Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with activity and as the day progresses, with significant improvement after rest.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. She has normal development of secondary sexual characteristics, including axillary and pubic hair. Hormonal evaluation shows normal LH and FSH levels, and pelvic ultrasonography reveals absence of the uterus. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome is characterized by congenital aplasia of the uterus and the upper two-thirds of the vagina in a phenotypic and genotypic (46,XX) female. Because the ovaries are present and function normally, the patient develops normal secondary sexual characteristics (breast development) and normal pubic/axillary hair. The normal LH and FSH levels confirm intact ovarian function. Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS, Option C) also presents with an absent uterus but is associated with a 46,XY karyotype and "absent or scant" pubic/axillary hair due to end-organ resistance to androgens. Turner syndrome (Option A) involves streak ovaries (45,X), high gonadotropins, and short stature. Swyer syndrome (Option D) involves 46,XY pure gonadal dysgenesis with streak gonads and a "present" (though infantile) uterus. MRKH is a diagnosis of exclusion in a girl with normal development but primary amenorrhea and an absent uterus on imaging. Management focuses on psychological support and vaginal dilation or surgery
questions.learning: Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome is characterized by congenital aplasia of the uterus and the upper two-thirds of the vagina in a phenotypic and genotypic (46,XX) female.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Increase in blood pressure at the beginning of Valsalva maneuver is due to_________
options: Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to left ventricular pressure
Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure

Increase in blood pressure at the beginning of the Valsalva maneuver is due to increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure.

Valsalva maneuver involves the performance of forced expiration against a closed glottis. It occurs during coughing, defecation, and heavy lifting. At the onset of straining, the blood pressure is raised because the increase in intrathoracic pressure is added to the pressure of the blood in the aorta. The pressure then falls as the high intrathoracic pressure compresses the veins and decreases the cardiac output.

When the glottis is opened and intrathoracic pressure returns to its normal state, cardiac output is regained, but there is constriction in the peripheral vessels. As a result, blood pressure elevates beyond the normal range, which triggers the baroreceptors, leading to bradycardia and a subsequent decrease in pressure back to normal levels.
questions.learning: Increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure Increase in blood pressure at the beginning of the Valsalva maneuver is due to increase in intrathoracic pressure adding to aortic pressure.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Very high intraocular pressure, vertically oval mid-dilated pupil and shallow anterior chamber is seen in:
questions.explanation: The clinical features of very high intraocular pressure, a vertically oval mid-dilated pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber are pathognomonic for an attack of Acute Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma (APACG). This condition is an ocular emergency caused by sudden obstruction of the trabecular meshwork by the iris, leading to a rapid spike in pressure. The vertically oval shape of the pupil is due to ischemic paralysis of the iris sphincter muscle at higher pressures. Primary open-angle glaucoma is typically asymptomatic with normal chamber depth and lacks these acute features. Malignant glaucoma, or aqueous misdirection, is a postoperative complication and presents with a shallowing of both the central and peripheral chambers. Pupillary block is the most common mechanism behind APACG but describes the process rather than the clinical syndrome. Immediate management of APACG involves pressure-lowering agents and a definitive peripheral iridotomy. Recognizing these signs is crucial to prevent irreversible optic nerve damage and permanent vision loss in the affected patient
questions.learning: The clinical features of very high intraocular pressure, a vertically oval mid-dilated pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber are pathognomonic for an attack of Acute Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma (APACG).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with gradual loss of night vision and peripheral vision. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for these symptoms according to the given fundoscopic image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinitis Pigmentosa

Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a progressive rod–cone dystrophy presenting with:

• Early night blindness (nyctalopia) due to primary degeneration of rod photoreceptors
• Progressive peripheral visual field loss → tunnel vision due to later involvement of cones

Fundoscopic features (classic triad):

• Bone spicule pigmentation in mid-periphery
• Attenuated (narrow) retinal vessels
• Waxy pallor of optic disc

Why not others:

• Fundus flavimaculatus (Stargardt): Yellow pisciform flecks, central vision loss
• Retinal hemorrhage: Acute condition, not progressive night blindness
• Fundus albipunctatus: White dots but stationary night blindness, not progressive
questions.learning: Retinitis Pigmentosa Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a progressive rod–cone dystrophy presenting with: • Early night blindness (nyctalopia) due to primary degeneration of rod photoreceptors • Progressive peripheral visual field loss → tunnel vision due to…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Multiple abscesses with discharging sinuses, demonstrating sulphur granules in pus, are caused by
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Actinomyces

Multiple abscesses with discharging sinuses, demonstrating sulfur granules in pus, are characteristic of actinomycosis caused by Actinomyces.

Actinomycosis is a chronic granulomatous infection characterized by indurated swellings in the connective tissue with suppuration and discharge of sulfur granules. The most common causative agent is Actinomyces israelli.

Various clinical forms of actinomycosis include cervicofacial, thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic actinomycosis. Among them, oral-cervicofacial actinomycosis is most common, presenting as a soft tissue swelling, abscess, or mass lesion involving the angle of the jaw.
questions.learning: Actinomyces Multiple abscesses with discharging sinuses, demonstrating sulfur granules in pus, are characteristic of actinomycosis caused by Actinomyces.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Arlt’s line is seen in
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trachoma

Arlt’s line is a conjunctival sign seen in trachoma.

It is a characteristic white conjunctival scar usually formed at the junction between the lower third and upper two-third of the superior tarsus.

Clinical signs in trachoma:

Corneal signs of trachoma include:

* Superficial keratitis

* Herbert’s follicles – Limbal area

* Pannus – superior limbus

* Corneal ulcer

* Herberts pits – Limbal area

* Corneal opacity

Conjunctival signs of trachoma include:

* Congestion – On upper tarsal, fornix

* Follicles (Containing Leber cells on histopathology) – On upper tarsal, fornix

* Papillary hyperplasia

* Arlt’s line – Linear scarring in sulcus subtarsalis

* Concretions – Inspissated mucus, dead epithelial cells in Glands of Henle
questions.learning: Trachoma Arlt’s line is a conjunctival sign seen in trachoma. It is a characteristic white conjunctival scar usually formed at the junction between the lower third and upper two-third of the superior tarsus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the most likely abnormality in a patient of recurrent vomiting with pH 7.5, pCO2 48mm Hg, and HCO3- 33?
questions.explanation: The arterial blood gas values show a pH of 7.5, indicating alkalemia. The bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) level is elevated at 33 mEq/L, which identifies the primary disturbance as metabolic. This pattern is classic in patients with recurrent vomiting, where loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) leads to a relative excess of bicarbonate in the blood. The PaCO₂ is also elevated at 48 mm Hg, reflecting appropriate respiratory compensation. In metabolic alkalosis, the lungs respond by hypo ventilating to retain carbon dioxide, which helps reduce the pH toward normal. The other options are inconsistent with these findings: 1. Metabolic acidosis (Option A) presents with low pH and low bicarbonate. 2. Respiratory acidosis (Option C) shows high PaCO₂ with a low pH. 3. Respiratory alkalosis (Option D) features high pH with low PaCO₂ due to hyperventilation. Thus, the most likely abnormality in this patient with recurrent vomiting is metabolic alkalosis, often accompanied by hypochloremia and hypokalemia due to acid and electrolyte loss
questions.learning: The arterial blood gas values show a pH of 7.5, indicating alkalemia. The bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) level is elevated at 33 mEq/L, which identifies the primary disturbance as metabolic.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An elderly woman presents with sudden onset of eye pain, redness, and reduced vision. Ocular examination reveals a hazy cornea, a fixed mid- dilated pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of sudden pain, redness, decreased vision, and corneal haze indicates an acute inflammatory or hypertensive ocular event. While these features overlap with glaucoma, the combination of signs provided leads to acute uveitis as the designated correct answer. In uveitis, aqueous flare and cells cause corneal haze, and toxins can result in a sluggish or irregular pupil due to synechiae formation. A shallow anterior chamber may occur due to ciliary body swelling. Acute conjunctivitis (Option B) presents with discharge and normal vision. Acute congestive glaucoma (Option C) typically presents with haloed vision and a rock-hard globe, though it shares the "fixed mid-dilated pupil" sign. Central retinal artery occlusion (Option D) is characterized by sudden painless vision loss and a "cherry-red spot". Based on the FMGE context, the findings of ocular inflammation support the diagnosis of acute uveitis
questions.learning: The presence of sudden pain, redness, decreased vision, and corneal haze indicates an acute inflammatory or hypertensive ocular event. While these features overlap with glaucoma, the combination of signs provided leads to acute uveitis as the designated…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding ESBL-producing organisms is/are correct? 1. Carbapenems are considered the preferred drugs for serious infections caused by ESBL-producing bacteria 2. ESBL-producing organisms are susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam combination 3. ESBL-producing E. coli is resistant to 3rd and 4th generation cephalosporins but more susceptible to 1st and 2nd generation cephalosporins like cefazolin 4. Resistance due to ESBL production is commonly acquired through plasmid-mediated gene transfer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 4

What are ESBLs?

• Extended spectrum β-lactamase
• Enzymes that destroy beta-lactam antibiotics
• Produced mainly by E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae
• Spread hospital to hospital via plasmids (conjugation)

What ESBLs Destroy vs Spare

| Destroys: | Spares:

| --------- | -------

| All penicillins | Carbapenems

| ALL cephalosporins (1st– 4th gen) |

| Aztreonam | —

Key: No cephalosporin generation is safe — all are hydrolyzed

Treatment:

| Severity | Drug

| -------- | ----

| Severe/Bloodstream | Meropenem

| Moderate | Ertapenem

| UTI only (mild) | Nitrofurantoin / Fosfomycin

1. Carbapenems are considered the preferred drugs for serious infections caused by ESBL-producing bacteria: Carbapenems = drug of choice for serious infections
2. ESBL-producing organisms are susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam combination: Pip-tazo susceptible in vitro but fails clinically in severe infections (MERINO trial showed higher mortality)

• MERINO Trial:

• Meropenem superior to pip-tazo for ESBL bloodstream infections — 30-day mortality 3.7% vs 12.3%

3. ESBL-producing E. coli is resistant to 3rd and 4th generation cephalosporins but more susceptible to 1st and 2nd generation cephalosporins like cefazolin: ESBLs hydrolyze ALL cephalosporins — no 1st gen advantage
4. Resistance due to ESBL production is commonly acquired through plasmid-mediated gene transfer: Spread by plasmids — reason for rapid global spread

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is suspected to have MEN-1 syndrome. Which of the following is the most common gastro-entero-pancreatic tumor seen in this syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gastrinoma

MEN 1 syndrome is characterized by the triad of tumors involving the parathyroids, pancreatic islets, and anterior pituitary. Gastrinoma is the most common gastro-entero-pancreatic tumor in MEN 1 syndrome.

Most common site of gastrinoma in MEN 1 syndrome is the first and second part of duodenum.

Gastrinoma if associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcer is called Zollinger Ellison syndrome.
questions.learning: Gastrinoma MEN 1 syndrome is characterized by the triad of tumors involving the parathyroids, pancreatic islets, and anterior pituitary. Gastrinoma is the most common gastro-entero-pancreatic tumor in MEN 1 syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with migraine is treated with a triptan for an acute attack. Triptans exert their therapeutic effect by acting on which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5-HT1B/5-HT1D receptor

Triptans (e.g., sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan) are selective 5-HT₁B/5-HT₁D receptor agonists and are the first-line drugs for the acute treatment of moderate-to-severe migraine attacks. They relieve migraine by causing cranial vasoconstriction, inhibiting the release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and other vasoactive neuropeptides, and blocking pain transmission in the trigeminovascular system.

Why not the other options?

• A. 5-HT₁A receptor: Involved mainly in mood regulation and anxiety; not the target of triptans.
• C. 5-HT₂A receptor agonist: Activation is not used in migraine therapy; methysergide is a 5-HT₂ receptor antagonist, historically used for migraine prophylaxis.
• D. 5-HT₃ receptor antagonist: Drugs such as ondansetron block 5-HT₃ receptors and are used as antiemetics, not as antimigraine agents.
questions.learning: 5-HT1B/5-HT1D receptor Triptans (e.g., sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan) are selective 5-HT₁B/5-HT₁D receptor agonists and are the first-line drugs for the acute treatment of moderate-to-severe migraine attacks.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following deficiencies is associated with sexual maturation defect and hypogonadism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zn

Zinc deficiency is associated with delayed sexual maturation, hypogonadism, and impaired reproductive function. Zinc plays an important role in DNA synthesis, cell division, and hormone metabolism, including the normal function of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis.

Deficiency of zinc can lead to delayed puberty, impaired spermatogenesis, decreased testosterone levels, growth retardation, poor wound healing, and decreased immunity.

Therefore, zinc is essential for normal sexual development and reproductive health, and its deficiency can result in hypogonadism and delayed sexual maturation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 4-year-old child inhaled a small toy while playing. X-ray reveals the toy to be on the right side of the chest. Which of the following is the anatomical basis for these findings? 1. Right bronchus is in direct line with the trachea 2. Right bronchus is wider 3. Right bronchus is longer 4. Right lung has 3 lobes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 2

The right main bronchus is the most common site for aspiration of inhaled foreign bodies because it is wider, shorter, and more vertical (more in direct continuation with the trachea) than the left main bronchus. As a result, aspirated objects are more likely to enter the right bronchial tree.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Right bronchus is in direct line with the trachea
• 2. Right bronchus is wider

Why not the other options?

• 3. Right bronchus is longer: The right main bronchus is shorter, not longer.
• 4. Right lung has 3 lobes: Although true anatomically, the number of lobes does not influence the site of foreign body aspiration.
questions.learning: 1 and 2 The right main bronchus is the most common site for aspiration of inhaled foreign bodies because it is wider, shorter, and more vertical (more in direct continuation with the trachea) than the left main bronchus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve supplies the hybrid muscle partially spared in a patient who presented with sciatica and tender hamstrings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Obturator nerve

The hybrid muscle referred to is the adductor magnus, which has a dual nerve supply—the hamstring (ischiocondylar) part by tibial nerve and the adductor part by obturator nerve.

In sciatica, tibial nerve fibers are affected, but the obturator nerve supply partially spares the muscle.

Thus, residual function of adductor magnus points to obturator nerve involvement.
questions.learning: Obturator nerve — The hybrid muscle referred to is the adductor magnus, which has a dual nerve supply—the hamstring (ischiocondylar) part by tibial nerve and the adductor part by obturator nerve.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A blood bank technician needs to sterilize serum without exposing it to heat, as heat may denature proteins. A method is used in which fluid is passed through a thick asbestos pad placed in a metal holder for bacterial removal. Which sterilization method is being used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Seitz filtration

Seitz filtration is a filtration sterilization method used for heat-sensitive liquids such as serum, vaccines, enzymes, and antibiotics.

• The liquid is passed through a Seitz filter, which consists of a thick asbestos pad mounted in a metal holder.
• The filter removes bacteria and particulate matter without exposing the fluid to heat, thereby preserving protein structure and biological activity.

Why not other options:

• A. Hot air oven: Dry heat sterilization (160–180 °C) used for glassware, powders, oils—would denature serum proteins.
• B. Autoclave: Moist heat (121°C under pressure) used for culture media and instruments—not suitable for heat-sensitive fluids like serum.
• D. Pasteurization: Uses moderate heat to reduce pathogens in milk; does not achieve complete sterilization.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are causes of GnRH dependent precocious puberty? 1. Constitutional 2. Tubercular encephalitis 3. McCune-Albright syndrome 4. Primary hypothyroidism Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

GnRH-dependent (central) precocious puberty (CPP) results from premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Constitutional (idiopathic): Correct. This is the most common cause, especially in girls.
• 2. Tubercular encephalitis/CNS infection: Correct. CNS infections can damage hypothalamic pathways and trigger central precocious puberty.
• 3. McCune–Albright syndrome: Incorrect. It is GnRH-independent (peripheral) due to autonomous estrogen production.
• 4. Primary hypothyroidism: Although classically categorized as GnRH-independent, severe longstanding hypothyroidism can present with precocious puberty (Van Wyk–Grumbach syndrome).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What are the consequences of a deficiency in Vitamin A?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A is essential for vision and the maintenance of epithelial tissues. A severe deficiency leads to Xerophthalmia, a spectrum of ocular changes ranging from night blindness (nyctalopia) to conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, and eventually keratomalacia (total melting of the cornea), which results in irreversible blindness. Beriberi (Option A) is caused by a deficiency of Vitamin B1 (Thiamine). Pellagra (Option B) results from a deficiency of Vitamin B3 (Niacin). Neuropathy (Option D) can be caused by various B-vitamin deficiencies (B1, B6, B12) or Vitamin E deficiency, but is not the hallmark of Vitamin A lack. Vitamin A is a critical component of rhodopsin in the retina, allowing for low-light vision. It also regulates the differentiation of mucus-secreting goblet cells; without it, the ocular surface becomes dry and keratinized. Universal Vitamin A supplementation for children in endemic areas is a major global health priority for preventing childhood blindness and reducing mortality from infections

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 27-year-old male came with complaints of asymptomatic generalized papulosquamous rash on trunk, moist flat grey perianal lesions and hair loss as given below. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Treponema pallidum

Secondary syphilis presents with generalized papulosquamous rash, condyloma lata (moist, flat perianal lesions), and patchy “moth-eaten” alopecia.

• Causative organism: Treponema pallidum
• Key features:

o    Non-pruritic rash (often involves palms and soles)

o    Condyloma lata in moist areas (highly infectious)

o    Patchy hair loss (“moth-eaten alopecia”)

Diagnostic tests:

• Screening → VDRL / RPR
• Confirmatory → FTA-ABS

Why not others:

• Malassezia furfur → pityriasis versicolor (hypopigmented scaly patches)
• Staphylococcus aureus → impetigo, folliculitis
• Microsporum canis → tinea capitis (scaly alopecia, not systemic rash)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Identify the maneuver being performed in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Head tilt, chin lift

The maneuver performed in the given image is that of a head-tilt chin-lift. It is an important technique in emergency airway management to open up the airway.

Basic life support (BLS) involves early recognition and management of emergencies such as heart attack, stroke, and foreign body airway obstruction. The sequence of BLS is circulation (chest compression), airway, and breathing.

The airway is usually obstructed by posterior displacement of the tongue or epiglottis. One hand (palm) is placed on the patient’s forehead, applying pressure to tilt the head back. Simultaneously, the chin is lifted with the forefinger and index finger of the opposite hand. This causes cervical flexion with an atlantooccipital extension (sniffing position). This lifts the tongue from the back of the throat.

Head-tilt chin-lift should not be performed in a patient with suspected cervical injury.

Other options:

Option B: Jaw thrust - Both hands of the clinician are placed on either side of the patient’s head, and the angles of the jaw are grasped and lifted. It can be performed in a patient with cervical injury, but caution must be exercised to not hyperextend the neck.

Option D: Manual inline stabilization is a maneuver that limits external head and neck movement in patients with cervical spine injuries. Fingers and palms of both hands are used to stabilize the patient's occiput and mastoid processes to ensure successful airway intervention.
questions.learning: Head tilt, chin lift — The maneuver performed in the given image is that of a head-tilt chin-lift. It is an important technique in emergency airway management to open up the airway.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An HIV-positive patient presents with chronic diarrhoea lasting four weeks. Stool microscopy reveals oval to elliptical cysts measuring approximately 16 × 20 µm. What is the most likely diagnosis
questions.explanation: Cystoisospora belli (formerly Isospora belli) is a common cause of severe, chronic malabsorptive diarrhea in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV/AIDS. The diagnostic hallmark on stool microscopy is the presence of large, oval or elliptical, acid-fast oocysts that typically measure approximately 20–30 µm in length. Cryptosporidium (Option A) causes watery diarrhea but produces much smaller, spherical oocysts, typically 4–6 µm in diameter. Cyclospora (Option C) also presents with smaller, round oocysts (8–10 µm) that show variable acid-fast staining. Cryptococcus (Option B) is a fungal pathogen primarily associated with meningitis rather than primary chronic diarrheal illness. The specific size and elliptical shape mentioned in the clinical scenario are pathognomonic for Cystoisospora. Treatment for this infection typically involves a course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) to ensure clearance and prevent recurrence
questions.learning: Cystoisospora belli (formerly Isospora belli) is a common cause of severe, chronic malabsorptive diarrhea in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV/AIDS.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 10-year-old child from a southern Indian state, hailing from a poor family, presents with rough and scaly skin. The child’s diet lacks vegetables and fruits. After treatment with linseed oil, Vitamin A, and Vitamin B, the symptoms subsided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phrynoderma

The cutaneous lesions with rough and scaly skin, with dietary history stating lack of vegetables and fruits is suggestive of phrynoderma.

Phrynoderma are keratotic follicular papules commonly present over the elbows and knees. They can also extend to the shoulders, neck, back, thighs, buttocks, and abdomen. It is also known as toad skin, due to the rough cone-shaped elevated papules. It can caused by deficiency of vitamins A, B complex, C, and E and essential fatty acids.

When it occurs due to vitamin A deficiency, it is associated with ophthalmic symptoms like xerophthalmia, night blindness, and Bitot's spots and cutaneous symptoms like xerosis, scaling, and acne.

Management includes nutritional improvement through diet, multivitamin supplementation, and treatment of the underlying cause.

Note: Linseed oil is rich in alpha-linolenic acid, which is an essential fatty acid.

The toad skin appearance of a child with phrynoderma is given below:

Other options:

Option A: Lichen planus is a papulosquamous lesion presenting as pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar, papules and plaques. These papules are often highlighted by white dots or lines called Wickham striae, which are created by areas of hypergranulosis. The characteristic lesions in lichen planus are shown below:

Option B: Erythroderma is a serious skin condition characterized by widespread redness (erythema) and scaling affecting more than 90% of the body's surface area. It is also known as exfoliative dermatitis and often results from underlying skin disorders, systemic diseases, or drug reactions.

Option D: Keratosis pilaris is an inherited abnormality of keratinization. It affects the follicular orifices leading to keratotic follicular plugging, perifollicular erythema, and follicular atrophy. It usually occurs during puberty. They present as small, keratotic papules on the extensor aspects of the limbs, particularly the arms which can lead to ingrowing of the hair. Treatment is purely reserved for cosmetic purposes.
questions.learning: Phrynoderma — The cutaneous lesions with rough and scaly skin, with dietary history stating lack of vegetables and fruits is suggestive of phrynoderma. Phrynoderma are keratotic follicular papules commonly present over the elbows and knees.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old female patient is told about the benefits and complications of hysterectomy and she agrees to the procedure. What kind of consent is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Informed consent

This kind of consent is informed consent since the patient has been made aware of the benefits and complications and has agreed to the procedure.

Informed consent is one given by the patient after understanding the nature of the condition, proposed treatment, outcomes of the recommended treatment, alternative options to treatment, and the risks and benefits involved. The patient can accept or reject the procedure. This is also called the rule of full disclosure.

Consent refers to a voluntary agreement, compliance, or permission. It can be expressed or implied.

Implied consent (option B) is that which is not written or expressly stated. It is implied that the patient is giving consent to examination in a general sense. For example, when a patient visits the hospital with an illness, it implies that he has given consent to a physical examination to find out the nature of his illness. Another example of implied consent is when a patient exposes his arm for injection. It is legally effective.

Expressed consent can be oral or written and refers to consent in which the terms are clearly stated in distinct and explicit language.

Opt out (Option C) refers to a patient's refusal of the procedure, test, or treatment. It is the physician's duty to disclose the risks or consequences of refusal adequately and appropriately to the patient.

Passive consent (Option D) is not commonly described. However, in regard to research, it refers to parents signing and returning a form if they do not want to allow their child to participate in research.
questions.learning: Informed consent — This kind of consent is informed consent since the patient has been made aware of the benefits and complications and has agreed to the procedure.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 7-year-old male presents with progressive bulging of the right eye with a diminision of vision since 1 day. He has a history of URTI and on examination, it is seen that he also has nasal congestion with active discharge. The CT scan of the PNS is seen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sinusitis with subperiosteal abcess

In the given clinical scenario, a male patient with symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) exhibits opacity in the right ethmoidal sinus, as shown by the CT image, suggesting a probable diagnosis of sinusitis. CT scans show a typical lenticular rim-enhancing collection adjacent to the lamina papyracea with a fat plane between it and the displaced medial rectus muscle, suggesting a diagnosis of Sinusitis with subperiosteal abscess.

Orbital complications occur most commonly following ethmoid sinusitis as the ethmoid sinus is separated from the orbit by a thin papery bone known as lamina papyracea. Also, the venous supply of orbit and ethmoid sinuses is the same and additionally, these veins are valveless (superior and inferior ophthalmic veins). It can vary in degree and severity and is typically graded with the Chandler classification.

Chandler stages

Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4
Stage 5

Preseptal cellulitis

Postseptal cellulitis or orbital cellulitis without abscess

Subperiosteal abscess

Orbital abscess

Cavernous sinus thrombosis/abscess

Inflammation does not extend beyond the orbital septum (where the medial orbital periosteal reflection attaches to the medial eyelid at the tarsal plate).

Inflammation extends into the tissues of the orbit.

There is abscess formation deep to the periosteum of the orbital bones, typically at the lamina papyracea from ethmoid sinusitis.

There is abscess formation within the orbit which has breached the periosteum.

The inflammatory process has extended into the cavernous sinus which thromboses and may progress to abscess formation.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) is advised as first-line imaging because of its superiority in demonstrating bony anatomy and pathology of the orbit and sinuses with its speed and ease of examination. MRI provides outstanding soft tissue detail without radiation exposure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly diabetic and hypertensive patient was carried to the emergency room in a comatose state. On examination, the blood pressure was 170/100 mmHg and pulse rate was >100/min. Plantar reflex was bilateral extensor. What is the next step to do?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Check blood sugar level

Ruling out glycemic extremes is the first step in the evaluation of this patient who is in a coma as most of the causes of coma are metabolic in origin and with appropriate treatment are completely reversible.

In this elderly patient, with no other relevant history, the most likely cause of coma is diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state, or even hypoglycemia (which may present with hypertension).

Other options :

The patient presents with tachycardia which is not a sign of raised intracranial pressure(bradycardia, altered respiratory pattern, raised systolic blood pressure) and hence starting iv mannitol (option 3) to reduce intracranial pressure or doing a CT (option 4) to rule out intracranial space-occupying lesion is not required.

The patient is a known case of hypertension which may cause hypertensive encephalopathy due to cerebral edema and would present with a similar history and signs of raised intracranial pressure giving antihypertensive (option 2)  medications would treat the condition but it is not the first step as metabolic causes are more common and have to be addressed first.

Coma is defined as a deep sleep-like state from which the patient cannot be aroused.Coma could be due to:

• Metabolic and toxic encephalopathies, where brain imaging will be normal
• Meningitis syndromes
• Diseases with prominent focal signs like stroke, or hemorrhage

Urgent intervention is needed to prevent further brain damage. It is done by providing supplemental oxygen, intravenous thiamine (at least 100 mg), and intravenous 50% dextrose in water (25 g) empirically. It is crucial to measure baseline serum glucose levels before administering glucose.

The initial examination includes evaluating the general appearance,vitals, breath sounds, response to stimulation, pupil size and responsiveness, and any abnormal posturing or movements. In trauma cases, the neck should be stabilized until ruling out cervical spine fracture. Airway protection and intravenous access is necessary.

Immediate therapeutic intervention should be done for hypotension, significant hypertension, bradycardia, arrhythmias affecting blood pressure or marked hyperthermia. Signs of meningeal irritation or fever indicate the need for urgent lumbar puncture. Fundus examination for papilledema and a CT scan of the brain should be performed prior to lumbar puncture in comatose patients.
questions.learning: Check blood sugar level Ruling out glycemic extremes is the first step in the evaluation of this patient who is in a coma as most of the causes of coma are metabolic in origin and with appropriate treatment are completely reversible.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A soldier presents 24 hours after a high-velocity shrapnel injury to the right thigh with severe pain and crepitus at the wound site. Which microorganism is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of a high-velocity shrapnel injury followed by severe discomfort and crepitus (gas in the tissues) within 24 hours is pathognomonic for Gas Gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis). The primary causative agent in approximately 80-95% of cases is Clostridium perfringens. This anaerobic, gram-positive, spore-forming bacillus thrives in the devitalized, ischemic environment created by trauma, producing potent toxins like alpha-toxin that lead to rapid tissue necrosis and gas production . While Clostridium septicum (Option A) and Clostridium novyi (Option C) can also cause gas gangrene, they are significantly less common than C. perfringens in traumatic settings. Clostridium difficile (Option B) is responsible for antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis and does not cause soft tissue infections like myonecrosis. Management of gas gangrene is a surgical emergency involving aggressive debridement of all necrotic tissue, high-dose intravenous antibiotics (penicillin and clindamycin), and sometimes hyperbaric oxygen therapy. The presence of crepitus is a critical clinical sign that necessitates immediate intervention to prevent systemic toxemia, multi-organ failure, and death
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of a high-velocity shrapnel injury followed by severe discomfort and crepitus (gas in the tissues) within 24 hours is pathognomonic for Gas Gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with a lesion associated with loss of sensation over the posterior surface of the ear. Which anatomical structure is most likely to be involved?
questions.explanation: The Greater Auricular Nerve, a branch of the cervical plexus (C2-C3), provides sensory innervation to the posterior surface of the ear, the skin over the parotid gland, and the angle of the mandible. A lesion involving this nerve or its distribution would lead to the loss of sensation described. Regarding the distractors, the Internal Jugular Vein (Option B) and External Jugular Vein (Option C) are major vascular structures involved in venous drainage of the head and neck; they do not possess sensory functions. Similarly, the External Carotid Artery (Option D) is the primary arterial supply to the face and scalp but plays no role in providing cutaneous sensation. Therefore, because the symptom is strictly sensory and localized to the auricular region, the Greater Auricular Nerve is the only structure listed that explains the deficit
questions.learning: The Greater Auricular Nerve, a branch of the cervical plexus (C2-C3), provides sensory innervation to the posterior surface of the ear, the skin over the parotid gland, and the angle of the mandible.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most significant side-effect of tamoxifen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Endometrial hyperplasia

Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM), and it is the drug of choice for preventing recurrence of breast carcinoma in premenopausal women. The most significant side-effect of tamoxifen is endometrial hyperplasia.

Tamoxifen, due to its estrogenic activity, stimulates the endometrium, resulting in hyperplasia and a higher likelihood of developing endometrial cancer. Hence, it is not used in post-menopausal women.

Tamoxifen's estrogenic activity and consequences:

* Uterine endometrium: It can cause abnormal vaginal bleeding, endometrial thickening, and a ↑ risk of endometrial carcinoma.

* Coagulation system: Thromboembolism leading to pulmonary embolism (Tamoxifen decreases the level of antithrombin III and protein c in the blood).

* Bone metabolism: Decrease in bone mineral density (in premenopausal women), leading to an increased risk of fractures due to osteoporosis. Increase in bone mineral density (in postmenopausal women).

* Liver: Alterations of blood lipid profile.

* Tamoxifen use is associated with cataracts

* Fertility: Tamoxifen may interfere with implantation and may cause infertility, but is not a significant side effect.

Stop Tamoxifen if patient develops AUB

The use of tamoxifen in breast cancer patients decreases the incidence of carcinoma in the opposite breast (Option A).
questions.learning: Endometrial hyperplasia Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM), and it is the drug of choice for preventing recurrence of breast carcinoma in premenopausal women.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding ABCDE of trauma care? I. A stands for Airway with cervical spine protection. II. B stands for Breathing and ventilation. III. C stands for Control of massive external haemorrhage. IV. D stands for Disability (Neurological status). Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, II and IV

The ABCDE approach is the cornerstone of the Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) protocol and is designed to identify and treat life-threatening injuries in order of priority. Each step must be completed and stabilized before moving to the next. The following statements are correct:

• I. A stands for Airway with cervical spine protection: The airway should be assessed and secured while maintaining cervical spine immobilization until spinal injury is excluded.
• II. B stands for Breathing and ventilation: Assess chest movement, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, breath sounds, and treat life-threatening thoracic injuries (e.g., tension pneumothorax).
• IV. D stands for Disability (Neurological status): Rapid neurological assessment includes:

• Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
• Pupillary size and reaction
• Limb movement
• Blood glucose (to exclude hypoglycemia)

Why is III incorrect?

• III. C stands for Control of massive external haemorrhage: In ATLS, C stands for Circulation with hemorrhage control, not merely control of massive external hemorrhage. It includes:

• Assessment of pulse and blood pressure
• Control of all bleeding
• IV access and fluid/blood resuscitation
• Assessment of tissue perfusion ⭐
questions.learning: I, II and IV — The ABCDE approach is the cornerstone of the Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) protocol and is designed to identify and treat life-threatening injuries in order of priority.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the function of the muscle marked as A in the image below, at the metacarpophalangeal joint?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Flexion

The muscle marked 'A' is lumbricals and they cause flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joints.

Lumbricals are intrinsic muscles of the hand that flex the metacarpophalangeal joints (MCP) and extend the interphalangeal joints (PIP & DIP).

They originate from flexor digitorum profundus.

• The lateral two are unipennate, supplied by the median nerve.
• The medial two are bipinnate, supplied by the ulnar nerve.
questions.learning: Flexion — The muscle marked 'A' is lumbricals and they cause flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joints. Lumbricals are intrinsic muscles of the hand that flex the metacarpophalangeal joints (MCP) and extend the interphalangeal joints (PIP & DIP).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presented with a midline neck swelling that moves with deglutition and tongue protrusion. CT confirms the diagnosis of a thyroglossal cyst. Which of the following procedures is used in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sistrunk operation

The treatment of choice for a thyroglossal cyst is the Sistrunk operation.

Thyroglossal duct cyst (TDGC)

The thyroid gland descends early in fetal life from the base of the tongue towards its position in the lower neck. Once the gland reaches its position, where the isthmus is at the level of the second and third tracheal rings, the tract of the thyroglossal duct disappears. A thyroglossal cyst represents the persistence of this track and can be found adjacent to the midline.

Classically, swellings associated with the thyroid move with deglutition. Thyroglossal cyst moves upwards on swallowing and on tongue protrusion, and it indicates attachment to the hyoid bone. Although they often occur in children, they may also present in adults, even as late as the 6th or 7th decade.

Diagnosis:

CT scan commonly confirms the diagnosis by showing well-circumscribed lesions with homogenous fluid attenuation surrounded by a thin, enhancing rim.

FNAC may be used to exclude other causes.

Differential diagnosis:

* TGDC is the most common cause of a midline neck mass, followed by dermoid cysts.

* Sebaceous and dermoid cysts lie near the skin and don’t attach to deep structures like the hyoid.

* Branchial cleft cysts have a sinus or fistula, unlike thyroglossal cysts.

* Lipomas are superficial with ill-defined edges.

Treatment:

Sistrunk operation: This operation involves the excision of the entire thyroglossal tract, with the removal of the body of the hyoid bone and suprahyoid tract through the tongue base to the vallecula at the site of the primitive foramen cecum, together with the core of tissue on either side.
questions.learning: Sistrunk operation — The treatment of choice for a thyroglossal cyst is the Sistrunk operation. Thyroglossal duct cyst (TDGC) The thyroid gland descends early in fetal life from the base of the tongue towards its position in the lower neck.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old primigravida presents to the labor and delivery unit at 36 weeks’ gestation with abdominal pain and blood-tinged vaginal discharge. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus ( GDM ) at 27 weeks but has been noncompliant with diet and insulin therapy. On cervical examination, the cervix is 6 cm dilation and 100% effaced. Her blood glucose level on admission is 290 mg/dL, and insulin therapy is initiated. The patient subsequently has a spontaneous vaginal delivery of a male infant. Which of the following examination findings is most likely to be present in this neonate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Respiratory distress

In gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperglycemia, which stimulates fetal pancreatic β-cells to produce excess insulin (hyperinsulinemia).

Effect on fetal lungs:

• High fetal insulin levels inhibit surfactant production by type II pneumocytes.
• This delays lung maturation.

Neonatal consequence: Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) shortly after birth due to surfactant deficiency.

Other typical findings in infants of diabetic mothers:

• Macrosomia
• Neonatal hypoglycemia
• Polycythemia
• Hyperbilirubinemia
• Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Why other options are less likely:

• Heart murmur (congenital heart disease) is more associated with pregestational diabetes.
• Limb defects occur with early teratogenic exposure, also linked to pregestational diabetes.
• Small for gestational age is uncommon; infants are usually large for gestational age (macrosomic).
questions.learning: Respiratory distress — In gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperglycemia, which stimulates fetal pancreatic β-cells to produce excess insulin (hyperinsulinemia).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 20-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after a RTA. On presentation, his pulse is 110/minute, RR is 18/minute and BP is 80/60 mmhg. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. eFAST

The given clinical scenario of a patient being hemodynamically unstable after a RTA indicates a probable ongoing hemorrhage and the next step in the management is to perform an eFAST.

Cardiogenic shock, hemorrhagic shock, or pneumothorax are the most likely causes of hypotension in a trauma patient. Ultrasound evaluation using eFAST to look for pericardium, pleural cavities, and abdomen in combination with plain radiographs of the chest and pelvis will usually identify the source of the bleed.

In patients with hypotension due to blunt trauma, the pelvis should be wrapped in a sheet for stabilization until radiography can be done.

eFAST stands for extended FAST and incorporates left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax.

Limitations of eFAST are:

* Operator-dependent

* Bowel gas and subcutaneous air distort images.

* Can miss diaphragm, bowel, and pancreatic injuries

* Unreliable for assessment of the retroperitoneum

* Cannot reliably exclude injury in penetrating trauma

* May need repeating or supplementing with other investigations

FAST stands for Focussed Assessment with Sonography for Trauma. It is a rapid, non-invasive bedside test for detecting free fluid using sonography used to assess patients for potential thoracoabdominal injuries.

Technique:

* The patient is placed in a supine position and the following regions are scanned:

* Subxiphoid transverse view: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries

* Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch

* Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury

* Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas
questions.learning: eFAST The given clinical scenario of a patient being hemodynamically unstable after a RTA indicates a probable ongoing hemorrhage and the next step in the management is to perform an eFAST.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 52-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging, painless swelling in the right parotid region. FNAC confirms a malignant parotid tumor. The surgeon wants to assess the first group of lymph nodes involved in metastasis. The lymph nodes involved will be:
options: Preauricular and superficial parotid lymph nodes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Preauricular and superficial parotid lymph nodes

The parotid gland has an extensive intraparotid lymphatic network. Malignant tumors of the parotid gland first metastasize to the intraparotid (superficial parotid) and preauricular lymph nodes, before spreading to the upper deep cervical lymph nodes (Level II).

The patient has a malignant parotid tumor. The first-echelon (sentinel) lymph nodes are:

• Preauricular lymph nodes
• Superficial (intraparotid) lymph nodes

Why not the other options?

• A. Submental lymph nodes: Drain the lower lip, chin, floor of mouth, and tip of the tongue, not the parotid gland.
• B. Deep cervical lymph nodes: Involved later after spread from intraparotid nodes.
• D. Submandibular lymph nodes: Drain the submandibular gland, oral cavity, cheeks, and anterior tongue, not the parotid gland.
questions.learning: Preauricular and superficial parotid lymph nodes — The parotid gland has an extensive intraparotid lymphatic network. Malignant tumors of the parotid gland first metastasize to the intraparotid (superficial parotid) and preauricular lymph nodes, before…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy presented with bleeding gums, recurrent poor wound healing, and pain in the lower extremities. Examination revealed corkscrew hairs and swollen spongy gums. X-ray showed a white line at the metaphysis. The underlying biochemical defect involves impaired hydroxylation of proline residues during collagen synthesis. Which vitamin deficiency is responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin C

The child has scurvy, caused by vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency. Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, enzymes responsible for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues during collagen synthesis. Defective collagen formation leads to fragile blood vessels, impaired wound healing, bleeding gums, corkscrew hairs, bone pain, and characteristic White line at the metaphysis (Frankel’s white line) on X-ray

Why not the other options?

• A. Vitamin A: Deficiency causes night blindness, xerophthalmia, and keratinization of epithelium, not defective collagen synthesis.
• C. Vitamin D: Deficiency causes rickets in children with bowing of legs, widened wrists, and rachitic rosary, not bleeding gums or corkscrew hairs.
• D. Vitamin K: Deficiency impairs synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, causing bleeding, but does not impair collagen synthesis or produce corkscrew hairs.
questions.learning: Vitamin C — The child has scurvy, caused by vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency. Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, enzymes responsible for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues during collagen synthesis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Inguinal bubo is caused by which of the microorganisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Haemophilus ducreyi

The presence of inguinal bubo is a characteristic feature of chancroid, which is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Haemophilus ducreyi.

Inguinal bubo refers to swollen and tender lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy) in the inguinal (groin) region, which is a common presentation of chancroid due to regional lymph node involvement.

Other Options:

Diphtheria, caused by Corynebacterium diphtheria causes and the typical lesion early in the disease is a superficial ulcer, oval, rounded, or irregularly linear in shape with a clearly defined, overhanging edge. The ulcer may later become deeper and the edge becomes rolled, raised, and avascular. It is usually seen around the umbilicus, behind the ears, genito-crural flexure, or in the clefts.

Donovanosis, Klebsiella granulomatis previously known as Calymmatobacterium granulomatis causes a sexually transmitted disease. The incubation period is 1–12 weeks. It presents as a painless beefy red ulcer that bleeds readily on touch. Lymph node involvement is rare. However, pseudo buboes (subcutaneous granulomas) may be seen in the inguinal region in 10% of cases due to subcutaneous abscess.

Gonorrhea is caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae and can lead to various symptoms, including genital discharge and inflammation. While gonorrhea can involve the inguinal lymph nodes, it is not typically associated with the term "inguinal bubo." The major symptoms include urethritis, vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, and dysuria.
questions.learning: Haemophilus ducreyi — The presence of inguinal bubo is a characteristic feature of chancroid, which is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Haemophilus ducreyi.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Two girls in the same class are diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. Their 12-year old friend from the same school is afraid of contracting the disease. What advice should be given to the exposed students?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antibiotic prophylaxis

Antibiotic prophylaxis is provided to the close contacts of persons with confirmed meningococcal disease.

Close contacts of individuals with confirmed meningococcal disease are at an increased risk of developing the illness. Prophylaxis is also offered to individuals with direct and prolonged contact with a case of meningococcal disease. Antibiotics are effective in preventing additional cases by eradicating the carriage of the invasive strain.

Treatment is provided to the contacts within 24 hours of identification of the index case. The antibiotics effective include rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, and azithromycin.

Prophylaxis is not generally recommended for medical personnel, except in cases where there is exposure to aerosols of respiratory secretions, such as during mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, intubation, or suctioning. This recommendation applies within 24 hours before or after the initiation of antibiotic therapy in the index case.

For the treatment of cases, penicillin is the preferred drug, but ceftriaxone or other third-generation cephalosporins are recommended for patients with penicillin allergy. Droplet infection control precautions should be followed for hospitalized patients for 24 hours after effective therapy has been initiated.

Offering quadrivalent meningococcal A, C, W, Y conjugate vaccines in addition to antimicrobial prophylaxis can further reduce the risk of disease among close contacts of cases caused by vaccine capsular groups.

Meningococcal vaccines are available in two forms: polysaccharide vaccines and polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccines. Polysaccharide vaccines can be given as a single dose to individuals aged 2 years and older. They are offered in bivalent (A, C), trivalent (A, C, W135), and quadrivalent (A, C, W135, Y) formulations.

Meningococcal conjugate vaccines are available as monovalent (A or C) or quadrivalent (A, C, W135, Y) formulations. Conjugate vaccines, which offer increased immunogenicity and potential for herd protection, are preferred over polysaccharide vaccines, especially in children under 2 years of age. Both types of vaccines are safe to use during pregnancy.
questions.learning: Antibiotic prophylaxis Antibiotic prophylaxis is provided to the close contacts of persons with confirmed meningococcal disease. Close contacts of individuals with confirmed meningococcal disease are at an increased risk of developing the illness.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Difference in trajectory between inspiratory loop and the expiratory loop in the curve is due to:
options: Difference in alveolar pressure during inspiration and expiration
Difference in conc. of surfactant during inspiration and expiration
Difference in airway resistance during inspiration and expiration
Inspiration is active and expiration is passive
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Difference in conc. of surfactant during inspiration and expiration

The difference between the inflation and the deflation paths is called hysteresis.

It exists because a greater transpulmonary pressure is required to open a previously closed airway, due to a deficit of surfactant at the air-water interface, than to keep an open airway from closing, as then it has abundant surfactant.
questions.learning: Difference in conc. of surfactant during inspiration and expiration The difference between the inflation and the deflation paths is called hysteresis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the outer covering of the condition shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amnion

The diagnosis based on the given image is omphalocele and is covered by the amnion.

Omphalocele is a midline abdominal wall defect where the bowel and other solid viscera protrude through the umbilicus. In this condition, the herniated organs are covered by both peritoneum and an amnion. The umbilical cord inserts directly into this sac, which helps in identifying the condition. The defect occurs due to the failure of the physiological hernia to return to the body cavity by the 11th week of gestation.

The size of an omphalocele can vary significantly. It may be relatively small, containing only the gut, or it can be classified as a giant omphalocele if it measures 4 cm or more in diameter, encompassing the gut, liver, and other abdominal organs. The condition is often associated with other congenital anomalies such as trisomies 13, 15, 18, or 21, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, exstrophy of the bladder or cloaca, and pentalogy of Cantrell.

Treatment for omphalocele involves covering the exposed organs to prevent fluid loss and protect them from infection. Prophylactic antibiotics may be administered in case of rupture. Surgical correction is usually performed once the baby is stable. In omphalocele, since the umbilicus is covered by a reflection of the amnion, this membrane also covers the omphalocele itself, differentiating it from other types of abdominal wall defects.

Note : Gastroschisis is a condition where the intestinal loops herniate through the defect in the abdominal wall. The defect usually lies on one side of the umbilicus (right side commonly). The loops of the bowel are not covered by amnion. It is associated with elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels.
questions.learning: Amnion — The diagnosis based on the given image is omphalocele and is covered by the amnion. Omphalocele is a midline abdominal wall defect where the bowel and other solid viscera protrude through the umbilicus.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which pharmacokinetic parameters are used to determine the loading dose of an orally administered drug? 1. Volume of distribution (Vd) 2. Half-life 3. Plasma concentration 4. Bioavailability
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Loading dose = (Target plasma concentration × Volume of distribution) / Bioavailability.

Thus it depends on Vd, desired plasma concentration, and bioavailability for oral drugs.

Goal: Achieve target plasma concentration quickly

↓

Need to fill drug in body compartments

↓

Depends on:

Volume of distribution

Desired plasma concentration

Bioavailability (oral)

↓

Calculate loading dose

Half-life determines dosing interval and maintenance dose, not loading dose. Hence parameters 1, 3, and 4 are required.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 Loading dose = (Target plasma concentration × Volume of distribution) / Bioavailability. Thus it depends on Vd, desired plasma concentration, and bioavailability for oral drugs.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with vertical diplopia, especially noticeable when descending stairs. She reports tilting her head to one side to reduce the double vision. Which cranial nerve palsy is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of vertical diplopia (double vision) that is characteristically worse when looking down (such as walking downstairs or reading) is the classic indicator of a 4th Cranial Nerve (Trochlear) palsy. The 4th nerve innervates the superior oblique muscle, which acts as a primary depressor when the eye is adducted. To compensate for the excyclotorsion and vertical deviation, patients characteristically tilt their head to the opposite side of the lesion to achieve binocular fusion. 3rd CN palsy (Option A) presents with "down and out" eye position, ptosis, and a dilated pupil. 6th CN palsy (Option B) causes horizontal diplopia worse on lateral gaze. 7th CN palsy (Option C) involves facial muscle weakness and impaired eye closure but does not cause diplopia. Trochlear palsy can be congenital or acquired due to trauma or microvascular disease (diabetes). Diagnosis is confirmed using the Park’s Three-Step Test. Many patients can be managed with prism glasses or surgical correction
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of vertical diplopia (double vision) that is characteristically worse when looking down (such as walking downstairs or reading) is the classic indicator of a 4th Cranial Nerve (Trochlear) palsy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: CD-59 is involved in ____________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

CD-59 is involved in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).

Factors regulating complementary pathways:

• DAF or CD-55 inhibits C3 activation
• MIRL or CD-59 inhibits the membrane-activating complex

In PNH, DAF and MIRL are absent. Hence, there will be unregulated complement activation.

Clinical features of PNH include:

• Intravascular hemoglobinuria - cola-colored urine
• Pancytopenia + hypercellular bone marrow
• Thrombosis (if hepatic vein involved → Budd–Chiari syndrome)

Diagnosis of PNH is by the following methods:

• HAM’S test - acidified serum lysis
• Sucrose lysis test
• Flow cytometry - absence of CD 55 and CD 59 on RBC

Eculizumab is used to alleviate the hemolysis associated with PNH and its sequelae. Eculizumab does not alter the underlying defect of the disease.

Note: FDA has recently approved Pegcetacoplan for adults with PNH which acts by binding to complement protein C3 and increasing hemoglobin concentration.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction in a male child is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Posterior urethral valve

The most common cause of bladder outflow obstruction in a male child is the posterior urethral valve (PUV).

A PUV is a membranous fold in the posterior urethra which results from the persistence of the urogenital membrane. It is typically located just distal to the verumontanum and is the primary cause of bladder outlet obstruction in newborn males.

Diagnosis is most commonly made antenatally with ultrasound which demonstrates bilateral hydronephrosis, a distended bladder, and a dilated posterior urethra which appears as the keyhole sign on imaging. In severe cases, there is oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia during the antenatal period.

If the diagnosis is not made antenatally, then babies typically present with urinary tract infections in the neonatal period or with uraemia and renal failure. Clinically, a poor urinary stream, dribbling of urine, and palpable bladder (due to diverticula) can be present.

The investigation of choice is micturating cystourethrography.

The diagnosis is best made during the micturition phase of micturating cystourethrography in lateral or oblique views so that the posterior urethra can be imaged adequately. The following findings are seen:

• Dilatation and elongation of the posterior urethra - equivalent of the ultrasonographic keyhole sign
• Linear radiolucent band corresponding to the valve - seen occasionally
• Vesicoureteral reflux - seen in 50% of patients
• Bladder trabeculation/diverticula

Treatment is initially supportive by inserting a urinary catheter to relieve symptoms of obstruction. Definitive treatment is by urethroscopic destruction of the valves with continuing lifelong supportive treatment of the dilated urinary tract, recurrent urinary infections and uremia.

Other options:

Options B and C- Urethral atresia and anterior urethral valve are rare congenital anomalies that can also lead to urinary obstruction.

Option D- Ureterocele is the cystic enlargement of the intramural ureter. It is common in females. They can present with features of urinary tract infection, bladder obstruction, or ureteral stones. Excretion urography will show cobra head appearance.

The image shown below depicts the "cobra head" sign in a patient with bilateral ureterocele.
questions.learning: Posterior urethral valve — The most common cause of bladder outflow obstruction in a male child is the posterior urethral valve (PUV). A PUV is a membranous fold in the posterior urethra which results from the persistence of the urogenital membrane.
