questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of botulinum toxin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prevents release of acetylcholine

Botulinum toxin prevents the release of acetylcholine.

The botulinum toxins produced by Clostridium botulinum are neurotoxins that cleave the SNARE (soluble NSF attachment protein receptor) family of proteins involved in vesicular fusion and subsequently neurotransmitter release. Preformed toxins when ingested can cause food-borne botulism. The botulinum toxins block the release of acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction and cause flaccid paralysis. Symptoms can include ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphonia, and dysphagia.

Eight different serotypes of toxin have been identified which are produced by Clostridium botulinum. All of them are neurotoxins except C2. The various SNARE proteins cleaved are:

* Synaptobrevin- cleaved by serotypes B, D, F, & G

* SNAP-25 - cleaved by serotypes A & E

* Syntoxin - cleaved by serotype C1

The image given below shows the site of action of botulinum toxin.

Infant botulism is also called floppy baby syndrome. It is usually seen in infants less than 6 months. It is acquired by ingestion of foods like honey contaminated with C. botulinum spores. It gets established in the gut and produces toxins. Affected children usually present with paralysis, constipation, difficulty breathing, poor feeding, weakness, altered crying, and loss of head control.

Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting toxins or spores in the stool. Gram staining shows gram-positive, sporing bacilli. It is managed by supportive care and assisted feeding only.

The image given below shows gram staining of Clostridium botulinum.

Other Options:

Option B: Inhibits acetylcholine esterase: Organophosphates, carbamates, and certain nerve agents like sarin prevent acetylcholine breakdown by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase.

Option C: Inhibits reuptake of acetylcholine: Hemicholinium blocks the reuptake of choline, preventing acetylcholine synthesis.

Option D: Blockage of postsynaptic receptors of acetylcholine: α-bungarotoxin, curare, and α-conotoxin act as competitive antagonists at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.

* Bacillus anthracis

* Vibrio cholerae - Cholera toxin

* Enterotoxigenic E.coli (ETEC) - heat labile toxin

* Enterotoxigenic E.coli (ETEC) - heat stable toxin

Inhibition of protein synthesis

* Diptheria toxin: inhibit elongation factor-2 (EF-2)

* Pseudomonas: inhibit elongation factor-2 (EF-2)

* Clostridium difficile

* Enterohemorrhagic E.coli (EHEC)-Shiga-like toxin: inhibit 60S

* Shigella dysenteriae- Shiga toxin: inhibit 60S

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following management techniques helps in standardising the methods of performing jobs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Work Sampling

Work sampling is a work measurement and management technique used to analyze how workers spend their time during a job. By making random observations of work activities, it helps identify inefficiencies and standardize the best method of performing a job, thereby improving productivity.

• A. Systems Analysis ✗

• Studies the functioning of an entire system and its components to improve overall efficiency.
• Does not standardize individual job methods.

• B. Decision Making ✗

• Refers to selecting the best course of action from available alternatives.
• It is a managerial function, not a method for standardizing work.

• C. Work Sampling ✓

• Uses random observations to determine how time is utilized.
• Helps establish standard methods, improve workflow, and increase efficiency.

• D. Personnel Management ✗

• Deals with recruitment, training, motivation, and appraisal of employees.
• It is not used to standardize job performance.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with meningitis, and the CSF sample was subjected to gram staining and microscopy and appears as shown in the microscopic image given below. Which of the following features/tests will be characteristic of the organism?
options: Oxidase and catalase negative, does not ferment inulin
Ferments glucose and maltose but not inulin
Oxidase and catalase positive and does not ferment maltose or glucose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Catalase negative, optochin sensitive

The given clinical vignette of meningitis with the grams stain slide showing gram-positive diplococci some in lancet-shaped and some arranged in chains narrows down the aetiological/ microbial agent to Pneumococcus / Streptococcus pneumoniae. It is catalase-negative and optochin sensitive.

The Gram stain would reveal Gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci, single cocci, or chains. Pneumococci undergo autolysis with the addition of surface-active agents like ox bile (10%) or sodium deoxycholate (2%). The Viridans streptococci do not lyse and are thus easily differentiated from pneumococci. The growth of pneumococci is inhibited by optochin (Ethyl hydrocuprein hydrochloride) while that of viridans streptococci is not. It is catalase-negative, ferments inulin, and optochin sensitive.

Pneumococci are commensals of the upper respiratory tract and can cause pneumonia, sinusitis, otitis, bronchitis, bacteremia, meningitis, peritonitis, and other infectious processes. The pneumococcal infection results in inflammation and exudation of fibrinous materials resulting in edema and consolidation. The onset of pneumococcal pneumonia is usually sudden, with fever, chills, and sharp pleural pain. The sputum is similar to the alveolar exudate, being characteristically bloody or rusty colored. Disseminated infection and bacteremia can present as meningitis, endocarditis, and septic arthritis.

The other diagnostic parameters include the C-polysaccharide found in the cell wall of all S. pneumoniae that can be detected in the urine and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and a positive Quellung reaction.  Quellung reaction/ Neufeld reaction is used to identify capsulated organisms such as pneumococci, Neisseria meningitis, Haemophilus influenza, etc. When a suspension of a capsulated bacterium is mixed with its specific anticapsular serum and examined under the microscope, the capsule becomes very prominent and appears 'swollen' due to an increase in its refractivity.

High-dose penicillin G is effective in treating pneumococcal infection.

The culture showing alpha hemolysis on blood agar, with optochin (Op) sensitivity, and microscopy showing gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci, suggests Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus).

The image shows a swollen capsule, which is demonstrated by the Quellung reaction

The flowchart demonstrates the algorithm used for identification of gram-positive organisms in the lab.

The primary clinical purpose of this instrument is menstrual regulation or the aspiration of the uterine cavity (Option D) . It is commonly used for early medical termination of pregnancy, management of incomplete abortions, or obtaining an endometrial biopsy. Hysterosalpingography (Option A) requires a different specialized cannula for injecting contrast under pressure. Measuring the uterine length (Option B) is performed using a uterine sound, which is a thin, graduated metal rod. Retraction (Option C) is a function of speculums or surgical retractors. Because the MVA provides a handheld, low-pressure suction mechanism specifically designed for intrauterine contents, it is the definitive tool for regulation and aspiration procedures. Recognizing this equipment is fundamental for practitioners providing reproductive health and outpatient gynecological services. .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An 11-year-old child who weighs 26 kg with a history of streptococcal pharyngitis presents to you with fever and arthralgia. There is no evidence of carditis. How often is benzathine penicillin recommended for prophylaxis of rheumatic heart disease?
options: 600000 IU Once in 3 weeks for next 5 years
600000 IU Once in 3 weeks for next 10 years
1200000 IU Once in 3 weeks for next 10 years
1200000 IU Once in 3 weeks for life
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 600000 IU Once in 3 weeks for next 10 years

This child has acute rheumatic fever without carditis and no established valvular disease. Benzathine penicillin G is used because it:

• Provides long-acting antibiotic coverage
• Prevents recurrent streptococcal infection

Administration: Intramuscular injection every 3 weeks

For secondary prophylaxis in ARF without carditis, benzathine penicillin is given for 5 years or until age 21 (whichever is longer). In this case, since the child is 11 years old, we will give prophylaxis for the next 10 years since (21-11 years) is longer than 5 years.

| Category | Duration from the last attack

| -------- | -----------------------------

| Rheumatic fever without carditis | 5 years or until 21 years of age (whichever is longer)

| Rheumatic fever with carditis but no residual heart disease | 10 years or until 21 years of age (whichever is longer)

| Rheumatic fever with carditis + residual heart disease | 10 years or until 40 years of age (whichever is longer)

In children weighing <30 kg, the recommended dose is 600,000 IU IM every 3 weeks.

Hence, 600000 IU once in 3 weeks for the next 10 years is correct.

The "Whichever is Longer" Rule — A Common Trap

Students often memorize "no carditis = 5 years" and stop there. But the full rule is:

5 years OR until age 21 — whichever gives MORE time

So you must always calculate both and pick the larger number:

| Child's Age | 5 years from now | Until age 21 | Choose

| ----------- | ---------------- | ------------ | ------

| 11 years | Age 16 | Age 21 = 10 more years | 10 years ✅

| 17 years | Age 22 = 5 more years | Age 21 = 4 years | 5 years ✅

| 18 years | Age 23 = 5 more years | Age 21 = 3 years | 5 years ✅

Why Not Option C (1.2 million IU)?

Add this explicitly since 20.9% chose it:

• 1,200,000 IU is for children ≥30 kg.
• This child weighs 26 kg < 30 kg → dose is 600,000 IU.

The weight cutoff is a second trap layered onto the duration trap — both must be applied correctly to reach B.

questions.text:
Match the following disorders with their genetic abnormalities.

Genetic abnormalities
Disorders

1. Trinucleotide repeat
a. Patau syndrome

2. Trisomy 18
b. Huntington chorea

3. Trisomy 13
c. Sickle cell anemia

4. Hb beta chain Glu→Val
d. Edward syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c

The correct match is:

Genetic abnormalities
Disorders

1. Trinucleotide repeat

b. Huntington chorea

2. Trisomy 18

d. Edward syndrome

3. Trisomy 13

a. Patau syndrome

4. Hb beta chain Glu→Val

c. Sickle cell anemia

Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant progressive brain disorder that causes uncontrolled movements, emotional problems, and loss of thinking ability. It occurs due to atrophy, with loss of neurons and gliosis in the caudate lobe, putamen, and globus pallidus. There is an abnormal expansion of the trinucleotide CAG in the Huntington gene on chromosome 4.

Trisomy 18 results in Edward’s syndrome in which a complete extra copy of chromosome 18 is inherited as a result of meiotic nondisjunction. The clinical features include micrognathia, low-set ears, prominent occiput, and rocker bottom feet. Patients have significant hypertonia including clenched hands with overlapping fingers. Cardiac anomalies (ventricular septal defects and patent ductus arteriosus) and gastrointestinal anomalies (Meckel’s diverticulum, malrotations) are common. Prenatal ultrasound reveals fetal growth restriction.

Trisomy 13 results in Patau syndrome which presents with midline facial clefts(Cleft lip/palate) and musculoskeletal abnormalities,eg-polydactyly. Phenotypic features include microcephaly, low-set ears, hypertelorism, and a broad nasal bridge.

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the point mutation in the β-globin gene, which results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS). Factors that predispose to sickling are infection, dehydration, and acidosis. Clinical features are moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice and painful bone crisis. The aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 70-year-old woman, admitted for right leg cellulitis, develops diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever three days into her hospital stay. Laboratory tests show a significantly elevated C-reactive protein (160 mg/L). Which pathogen is most likely causing her current symptoms?
questions.explanation: (Note: There is a nomenclature error in the source options; the intended answer is Clostridium difficile, which causes pseudomembranous colitis. "C. coli" is not a standard pathogen in this context.) The patient's development of diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain three days after admission for a different infection (cellulitis) is the classic presentation of healthcare-associated (nosocomial) diarrhea. The primary culprit is Clostridium difficile, which typically occurs after antibiotic therapy for a primary infection (like cellulitis) disrupts the normal gut flora. E. coli (Option B) is more common in community-acquired diarrhea or food poisoning. Norovirus (Option C) and Rotavirus (Option D) are viral causes that usually present in outbreaks or specific age groups (infants) and would not be as strongly linked to a hospital admission for cellulitis. C. difficile toxins cause significant inflammation, explaining the high CRP of 160 mg/L. Therefore, antibiotic-associated colitis from Clostridium is the definitive clinical diagnosis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young girl presents with irregular menstrual cycles, acne, hirsutism, and ultrasound evidence of multiple ovarian follicles. In this clinical setting, which hormone or biochemical parameter is most likely to be elevated?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of irregular periods, acne, and hirsutism (increased facial hair), combined with the ultrasound finding of polycystic ovaries, is pathognomonic for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). The characteristic biochemical abnormality in PCOS is an increase in androgens; therefore, Serum testosterone levels would be elevated. Sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) (Option A) levels are characteristically decreased in PCOS (due to insulin resistance), which further increases the bioavailability of free testosterone. FSH levels (Option C) are often normal or low. The LH:FSH ratio is typically increased (often ), but Option D incorrectly lists the "FSH/LH ratio," which would be decreased. Insulin resistance is a central feature of the syndrome, leading to the compensatory hyperinsulinemia that stimulates the ovarian theca cells to produce more testosterone. Management focuses on lifestyle modification, hormonal contraceptives to regulate cycles, and anti-androgens like spironolactone to treat the cutaneous symptoms of hirsutism and acne

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B

Lab investigations in vitamin D-dependent rickets will reveal normal/decreased serum calcium, decreased phosphorous, elevated PTH, and increased ALP levels.

Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1 is due to 1 α hydroxylase deficiency resulting in decreased hydroxylation of 25 hydroxy vitamin D leading to increased levels of 25 OH vitamin D and decreased levels of 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D.

Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2 is due to the resistance of the vitamin D receptors to vitamin D in both bone and intestine. Here, the levels of 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D are raised, but despite this, the serum calcium and phosphate levels are low due to the lack of action of vitamin D.

Decreased vitamin D leads to decreased calcium and phosphate due to reduced absorption. The decreased calcium stimulates increased PTH production. PTH tries to normalise the calcium and further decreases the phosphate because of renal elimination. ALP level is increased as it is involved in bone mineralization.

X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH) occurs because of a defect in the PHEX gene. Since the PHEX gene is responsible for inactivating FGF-23, there is an increased FGF-23 in XLH. Increased FGF-23 inhibits phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule of the kidney and causes phosphaturia. It also inhibits 1-α-hydroxylase, leading to decreased production of activated vitamin D.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common primary source of brain metastases?
questions.explanation: Brain metastases are the most common intracranial tumors in adults, and the lung (Option B) is the primary site of origin in approximately 40% to 50% of all cases. Lung cancer cells frequently spread hematogenously to the brain due to the direct vascular pathway from the pulmonary circulation. Breast cancer (Option D) is the second most common source, particularly in women. Thyroid cancer (Option A) and liver cancer (Option C) can occasionally metastasize to the brain, but they are significantly less frequent primary sources compared to the lung and breast . Brain metastases often present with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure, such as headaches, or focal neurological deficits and seizures. Multiple lesions are more common than solitary ones in metastatic disease. Radiologically, these typically appear as ring-enhancing lesions with significant surrounding edema. Therefore, when an adult presents with new-onset neurological signs and multiple brain lesions, a primary lung malignancy is the first suspicion
questions.learning: Brain metastases are the most common intracranial tumors in adults, and the lung (Option B) is the primary site of origin in approximately 40% to 50% of all cases.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is admitted to the ICU two days after a femur fracture. They are on a rebreathing oxygen unit with an arterial oxygen saturation of 100%, but pulse oximetry (SpO₂) reads 60%. The patient is confused, and chest X-ray shows clear lung fields. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of a recent long-bone (femur) fracture, confusion (neurological symptoms), and severe hypoxemia ( 60%) in the presence of a clear chest X-ray is pathognomonic for Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES). FES occurs when fat globules from the marrow are released into the systemic circulation. Pulmonary embolism (Option A) typically presents with chest pain and would show signs on CT, not just a clear X-ray. ARDS (Option C) would show diffuse, bilateral "white-out" or infiltrates on X-ray, rather than clear fields. Occult pneumothorax (Option D) would show localized findings or mediastinal shift. The "mismatch" between the profound hypoxemia and the normal initial radiograph is a key diagnostic clue for FES. Therefore, based on the specific orthopedic trauma history and the multi-system clinical picture, Fat Embolism is the definitive diagnosis. Treatment is primarily supportive with oxygen and stabilization
questions.learning: The clinical triad of a recent long-bone (femur) fracture, confusion (neurological symptoms), and severe hypoxemia ( 60%) in the presence of a clear chest X-ray is pathognomonic for Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following muscle is responsible for ptosis in horner's syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Muller's muscle

Ptosis in Horner's syndrome is due to the paralysis of Muller's muscle. Muller's muscle(superior tarsal muscle) maintains the elevation of the upper eyelid. It is innervated by the sympathetic nervous system.

Fasanella-Servat operation is indicated in cases having mild ptosis(< 2 mm) and good levator function. In this surgery, the upper tarsal border along with its attached Muller’s muscle and conjunctiva are resected.

questions.text: A young woman, following an intense workout involving heavy weight lifting, presents with lower back pain radiating to her right hip and extending down to her right ankle. MRI shows the following finding. Based on the location and radiation of her pain, which of the following nerve roots is most likely involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. L5

Based on the clinical presentation of lower back pain radiating to the right hip and ankle, along with an MRI showing L4-L5 disc prolapse, the likely nerve root involved is L5. In a typical L4-L5 disc herniation, the L5 nerve root is most commonly compressed.

Other options:

Option A: L4: Involvement typically causes symptoms around the knee and anterior lower leg, but not the ankle.

Option C: S1: Compression here causes symptoms in the posterior leg, calf, and heel, differing from this case's distribution of pain.

Option D: L3: Affects the anterior thigh, with no radiating pain below the knee.

The label marked 2 represents the LH surge ,which is responsible for ovulation.

Phases of the menstrual cycle :

Follicular phase (days 0–14)

* A primordial follicle develops to the Graafian stage, with atresia of neighboring follicles.

* LH and FSH receptors are up-regulated in theca and granulosa cells.

* Estradiol levels increase and cause proliferation of the uterus.

* FSH and LH levels are suppressed by the negative feedback effect of estradiol on the anterior pituitary.

* Progesterone levels are low.

Ovulation (day 14)

* Occurs 14 days before menses, regardless of cycle length. Thus, in a 28-day cycle, ovulation occurs on day 14; in a 35-day cycle, ovulation occurs on day 22.

* A burst of estradiol synthesis at the end of the follicular phase has a positive feedback effect on the secretion of FSH and LH (LH surge).

* Ovulation occurs as a result of the estrogen-induced LH surge.

* Estrogen levels decrease just after ovulation (but rise again during the luteal phase).

* Cervical mucus increases in quantity; it becomes less viscous and more penetrable by sperm.

Luteal phase (days 14–28)

* Progesterone levels are high.

* The corpus luteum begins to develop, and it synthesizes estrogen and progesterone. Vascularity and secretory activity of the endometrium increase to prepare for receipt of a fertilized egg.

* Basal body temperature increases because of the effect of progesterone on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center.

* If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses at the end of the luteal phase. As a result, estradiol and progesterone levels decrease abruptly.

Menses (days 0–4)

* The endometrium is sloughed because of the abrupt withdrawal of estradiol and progesterone.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following is the first intermediate host for the parasitic fluke Clonorchis sinensis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Snail

Clonorchis sinensis (Chinese liver fluke) is a trematode that infects the biliary tract of humans. Its life cycle requires two intermediate hosts: the freshwater snail as the first intermediate host and freshwater fish as the second intermediate host. Humans acquire infection by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish containing metacercariae.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Dog: Dogs are reservoir/definitive hosts, not intermediate hosts.
• C. Encysts on vegetation: Encystment on aquatic vegetation occurs in Fasciola hepatica, not Clonorchis sinensis.
• D. Sheep: Sheep are the definitive host of Fasciola hepatica, not Clonorchis sinensis.
questions.learning: Snail Clonorchis sinensis (Chinese liver fluke) is a trematode that infects the biliary tract of humans. Its life cycle requires two intermediate hosts: the freshwater snail as the first intermediate host and freshwater fish as the second intermediate host.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A young boy with fatigue is found to have a haemoglobin of 9 g/dl. Peripheral smear showed sickle-shaped RBCs. What is the next best step in managing this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Blood transfusion

The given clinical scenario and image are diagnostic of sickle cell anemia. The next best step is blood transfusion.

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the T-to-A point mutation in the sixth codon of the β-globin gene. This results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS).

The clinical features of sickle cell disease are due to the tendency of HbS molecules to stack into polymers when deoxygenated. The features are:

* Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice.

* Painful bone crisis- hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet.

* Acute chest syndrome typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates.

* Hyposthenuria- inability to concentrate urine.

* Aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia.

* Spleen

* In children- splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion.

* Adolescence or early adulthood- autosplenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage.

* Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms like pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza septicemia, but can be reduced by vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics.

* Other clinical features- priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation.

The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical findings, the presence of irreversibly sickled RBCs on peripheral smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis showing increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike.

Disease-modifying drugs such as hydroxyurea can be given to patients with sickle cell anemia since it reduces the incidence of adverse vaso-occlusive vents. Blood transfusions are used to treat and prevent complications of sickle cell disease, including preparation for surgery, symptomatic anemia, acute stroke, multi-organ failure and acute chest syndrome

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient is admitted with tachycardia and arrhythmias. On examination, multiple scratch marks are noted on the body. Which drug of abuse is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of tachycardia, arrhythmias, and multiple scratch marks on the body is highly suggestive of Cocaine abuse. The scratch marks are a result of Magnan's sign (formication), a specific type of tactile hallucination where the user feels like insects are crawling under their skin ("cocaine bugs"). This leads to frantic, compulsive scratching. Cocaine is a potent sympathomimetic that also causes severe cardiovascular effects, including hypertension, tachycardia, and potentially fatal arrhythmias. Morphine (Option B) is an opioid that typically causes bradycardia, respiratory depression, and "pinpoint" pupils. Datura (Option C) causes an anticholinergic syndrome ("mad as a hatter, red as a beet"). Cannabis (Option D) usually causes relaxation and reddened eyes (conjunctival injection). Understanding these specific "behavioral clues" is essential for emergency physicians and psychiatrists to identify the hidden drug of abuse when a patient presents with non-specific systemic symptoms

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Surgical correction of VSD is performed in an infant. This will help in relieving which of the following features?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Failure to thrive

Surgery for ventricular septal defect (VSD) mainly helps to relieve congestive cardiac failure which manifests as a failure to thrive in an infant. The main aim of performing surgery in VSD is to get the symptoms of heart failure in control and to prevent the development of pulmonary vascular disease.

Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart disease. The most common subtype is the membranous type.

Small VSDs with trivial left-to-right shunts and normal pulmonary artery pressure (PAP) are the most common. These patients are asymptomatic. A loud, harsh, or blowing holosystolic murmur is present and heard best over the lower left sternal border, and it is accompanied by a thrill.

Small VSDs close spontaneously, especially within the first two years of life. Muscular VSDs have a higher closure rate (up to 80%) compared to membranous VSDs.

Large VSDs with excessive pulmonary blood flow and pulmonary hypertension can lead to signs of congestive heart failure in early infancy. These signs may include dyspnea, feeding difficulties, poor weight gain, profuse perspiration, irritability, weak crying, and recurrent pulmonary infections. The holosystolic murmur associated with a large VSD is less harsh and more blowing compared to that of a small VSD. This is due to the absence of a significant pressure gradient across the defect.

The indications of surgery in VSD are:

• Large defects in patients of any age with uncontrolled symptoms or failure to thrive.
• Moderate to large defects associated with pulmonary hypertension in infants between 6 and 12 months, even if symptoms are controlled by medication.
• Patients older than 24 months with a Qp: Qs ratio greater than 2:1 (ratio of total pulmonary blood flow-Qp to total systemic blood flow-Qs).
• Supracristal VSDs of any size, due to the higher risk of developing aortic valve regurgitation.

Severe pulmonary vascular disease nonresponsive to pulmonary vasodilators is a contraindication to VSD closure.

Other options:

Options A and C: Respiratory alkalosis and arrhythmia are other rare complications of VSD.

Options D: Heart block may occur perioperatively in VSD.
questions.learning: Failure to thrive Surgery for ventricular septal defect (VSD) mainly helps to relieve congestive cardiac failure which manifests as a failure to thrive in an infant.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents to the orthopedic clinic with a fracture as shown in the image. Which nerve is most likely involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior interosseous nerve

Supracondylar fractures of the humerus commonly injure the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN), the most frequently affected branch of the median nerve. AIN palsy causes motor deficits without sensory loss, characterized by inability to make the “OK” sign due to paralysis of the flexor pollicis longus, the radial half of flexor digitorum profundus, and pronator quadratus.

FMGE/NEET PG Pearl

• Supracondylar fracture → Most common nerve injured: Anterior interosseous nerve (median nerve branch).
• AIN injury → Pure motor; no sensory deficit.
• Median nerve injury → Sensory loss over the lateral 3½ fingers and thenar weakness.
• Cubital tunnel/medial epicondyle injury → Ulnar nerve involvement.
• Radial nerve is more commonly injured in shaft fractures of the humerus.
questions.learning: Anterior interosseous nerve Supracondylar fractures of the humerus commonly injure the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN), the most frequently affected branch of the median nerve.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: According to the Difficult Airway Society (DAS) guidelines for unanticipated difficult intubation in adults, which of the following represents the correct sequence of airway interventions prioritizing oxygenation?
options: Intubation → Front of neck access → SAD → Face mask ventilation
Intubation → SAD → Face mask ventilation → Front of neck access
Face mask ventilation → Intubation attempts → SAD → Front of neck access
SAD → Intubation → Front of neck access → Face mask ventilation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intubation → SAD → Face mask ventilation → Front of neck access

The DAS algorithm consists of four sequential plans:

• Plan A: Tracheal intubation

• Optimize first-pass success (positioning, bougie/videolaryngoscope if needed).
• Limit attempts (generally ≤3, with one additional attempt by an experienced operator).

• Plan B: Maintain oxygenation using a supraglottic airway (SGA)

• Insert a second-generation SGA.
• Consider intubation through the SGA only in appropriate circumstances.

• Plan C: Face-mask ventilation and wake the patient

• If intubation and SGA fail but mask ventilation is possible, maintain oxygenation and abandon the procedure if feasible.

• Plan D: Emergency front-of-neck access (eFONA)

• Performed in a Can't Intubate, Can't Oxygenate (CICO) situation.
• The recommended technique is scalpel-bougie cricothyroidotomy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida presents to the emergency department with a cervical dilation of 5 cm at 1 pm and 6 cm at 4 pm. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation: In a primigravida, normal cervical dilation in the active phase is about ≥1 cm/hour. Here, dilation increases from 5 cm at 1 pm to 6 cm at 4 pm—only 1 cm in 3 hours, indicating protracted labor. On a partograph, this rate crosses the alert line and approaches the action line, signaling abnormal progress. At this point, simply labeling it as slow progress is not enough—the next step is active management. Management includes: 1. Assessing the 3 Ps (power, passenger, passage) 2. Amniotomy (ARM) if membranes are intact 3. Oxytocin augmentation if contractions are inadequate Why other options are incorrect: (A) Slow progress of labor: This is only a diagnosis, not the next management step. (B) Wait for complete dilation: Unsafe in abnormal labor; may risk fetal/maternal complications. (C) Induce labor: Induction is for initiating labor, not for a patient already in labor

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old child is diagnosed with amblyopia affecting the right eye. To promote visual development in the weaker eye, which management option is most appropriate to recommend?
options: Spectacles or refraction with a near addition
questions.explanation: Amblyopia, often called "lazy eye," is a developmental disorder where the brain fails to process inputs from one eye, favoring the other. At age three, the visual system is still plastic, making early intervention critical. Occlusion therapy, which involves patching the stronger "good" eye for several hours a day, is the gold-standard treatment. By forcing the brain to use the weaker, amblyopic eye, it stimulates the development of the corresponding visual cortex. Observation (Option A) is inappropriate as amblyopia does not resolve spontaneously and can lead to permanent vision loss. While refractive correction (Option B) is often the first step if an error exists, it is frequently insufficient on its own and must be followed by patching. Radial keratotomy (Option D) is an obsolete refractive surgery for myopia and is never used in pediatric amblyopia management. Therefore, occlusion therapy remains the most effective and widely used method to restore balanced vision in young children before the critical period of visual development ends around age seven to nine
questions.learning: Amblyopia, often called "lazy eye," is a developmental disorder where the brain fails to process inputs from one eye, favoring the other. At age three, the visual system is still plastic, making early intervention critical.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Patients with which of the following conditions are more susceptible to infections caused by catalase-positive organisms:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic granulomatous disease

Susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms is a hallmark of Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD).

• Defect in NADPH oxidase → impaired respiratory burst
• Phagocytes cannot generate reactive oxygen species to kill ingested microbes

Catalase-positive organisms degrade their own hydrogen peroxide using catalase. Phagocytes cannot utilize microbial H₂O₂ → failure of intracellular killing

Common organisms:

• Staphylococcus aureus
• Serratia marcescens
• Aspergillus species
• Nocardia

Differentiation:

• Hyper IgM → defective class switching
• Job syndrome → impaired neutrophil chemotaxis, recurrent staph infections but not specifically catalase-positive pattern

Chediak-Higashi → lysosomal trafficking defect

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman who underwent dilatation and curettage previously, now presents with amenorrhea. The urine pregnancy test is negative. HSG revealed a honeycomb appearance in the uterine cavity.What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Asherman syndrome

The given clinical features, history and hysteroscopy are suggestive of Asherman syndrome.

Asherman syndrome refers to the presence of adhesion within the endometrial cavity. It is also called uterine synechiae and can be asymptomatic tiny bands or can completely or almost completely obliterate the endometrial cavity. It can occur as a result of trauma to the endometrium following vigorous uterine curettage, tuberculous endometritis, pelvic radiation, or endometrial ablation.

It causes secondary amenorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea, dysmenorrhoea, habitual abortion and infertility depending upon the extent of uterine cavity obliteration.

Asherman syndrome (uterine synechiae) is classified as follows:

* Mild: <25% adhesion involves the uterine cavity, flimsy adhesions involving the fundus and tubal ostia.

* Moderate: 25–70% adhesion of the endometrial surfaces, but no agglutination of the uterine wall.

* Severe: 75% adhesions with agglutination and thick adhesions.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) may show honeycomb or moth-eaten appearance. Definitive diagnosis requires hysteroscopy as polyps, leiomyomas, air bubbles and blood clots may masquerade as adhesions.

Treatment involves hysteroscopic lysis of the adhesions.

The image below shows a moth-eaten appearance on hysterosalpingography

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not included in MMR?
questions.explanation: The Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) tracks the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and site of the pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management. Direct obstetric causes, such as death due to preeclampsia (Option B) or complications of an ectopic pregnancy (Option C), are included. Similarly, a death on the 14th day postpartum (Option D) falls well within the 42-day window and is included if it resulted from obstetric causes. However, deaths resulting from accidental or incidental causes, such as a Road Traffic Accident (RTA) (Option A), are not included in the calculation of MMR. MMR is a key indicator of a nation's reproductive health status and the quality of its obstetric care system. India has made significant progress in reducing its MMR through improved access to institutional deliveries and high-quality antenatal care
questions.learning: The Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) tracks the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, irrespective of the duration and site of the pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient presents with headache, vomiting and nuchal rigidity. Guarded LP was done and shows turbid CSF. Microscopy shows 90% PMN cells with sugar of 40 mg/dL and protein of 200 mg/dl. Which is correct about the management of this case? LP-Lumbar puncture CSF-Cerebro spinal fluid PMN-Polymorpho nuclear cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin

The given clinical scenario of a patient presenting with headache, vomiting, and nuchal rigidity and a guarded lumbar puncture revealing turbid CSF with 90% PMN cells, a sugar level of 40 mg/dL, and protein of 200 mg/dL is suggestive of bacterial meningitis and the appropriate management includes treatment with ceftriaxone plus vancomycin.

The most common cause of meningitis in adults over 20 years of age is Streptococcus pneumoniae.

The classic clinical triad of meningitis includes fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity. Other common symptoms include decreased consciousness, nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and seizures. Cutaneous signs such as petechiae, purpura, or an erythematous macular rash may be present.

Brudzinski's sign and Kernig's sign can indicate meningeal irritation.

* Brudzinski's sign is positive when there is involuntary flexion of the hips and knees in response to passive neck flexion.

* Kernig's sign is positive when there is resistance and pain in extending the knee with the hip flexed at 90 degrees (given below)

When bacterial meningitis is suspected, blood cultures should be obtained, and empirical antimicrobial therapy should be initiated without delay. The diagnosis is confirmed by examining cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). CSF analysis shows increased polymorphonuclear leukocytes, decreased glucose concentration, increased protein concentration, and increased opening pressure. CSF bacterial cultures and Gram stain are used to identify the causative organism.

Prompt initiation of empirical antimicrobial therapy is crucial in suspected cases of bacterial meningitis. Commonly used antibiotics include third- or fourth-generation cephalosporins (such as ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or cefepime) that cover Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae and Vancomycin if there is a high suspicion of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection. Ampicillin with metronidazole is added when Listeria monocytogenes is suspected, particularly in neonates, pregnant women, individuals over 50 years, and immunocompromised individuals.

Other Options:

Option A: Amphotericine B plus flucystosine for at least 2 weeks is used as Induction agent for Cryptococcus with CNS involvement in HIV patient.

Option B: Acyclovir is used as a drug of choice for treating Viral meningitis  especially caused by HSV and is not useful in managing bacterial meningitis.

Option D: Tubercular meningitis can be treated with Rifamapicin plus isoniazid. But they are not indicated in bacterial meningitis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A woman presents with impaired hearing. Her tympanogram findings are given below. Pick the right combination of tuning fork test results that would be seen in this patient.
options: Left Rinne's test negative, Weber's test lateralized to right ear
Left Rinne's test negative, Weber's test lateralized to left ear
Left Rinne's test positive, Weber's test lateralized to right ear
Left Rinne's test positive, Weber's test lateralized to left ear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Left Rinne's test positive, Weber's test lateralized to right ear

The given tympanogram findings indicate sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear. Tuning fork tests in this patient would show left Rinnie's positive and Weber lateralized to the right ear.

In left sensorineural hearing loss, Rinne's test will be positive on both left and right ears, and Weber's test will be lateralized to the better ear, which is the right.

Tuning fork tests are performed commonly with tuning forks of frequencies such as 128, 256, 512, 1024, etc. The tuning fork of 512 Hz is considered ideal as forks of lower frequencies produce a sense of bone vibration, while those of higher frequencies have a shorter decay time.

Rinne’s test is done by placing a vibrating tuning fork on the patient’s mastoid and when he/she stops hearing, it is brought beside the external auditory meatus (EAC). If he/she still hears the sound, air conduction (AC) is better than bone conduction (BC).

Weber test is done by placing a vibrating tuning in the middle of the forehead or the vertex and the patient is asked in which ear the sound is better heard.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the condition shown in the image given below:
questions.explanation: The image depicts a carbuncle (Option D), which is a deep-seated bacterial infection of a cluster of hair follicles. It is characteristically formed by several interconnected furuncles (boils) and is identified by its multiple draining sinus tracts on the skin surface, often referred to as a "sieve-like" appearance. These are most common in areas with thick skin, like the back of the neck or the back. Botryomycosis (Option A) is a rare chronic granulomatous bacterial infection that mimics fungal lesions. Erysipelas (Option B) is a superficial cellulitis with well-defined, raised borders and intense erythema. Ecthyma (Option C) is an ulcerative form of impetigo that extends into the dermis, resulting in "punched-out" ulcers. Carbuncles are frequently associated with underlying immunosuppression or diabetes mellitus. Treatment requires incision and drainage along with systemic antibiotics to manage the extensive staphylococcal infection

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following head and neck cancers is most commonly associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oropharyngeal carcinoma

HPV infection is most commonly associated with oropharyngeal carcinoma.

HPV 16 and 18 are considered high-risk subtypes and are associated with cervical cancer and precancerous cervical lesions. There is also evidence linking HPV 16 and 18 with cancers of the anus, vulva, vagina, penis, and oropharynx.

The E6 protein of high-risk types binds to the p53 gene, while the E7 protein inactivates the pRb gene. p53 and pRb are tumour suppressor genes that, when inactivated, result in uncontrolled cell proliferation. The presence of koilocytes is a histopathological marker of the virus. These cells have a perinuclear halo in the cytoplasm, and these cells disappear when dysplasia advances.

Laryngeal papillomas are benign tumours of the larynx caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV types 6 and 11), which is most likely acquired at birth from mothers who had vaginal HPV disease. Juvenile papillomatosis, or respiratory papillomatosis, is the most common benign laryngeal neoplasm in children.

Important agents associated with malignant conditions:

* HHV-8 (mainly), cytomegalovirus - Kaposi’s sarcoma

* Epstein-Barr virus – Burkitt’s lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma

* HPV 16 and 18 – Cancer cervix

* HBV and HCV – Hepatocellular carcinoma

* Schistosoma – Bladder carcinoma

The head and neck cancers include cancers of the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, paranasal sinuses, nasal cavity, and salivary glands. Squamous cell cancer is the most common head and neck malignancy, often linked to tobacco and alcohol use. Non-squamous malignancies include thyroid cancer, salivary gland cancer, and sarcomas.

The risk factors for head and neck malignancies are listed below:

* Oral cavity cancer:

* Tobacco, smokeless tobacco like Bidi, Chutta, Paan (oral tobacco mixed with betel leaf, areca nut, and salted lime), Khaini, and marijuana

* Alcohol, poor oral hygiene, and intake of red meat and salted meat

* Infections with human papillomavirus and HIV

* Genetic conditions like Li-Fraumeni, ataxia telangiectasia, Bloom syndrome, and Fanconi's anaemia

* Oropharyngeal cancer:

* Smoking and alcohol

* HPV 16 and 18

* Cancer of the larynx and hypopharynx (Option D):

* Tobacco and alcohol

* Nickel, mustard gas, and asbestos exposure

* Long-term exposure to sulphuric acid and hydrochloric acid in battery plant workers.

* Postcricoid carcinoma is associated with previous radiation and sideropenic dysphagia

* HPV infection and immunosuppression

* Nasopharyngeal cancer: (Option A)

* Chinese population

* Epstein-Barr virus infection

* Nitrosamines in salted fish and meat

* Vitamin C deficiency

* Cancers of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinus:

* Tobacco

* Occupational exposure to dust from wood, textiles, and leather. Nickel and chromium dust and mustard gas exposure.

* HPV 16 and 18

Option B: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is a known risk factor for post-cricoid hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.learning: Oropharyngeal carcinoma HPV infection is most commonly associated with oropharyngeal carcinoma. HPV 16 and 18 are considered high-risk subtypes and are associated with cervical cancer and precancerous cervical lesions.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What are the potential effects of folic acid deficiency during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Folic acid is a crucial B-vitamin required for DNA synthesis and rapid cell division during fetal development. A deficiency in maternal folic acid is strongly linked to the development of neural tube defects (NTDs), such as spina bifida and anencephaly, which occur when the neural tube fails to close properly within the first 28 days of gestation. While severe deficiency might contribute to general pregnancy complications, Option B (preterm labor) is not the primary direct outcome of folate lack. Pernicious anemia (Option C) is specifically caused by Vitamin B12 deficiency due to a lack of intrinsic factor, not folic acid. Iron deficiency anemia (Option D) results from inadequate iron levels and is a separate nutritional pathology. Due to its critical role, universal periconceptional folic acid supplementation is recommended for all women planning pregnancy to significantly reduce the risk of NTDs
questions.learning: Folic acid is a crucial B-vitamin required for DNA synthesis and rapid cell division during fetal development. A deficiency in maternal folic acid is strongly linked to the development of neural tube defects (NTDs), such as spina bifida and anencephaly,…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with chronic kidney disease underwent a nephrectomy. Which of the following can be administered as a postoperative analgesic in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acetaminophen

Acetaminophen can be given as an analgesic for the patient as it is the least nephrotoxic among the given options.

Analgesia in CKD patients:

Acetaminophen is considered a safer non-narcotic analgesic in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. For more severe pains opioid analgesics like tramadol or fentanyl are used.

Even though acetaminophen is considered safe, with chronic high dosage it can also become nephrotoxic.

NSAIDs like naproxen, indomethacin, diclofenac, etc are not used in CKD patients because of their direct nephrotoxic effects. In healthy normal individuals, NSAIDs have little effect on renal function and blood pressure. But in conditions where the regulatory systems are impaired as hypovolemia, congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, or other conditions where the renin-angiotensin system is activated, renal function by the formation of prostaglandins are very important.

NSAIDs cause impairment of prostaglandin-induced inhibition of chlorine reabsorption and antidiuretic hormone action. This will cause salt and water retention. It also inhibits COX-2 derived prostaglandins which regulate the renal medullary blood flow and would lead to a rise in blood pressure, increased cardiovascular thrombotic events, and cardiac failure. It can also cause electrolyte abnormalities like hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.
questions.learning: Acetaminophen Acetaminophen can be given as an analgesic for the patient as it is the least nephrotoxic among the given options. Analgesia in CKD patients: Acetaminophen is considered a safer non-narcotic analgesic in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Fibers from the marked structure terminate at which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Red nucleus

The peduncle highlighted in the image is the superior cerebellar peduncle. The superior cerebellar peduncle includes fibers from deep cerebellar nuclei that project to the brainstem, red nucleus, and thalamus. It also contains the ventral spinocerebellar tract fibers.

The superior cerebellar peduncle contains all the efferent fibers from the dentate, emboliform, and the globose nuclei, and a small fascicle from the fastigial nucleus. Its fibers decussate in the caudal mesencephalon and are destined to synapse in the contralateral red nucleus and thalamus. The middle cerebellar peduncle contains only afferent fibers from the contralateral pontine nuclei. The inferior cerebellar peduncle is a mixture of afferent fibers from the brainstem and spinal cord and efferent fibers to the vestibular nuclei.

The image below summarizes the various tracts in the cerebellar unit.

The cerebellum consists of two hemispheres (right and left) joined by a median vermis. It is divided into three lobes:-

• Anterior lobe - lies superiorly above the primary fissure
• Middle lobe - lies inferiorly below the primary fissure. It is the largest lobe. It is also called the posterior lobe.
• Flocculonodular lobe - lies posterior to the uvulonodular fissure

It has two surfaces - superior and inferior separated by a horizontal fissure. It is connected to the other parts of the central nervous system via three peduncles

• Superior cerebellar peduncle -connecting to the midbrain
• Middle cerebellar peduncle - connecting to the pons
• Inferior cerebellar peduncle - connecting to the medulla oblongata
questions.learning: Red nucleus — The peduncle highlighted in the image is the superior cerebellar peduncle. The superior cerebellar peduncle includes fibers from deep cerebellar nuclei that project to the brainstem, red nucleus, and thalamus.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the most reliable confirmatory method to verify correct placement of a central venous catheter in the internal jugular vein?
questions.explanation: After inserting a central venous catheter (CVC) into the internal jugular or subclavian vein, a chest X-ray (Option A) is the gold standard and best confirmatory method. It ensures that the tip of the catheter is correctly positioned at the junction of the superior vena cava and the right atrium. Crucially, it also rules out procedural complications such as a pneumothorax. Blood color (Option C) and pH (Option B) are unreliable indicators, especially in hypoxic or acidotic patients, as venous blood can sometimes appear arterial and vice versa. ETCO2 (Option D) is used to confirm the correct placement of an endotracheal tube in the lungs, not a vascular catheter . While ultrasound is used to guide the initial insertion, the post-procedure X-ray remains mandatory to verify the final location and safety of the line. Therefore, X-ray is the definitive clinical step before using the line for high-volume infusion or medications
questions.learning: After inserting a central venous catheter (CVC) into the internal jugular or subclavian vein, a chest X-ray (Option A) is the gold standard and best confirmatory method.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which nerve will be involved in the following finding on rest?
questions.explanation: The image depicts an "Ulnar Claw Hand," which occurs due to an injury to the ulnar nerve. This deformity is characterized by hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and flexion at the proximal and distal interphalangeal (PIP/DIP) joints, most prominently in the 4th and 5th fingers. It results from the loss of function in the medial lumbricals and interosseous muscles. Median nerve injury (Option B) leads to "Hand of Benediction" (seen only when attempting to make a fist) or "Ape Hand" deformity due to loss of thumb opposition. The musculocutaneous nerve (Option C) primarily controls elbow flexion and does not cause a specific hand deformity. The "ulnar paradox" states that higher lesions of the ulnar nerve result in less obvious clawing because the long finger flexors are also paralyzed. Therefore, the specific resting position of the medial two fingers is diagnostic of distal ulnar palsy

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presents with history of having ingested a button battery. What is your next course of action?
options: Reassure and to check whether passed in stools
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Remove endoscopically

This case should be managed by removing the button battery endoscopically after confirming its position on X-Ray.

Button battery ingestion causes alkaline caustic injury, more in the areas surrounding the negative pole.

Management :

• The child is to be kept NPO until the oesophageal position of the battery is ruled out by X-ray scan. Vomiting should never be induced since the battery, which has passed through the esophagus, might lodge back again into it. Reassurance can be done only if the position of the battery is confirmed and if there are no symptoms.
• Since the question does not mention that the child is asymptomatic, the management of choice would be removing the battery endoscopically.
• Management also depends on battery life. Fresh batteries need to be removed as soon as possible as they have a higher concentration of injurious substances.
questions.learning: Remove endoscopically — This case should be managed by removing the button battery endoscopically after confirming its position on X-Ray. Button battery ingestion causes alkaline caustic injury, more in the areas surrounding the negative pole.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not applicable or permissible during cross- examination in a court of law?
options: Witness is examined by the defense lawyer
Objective of cross-examination is to weaken case of opponent
There is no time limit to cross examination
questions.explanation: In a legal trial, cross-examination is the stage where the opposing party’s lawyer questions the witness. A key feature of cross-examination is that leading questions ARE allowed and are frequently used to challenge the witness's credibility or to elicit specific answers. This distinguishes it from the "examination-in-chief," where leading questions are strictly prohibited. The witness is indeed examined by the defense (or opposing) lawyer (Option A). The primary objective is to weaken the opponent's case or to reveal inconsistencies in the testimony (Option C). While the judge has the authority to prevent irrelevant or repetitive questioning, there is generally no strict "time limit" fixed by law for this process (Option D). Therefore, statement B is incorrect because leading questions are a fundamental tool during cross-examination

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which agency collects data and publishes large scale surveys continuously regarding morbidity, family planning, vital events?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. National Sample Survey

The National Sample Survey collects data and publishes large-scale surveys continuously regarding morbidity, family planning, vital events.

The National Sample Survey(NSS), headed by a Director-General, is responsible for the conduct of large-scale sample surveys in diverse fields all over India.

Data are collected through national household surveys on various socio-economic subjects. Besides these surveys, NSS collects data on rural and urban prices and plays a significant role in the improvement of crop statistics through supervision of the area enumeration and crop estimation surveys of the State agencies.  It also maintains a frame of urban area units for use in sample surveys in urban areas.

The four types of survey methods are :

* Health interview (face-to-face) survey

* Health examination survey

* Health records survey

* Mailed questionnaire survey

The cause of death is noted by the Sample registration system (SRS), the Death certificate, and via lay reporting

Other Options:

Option A: Civil Registration System also known as Vital Registration System, is managed under the Ministry of Home Affairs by the Office of the Registrar General of India. Birth and death registration in India is undertaken by this system and is registered within 21 days.

Option C: Sample Registration System, a Biannual system conducted every 6 months, and assess indicators such as crude birth rate, death rate, Infant mortality rate, Maternal mortality rate, and so on.

Option D: Central Bureau of Health functions as the national health data repository, responsible for the collection, analysis, and dissemination of health statistics to support evidence-based policy and planning.
questions.learning: National Sample Survey — The National Sample Survey collects data and publishes large-scale surveys continuously regarding morbidity, family planning, vital events.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: True statement regarding the given nerve action potential curve is?
options: At point E, the nerve is more excitable
Point C to D is due to opening of Na+ and closure of K+ channels
Point B to D is refractory period
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Point B to D is refractory period

Points B to D span depolarization through early repolarization, corresponding to the absolute refractory period. During this phase, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated and a new action potential cannot be generated. Excitability is reduced until repolarization progresses. Hence B to D represents the refractory period.

| Option | Statement | Correct/Incorrect | Explanation

| ------ | --------- | ----------------- | -----------

| A | Threshold at A | ❌ Incorrect | A = resting potential, threshold at B

| B | At E nerve is more excitable | ❌ Incorrect | E = hyperpolarization → less excitable

| C | C–D due to Na⁺ opening & K⁺ closure | ❌ Incorrect | Opposite: Na⁺ closes, K⁺ opens

| D | B–D is refractory period | ✅ CORRECT | Covers absolute + most of refractory phase
questions.learning: Point B to D is refractory period Points B to D span depolarization through early repolarization, corresponding to the absolute refractory period. During this phase, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated and a new action potential cannot be generated.

• Acute monoarthritis (knee effusion)
• Sterile joint aspirate

Reactive arthritis is:

• A seronegative spondyloarthropathy
• Triggered by GI infections (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter) or GU infections (Chlamydia)
• Strongly associated with HLA-B27

Clinical features may include:

• Asymmetric oligoarthritis (lower limbs)
• Conjunctivitis or uveitis
• Urethritis
• Sacroiliitis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old male intravenous drug user presents with fever of 38.5 °C and fundal spots. CBC shows a leukocyte count of 20,000/cu mm, and blood cultures have been sent. In this scenario, how many minor Duke’s criteria are met for the diagnosis of infective endocarditis?
questions.explanation: The Duke’s criteria are used to diagnose infective endocarditis by identifying a combination of major and minor criteria. In this patient, only minor criteria can be assessed based on the given information. The following three minor criteria are fulfilled: 1. Predisposing condition: The patient is an intravenous drug user, which is a known risk factor for infective endocarditis. 2. Fever ≥ 38°C: The patient has a temperature of 38.5°C, meeting the fever criterion. 3. Immunologic phenomenon: The presence of fundal spots (Roth spots) indicates an immunologic manifestation. Although blood cultures have been sent, their results are not yet available, so microbiological evidence cannot be counted at this stage. Why other options are incorrect: (A) 6 :Too many; only three criteria present (C) 4 : Assumes positive blood culture, which is not given (D) 2 : Misses one valid criterion
questions.learning: The Duke’s criteria are used to diagnose infective endocarditis by identifying a combination of major and minor criteria. In this patient, only minor criteria can be assessed based on the given information.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the characteristic lesion of Kaposi sarcoma?
options: A white, striated lesion that cannot be scraped off
questions.explanation: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a malignancy caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals such as those with HIV/AIDS. The characteristic lesions typically begin as flat, reddish-purple macules and progress into raised, palpable plaques and nodules. This violaceous (purple-red) appearance is a pathognomonic sign resulting from the deposition of hemosiderin and extravasated red blood cells within the tumor. A yellow lesion with pus (Option A) indicates a bacterial infection like an abscess. A white, striated lesion (Option B) describes lichen planus or oral hairy leukoplakia. Small red erosions (Option D) are non-specific findings for various inflammatory skin conditions. Therefore, the raised purple-red morphology is the definitive clinical description for Kaposi sarcoma lesions
questions.learning: Kaposi Sarcoma (KS) is a malignancy caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals such as those with HIV/AIDS.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A mother brings her 9-month-old infant for evaluation, concerned that no BCG scar has developed despite the child having received the BCG vaccine at birth. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Do the Mantoux test & wait for the result
Refer the baby for a chest X-ray & further evaluation
questions.explanation: Following BCG vaccination, approximately 10% of children may not develop a visible scar; however, the absence of a scar is not an indicator of lack of immunity. National and WHO immunization guidelines state that if a child has a documented history of receiving the vaccine at birth and is otherwise healthy, no further action or revaccination is necessary. Therefore, the doctor should simply reassure the mother. Giving the vaccine again (Option B) is not recommended. Performing a Mantoux test (Option C) is unnecessary in an asymptomatic, previously vaccinated child. A chest X-ray (Option D) is only indicated if the child exhibits clinical symptoms suggestive of tuberculosis infection. The BCG vaccine is a live-attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis intended to protect infants from severe forms of TB like miliary TB and meningitis
questions.learning: Following BCG vaccination, approximately 10% of children may not develop a visible scar; however, the absence of a scar is not an indicator of lack of immunity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The mechanism by which glucose is absorbed in the intestine is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Secondary active transport

Glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport.

On the basolateral side, there is active transport of sodium ions out of the cell into the interstitial fluid. This depletes sodium inside the cell. Because of this Na+ concentration difference, more Na+ binds to the SGLT on the luminal side. This increases the affinity of SGLT for glucose and glucose binds to it.

Then, both the Na+ and glucose are transported together to the interior of the cell. Thus, glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport. The energy for glucose transport is provided indirectly, by the active transport of Na+ out of the cell. The glucose moves out of the cell into the blood across the basolateral membrane by facilitated diffusion mediated via GLUT.
questions.learning: Secondary active transport Glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport. On the basolateral side, there is active transport of sodium ions out of the cell into the interstitial fluid.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A patient presents with chronic small bowel diarrhea and says that he is allergic to wheat. Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy. Anti-endomysial antibodies and tTG IgA antibodies are positive. What is the diagnosis? tTG - tissue transglutaminase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Celiac sprue

Villous atrophy on duodenal biopsy together with a positive serological test for anti-endomysial antibodies and IgA anti-TTG antibodies suggests the diagnosis of celiac sprue.

Celiac disease is triggered by the ingestion of gluten, which is the major storage protein of wheat and similar grains. It usually affects the second portion of the duodenum or proximal jejunum. Antibodies associated with celiac disease are anti-gliadin antibodies, anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, and anti-endomysial antibodies.

The histopathology is characterized by villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial CD8+T lymphocytes. An increase in the number of intraepithelial lymphocytes is a sensitive marker of celiac disease, even in the absence of epithelial damage and villous atrophy. MARSH's Score is used to assess celiac disease histologically.

Dermatitis herpetiformis can occur in as many as 10% of patients.

The main stay of treatment is a gluten-free diet.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents with multiple swellings and multiple brown rashes. She has increased uptake on bone scans over the femur, skull, and ribs. Biochemical parameters are abnormal. She also has a history of hypothyroidism. An X-ray of her femur is given below. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. McCune-Albright syndrome

The above X-ray shows the bending of the femur known as Shepherd's crook deformity. It is seen in fibrous dysplasia of the proximal femur. The diagnosis based on the x-ray and clinical scenario points to McCune-Albright syndrome.

McCune Albright syndrome presents as a triad of cafe-au-lait spots (cutaneous pigmentation), polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and precocious puberty. It is also associated with multiple endocrinopathies like hyperthyroidism, acromegaly, etc. The locus of involvement is the GNAS1 gene.

Cutaneous pigmentation is more prominent on the side with severe bone involvement. Fibrous dysplasia is a condition that affects bone development and is characterized by the replacement of the bone with fibrous tissue. The patient presents with a progressive limb deformity or a fracture through a previously asymptomatic lesion. The presentation often occurs in the second decade. Other symptoms include nonspecific bone pain, tenderness, and swelling in the affected area. The commonly involved sites are the proximal femur, tibia, pelvis, and foot.

Radiological findings include:

• Well-defined, expansile intramedullary lesions
• Hazy ground glass appearance is seen in the majority of cases
• Shepherd's crook deformity - expansion with marked varus in the proximal femur.

Other options:

Option A: Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) occurs due to the proliferation of a special type of immature dendritic cells, called Langerhans cells. Their normal function is to present antigens. The most common mutation is the BRAFV600E gain-of-function mutation.

It is characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions and can also infiltrate nearly every organ, like the skin (of the scalp), lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, or the central nervous system. It presents with pain and swelling in the affected area. Spinal involvement results in compression fractures and neurological involvement. Vertebral involvement results in a rapid flattening of the vertebral body (vertebra plana).

LCH can present as the following clinical entities:

• Multifocal multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (Letterer-Siwe disease) which is mostly seen in infants
• Unifocal and multifocal system Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma) - The combination of bone defects, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos is called the Hand-Schüller-Christian triad that is mostly seen in younger children
• Pulmonary LCH is mostly seen in adults.

Option D: Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid (PTC) presents as a painless nodule or mass in the neck or enlargement of cervical lymph nodes. It usually occurs in women between 25 to 50 years of age. PTC is the most common thyroid cancer associated with previous exposure to ionizing radiation. Conventional PTCs have translocations involving RET or NTRK, and point mutations involving the BRAF gene.

Patients present with painless swelling. Initial presentation may be with cervical lymphadenopathy due to lymph node metastases.
questions.learning: McCune-Albright syndrome — The above X-ray shows the bending of the femur known as Shepherd's crook deformity. It is seen in fibrous dysplasia of the proximal femur.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Nitrogenous waste is excreted from the body in the form of __?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Urea

Nitrogenous wastes are excreted from the body in the form of urea.

Depending on their ecology and physiology, different animals excrete excess nitrogen as ammonia, uric acid, or urea.

In aqueous animals nitrogenous waste is excreted as ammonia. The constant excretion of water permits them to excrete the highly toxic ammonia, as it highly water soluble. Birds must both conserve water and maintain low weight and hence excreting nitrogen-rich uric acid. Many land animals, including humans, excrete nontoxic, highly water-soluble urea. High blood levels in renal disease are a consequence of impaired renal function.

Pearl PF0082: Urea Cycle and its disorders
questions.learning: Urea Nitrogenous wastes are excreted from the body in the form of urea. Depending on their ecology and physiology, different animals excrete excess nitrogen as ammonia, uric acid, or urea.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A diagnostic test has a sensitivity of 80% and a specificity of 90%. If the prevalence of the disease is 1% in a population of 10,000, what is the positive predictive value?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 7.5%

PPV is the probability that a person with a positive test truly has the disease.

Population = 10,000

Disease prevalence = 1% = 100 diseased, 9,900 non-diseased

• True positives (TP) = 80% of 100 = 80
• False positives (FP) = 10% of 9,900 = 990

PPV = TP / (TP + FP)

= 80 / (80 + 990)

= 80 / 1070

= 7.5%
