questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman with schizophrenia had been regularly taking olanzapine for several months but eventually stopped the medication. Which of the following adverse effects is the most likely reason for discontinuing this treatment?
questions.explanation: Olanzapine is a second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic highly effective for schizophrenia but is notoriously associated with significant metabolic side effects. The most frequent reason for non-compliance and treatment discontinuation is excessive weight gain, often accompanied by increased appetite and a high risk of metabolic syndrome, including dyslipidemia and diabetes. While extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) like acute dystonia (Option B) and akathisia (Option C) occur, they are much more common with first-generation (typical) antipsychotics like haloperidol. Tardive dyskinesia (Option D) is a late-onset neurological side effect also primarily linked to long-term use of typical antipsychotics. Because olanzapine has a lower affinity for D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway, it causes fewer motor side effects but remains a leading cause of treatment-limiting weight gain
questions.learning: Olanzapine is a second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic highly effective for schizophrenia but is notoriously associated with significant metabolic side effects.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with low-grade fever, headache, and malaise for the past 2 weeks. Lumbar puncture is performed. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis reveals lymphocytic predominance and low glucose levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tubercular meningitis

Differentiate the common causes of meningitis based on CSF analysis. Tubercular meningitis (TBM) typically presents with a subacute onset (days to weeks) of fever, headache, and malaise. CSF classically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose, reflecting chronic granulomatous inflammation caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Bacterial meningitis: Usually presents acutely with neutrophilic predominance, markedly low glucose, and very high protein.
• B. Viral meningitis: CSF shows lymphocytic predominance, but glucose is usually normal with only mildly elevated protein.
• D. Fungal meningitis: Can also show lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose, but it is more commonly seen in immunocompromised patients (e.g., cryptococcal meningitis), whereas the clinical presentation here is most typical of TBM.

High-yield Pearl

| Type of Meningitis | Cells | Protein | Glucose

| ------------------ | ----- | ------- | -------

| Bacterial | Neutrophils ↑ | ↑↑ | ↓↓

| Viral | Lymphocytes ↑ | Mild ↑ | Normal

| Tubercular | Lymphocytes ↑ | ↑↑ | ↓

| Fungal | Lymphocytes ↑ | ↑ | ↓

Exam Tip:

• Subacute meningitis + Lymphocytic CSF + Low glucose = Think Tubercular meningitis.
• Acute meningitis + Neutrophils + Very low glucose = Bacterial meningitis.
questions.learning: Tubercular meningitis Differentiate the common causes of meningitis based on CSF analysis. Tubercular meningitis (TBM) typically presents with a subacute onset (days to weeks) of fever, headache, and malaise.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzyme activities can be estimated in red blood cells to diagnose vitamin B2 deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutathione reductase

Glutathione reductase activity in red blood cells can be estimated to diagnose vitamin B2 deficiency.

Vitamin B2, also known as riboflavin, is a water-soluble vitamin. Its active forms are FMN (flavin mononucleotide) and FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide). Glutathione reductase is a FAD-containing enzyme (flavoenzyme). Hence, riboflavin deficiency can be detected by measuring erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity. Red blood cell and urinary concentrations of riboflavin can also be estimated to detect a deficiency.

Deficiency of riboflavin can present as anemia, corneal vascularization, mucocutaneous lesions, and personality changes. Milk and other dairy products are important dietary sources.

Other options:

Option A - Transketolase contains thiamine diphosphate as a coenzyme. Estimation of erythrocyte apotransketolase (enzyme protein) after in vitro addition of thiamine diphosphate, can be used to assess thiamine nutritional status. Thiamine deficiency can result in peripheral neuritis, beriberi, and Wernicke encephalopathy with Korsakoff psychosis.

Option C - Kynureninase is an enzyme that requires pyridoxal phosphate as a coenzyme. It converts 3-hydroxykynurenine, a tryptophan metabolite, to 3-hydroxyanthranilate. In vitamin B6 deficiency, this is impaired and results in the formation and subsequent urinary excretion of xanthurenate. This can be used for diagnosis.

Option D - Pyruvate is decarboxylated by pyruvate dehydrogenase for which thiamine diphosphate acts as the cofactor. Therefore thiamine deficiency results in the accumulation of pyruvate. This leads to pyruvic and lactic acidosis, commonly seen in alcoholics.
questions.learning: Glutathione reductase Glutathione reductase activity in red blood cells can be estimated to diagnose vitamin B2 deficiency. Vitamin B2, also known as riboflavin, is a water-soluble vitamin.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 65-year-old female patient presented with sudden painless loss of vision. She has been a known diabetic for 12 years. Ophthalmoscopy shows evidence of loss of fundal features, floating debris and a dark red glow. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitreous haemorrhage

This patient with long-standing diabetes with sudden, painless vision loss, floating debris and a dark red glow on fundoscopic examination is most likely suffering from vitreous haemorrhage.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy, which can arise in people with long-term diabetes mellitus, is a common risk factor for vitreous haemorrhage caused by the breakage of the fragile blood vessels on the retina's surface. Intravitreal blood blocks light from reaching the retina, resulting in patients experiencing sudden onset cloudy vision, sometimes with a red tint, or vision loss.

Vitreous haemorrhage has a variable presentation depending on the severity of the haemorrhage. The mild haemorrhage causes sudden onset floaters and diffuse blurring of vision, but may not affect visual acuity, whilst a dense bleed may result in sudden painless loss of vision.

Causes: Acute posterior vitreous detachment is associated either with a retinal tear or avulsion of a peripheral vessel. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion and sickle cell disease.

The investigation of choice for vitreous haemorrhage is an ultrasound B-scan.

Treatment: Patients with vitreous haemorrhage can be adequately managed with bed rest to prevent additional bleeding and elevation of the head to promote blood settling away from the visual axis and correcting the underlying cause of the bleeding. (eg. photocoagulation for proliferative retinopathy). Vitreoretinal surgery with photocoagulation is indicated in patients with persistent vitreal haemorrhage.

Other options

Option A: Patients with retinal detachment can develop floaters and have acute vision loss. However, photopsia is common and fundoscopy reveals an elevated retina with folds or tears. An image showing retinal detachment at the fovea and the macula is shown below.

Option C:  Patients with macular degeneration typically have painless central blurring of vision which is progressive as opposed to vitreous hemorrhage which is acute in its presentation. An image depicting age-related macular degeneration with the presence of drusens is shown below.

Option D: Patients with central retinal vein occlusion can also present with sudden, painless loss of vision but would have scattered, diffuse hemorrhages, disc swelling and cotton wool spots. Image showing central retinal vein occlusion is as follows.
questions.learning: Vitreous haemorrhage — This patient with long-standing diabetes with sudden, painless vision loss, floating debris and a dark red glow on fundoscopic examination is most likely suffering from vitreous haemorrhage.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Revised Which of the following is not a component of the global hunger index (GHI)?
options: Percentage of undernourished children under 5 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Infant mortality rate

The infant mortality rate is not a component of the global hunger index.

The Global Hunger Index (GHI) has three dimensions. These dimensions are measured by indicators.

Dimensions
Indicators

Inadequate food supply
Proportion of the population undernourished

Child mortality
Under 5 mortality rate

Child undernutrition
Wasting in children under 5 years
Stunting in children under 5 years

GHI score = (1/3 X standardized PUN) + (1/6 X standardised CWA) + (1/6 X standardised CST) + (1/3 X Standardised CM)

Where,

* PUN is the proportion of the population that is undernourished

* CWA is the prevalence of wasting in children under 5 years of age

* CST is the prevalence of stunting in children under 5 years of age

* CM is the proportion of children dying under the age of 5 years of age.

The result lies on a scale from 0 to 100, with 0 meaning no hunger and 100 being the worst score. The GHI is given by the International Food Policy Research Institute. In 2021, India's GHI was 27.5. It ranks 101 among 116 countries. In 2022, India's GHI stands at 29.1, and India ranks 107th out of the 121 countries. In 2024, India's GHI was 27.3, and it ranked 105 out of 127 countries.
questions.learning: Infant mortality rate — The infant mortality rate is not a component of the global hunger index. The Global Hunger Index (GHI) has three dimensions.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During a forensic autopsy of a gunshot victim, the firearm wound is noted to have a stellate (star-shaped) appearance. What does this finding indicate about the range of the gunshot?
questions.explanation: A stellate or star-shaped entrance wound is a pathognomonic feature of a "hard contact" gunshot wound, particularly when the weapon is pressed against skin overlying a flat bone, such as the skull. When the muzzle is in tight contact with the skin, the rapidly expanding gases produced by the gunpowder combustion are forced into the subcutaneous space between the skin and the bone. This gas pressure causes the skin to bulge outward and eventually burst or tear in a radiating, irregular pattern, creating the classic stellate appearance. In a close shot (Option A) or near shot (Option C), usually within a few centimeters to a meter, one would expect to see singeing, smudging, or tattooing (stippling) around a more circular hole rather than a stellate tear. A distant shot (Option D) typically produces a neat, circular or oval hole with an abrasion collar but lacks the gas-expansion effects required to create a stellate-shaped entrance wound
questions.learning: A stellate or star-shaped entrance wound is a pathognomonic feature of a "hard contact" gunshot wound, particularly when the weapon is pressed against skin overlying a flat bone, such as the skull.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An alcoholic patient presents with palpitations, dizziness, and episodes of syncope. On examination, the pulse is irregularly irregular. What finding is most likely to be observed on jugular venous pressure (JVP) examination?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of an irregularly irregular pulse in a chronic alcoholic is highly suggestive of atrial fibrillation (AF), often referred to as "Holiday Heart Syndrome" in this context. The jugular venous pulse (JVP) reflects pressure changes in the right atrium; specifically, the 'a' wave is produced by active atrial contraction. In atrial fibrillation, the atria do not contract effectively in a coordinated manner; instead, they undergo rapid, disorganized electrical activity. Consequently, there is a complete loss of the organized atrial systole required to produce the 'a' wave, leading to its disappearance on the JVP tracing. Large 'a' waves (Option B) occur during resistance to atrial emptying, such as in tricuspid stenosis. Cannon 'a' waves (Option C) are seen when atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve, as in complete heart block. A steep 'y' descent (Option D) is characteristic of constrictive pericarditis. Thus, the absent 'a' wave is the definitive JVP finding for AF
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of an irregularly irregular pulse in a chronic alcoholic is highly suggestive of atrial fibrillation (AF), often referred to as "Holiday Heart Syndrome" in this context.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In what proportion of cases is a complete vesicular mole found to be associated with Theca lutein cysts? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Between 20% and 30%

Theca lutein cysts are bilateral ovarian cysts caused by excessive ovarian stimulation from markedly elevated β-hCG levels. They are commonly associated with:

• Complete hydatidiform mole
• Multiple gestation
• Choriocarcinoma

In complete vesicular mole: Theca lutein cysts occur in approximately 20–30% of cases

Characteristics:

• Usually bilateral and multiloculated
• Caused by luteinization of theca interna cells
• Often regress spontaneously after evacuation of the mole and normalization of β-hCG levels
questions.learning: Between 20% and 30% — Theca lutein cysts are bilateral ovarian cysts caused by excessive ovarian stimulation from markedly elevated β-hCG levels. They are commonly associated with: • Complete hydatidiform mole • Multiple gestation • Choriocarcinoma In…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man diagnosed with Addison’s disease presents with typical features of adrenal hormone deficiency but also reports an unexpected rise in blood glucose levels. Considering the usual clinical presentation of Addison’s disease, which of the following features is not commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Addison’s disease, or primary adrenal insufficiency, results from the destruction of the adrenal cortex, leading to a deficiency in cortisol and aldosterone. Cortisol is a "stress hormone" that increases blood glucose; therefore, a deficiency characteristically leads to hypoglycemia rather than hyperglycemia. The aldosterone deficiency causes the kidneys to lose sodium and retain potassium, leading to the hallmark electrolyte abnormalities of hyponatremia (Option B) and hyperkalemia (Option C). Chronic mineralocorticoid deficiency also results in reduced blood volume and hypotension (Option D). The patient’s report of hyperglycemia is contradictory to the pathophysiology of the disease. Other common symptoms include skin hyperpigmentation (due to elevated ACTH) and profound fatigue. A diagnosis of Addison's is confirmed with a low morning cortisol level and a failure to respond to the ACTH stimulation test
questions.learning: Addison’s disease, or primary adrenal insufficiency, results from the destruction of the adrenal cortex, leading to a deficiency in cortisol and aldosterone.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department six hours after sustaining burns involving 22% of his body surface area. On examination, he has cool extremities, blood pressure of 92/50 mmHg, a pulse rate of 56 beats per minute, and a urine output of only 30 mL since the burn injury. What is the next appropriate step in management?
questions.explanation: This child is experiencing burn shock, characterized by hypotension, low urine output, and cool extremities. In pediatric patients, burns exceeding 15% BSA require urgent intravenous fluid resuscitation. Because the patient is already 6 hours post-injury with signs of significant dehydration, a bolus of 10 ml/kg of Ringer’s lactate is the appropriate next step to stabilize circulation. Colloid boluses (Option B) are contraindicated in the first 24 hours of a major burn because increased capillary permeability causes them to leak into tissues, worsening edema. Definitive surgical intervention (Option C) must wait until the patient is hemodynamically stable. A high-volume bolus of 30 ml/kg/hr (Option D) is dangerous in children as it can rapidly lead to pulmonary edema or abdominal compartment syndrome. Therefore, cautious resuscitation with a 10 ml/kg bolus followed by maintenance fluids is the gold standard
questions.learning: This child is experiencing burn shock, characterized by hypotension, low urine output, and cool extremities. In pediatric patients, burns exceeding 15% BSA require urgent intravenous fluid resuscitation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoxia

Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive to hypoxia.

Peripheral Chemoreceptors are located in the carotid bodies (at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries) and aortic bodies (near the aortic arch). They are sensitive to changes in pO2, pCO2, and pH of the blood. In response to changes in these parameters, they send impulses to the medullary respiratory centers and modify the duration and frequency of respiratory cycles.

Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive to a drop in partial pressure of oxygen (PaO₂) in arterial blood.

Mechanism:

Type I glomus cells in the carotid and aortic bodies have O2-sensitive K+ channels, which are inactivated in response to hypoxia. This reduces the K+ efflux, depolarizing the cell and causing Ca2+ inﬂux, via L-type voltage-gated calcium channels. The Ca2+ influx triggers action potentials and consequent excitation of the afferent nerve endings in the peripheral chemoreceptors.

Hypoxia (PaO₂ < 60 mmHg) strongly stimulates these receptors, leading to an increase in respiratory rate and depth to improve oxygenation.

Other Options:

Peripheral chemoreceptors also respond to hypercapnia (Option A) and acidosis (Option C). However, these are primarily detected by central chemoreceptors, located in the medulla, which monitor CO₂ levels in cerebrospinal fluid.

Alkalosis (Option D) causes a weaker response from peripheral chemoreceptors compared to hypoxia.
questions.learning: Hypoxia Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive to hypoxia. Peripheral Chemoreceptors are located in the carotid bodies (at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries) and aortic bodies (near the aortic arch).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Beta hCG is structurally similar to which biochemical moiety?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. LH

Beta hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) has biological activity similar to that of luteinizing hormone (LH).

hCG is a glycoprotein produced by syncytiotrophoblasts. It is made up of α and β subunits. Though the α subunit of hCG is similar to the α subunits of LH, FSH, and TSH, the β subunit has structural similarity to LH only. Hence, LH is a better answer than FSH.

hCG is primarily luteinizing and luteotrophic. It appears to act on the same receptor as that of LH. The function of hCG is to prevent regression of the corpus luteum. It can be detected in blood as early as 6 days after conception and forms the basis of various tests used to identify pregnancy.

Its level peaks at gestational week 9 and then declines gradually but is present in lower concentration till the end of pregnancy. But hCG is not specific for pregnancy as it is secreted in a variety of gastrointestinal and genital tumors in both males and females.
questions.learning: LH Beta hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) has biological activity similar to that of luteinizing hormone (LH). hCG is a glycoprotein produced by syncytiotrophoblasts.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with difficulty in left gaze; right gaze is normal, but on attempting left gaze, the right eye shows limited movement while the left eye exhibits nystagmus. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Right Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia

Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO) results from a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), which coordinates conjugate horizontal eye movements between the two eyes.

• On gaze toward the side opposite the lesion:

• Ipsilateral eye (to lesion) → impaired adduction
• Contralateral eye → abducting nystagmus

• Convergence is typically preserved (helps differentiate from 3rd nerve palsy)

In this question:

• Difficulty in left gaze
• Right eye fails to adduct + left eye shows nystagmus

→ Indicates right-sided MLF lesion → Right INO

Why not others:

• Thyroid eye disease: Restrictive myopathy, not abducting nystagmus pattern
• 3rd nerve palsy: Affects multiple movements + ptosis, pupil involvement
• Esotropia: Static deviation, not gaze-specific internuclear defect

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the initial indication of alcohol withdrawal?
questions.explanation: The clinical stages of alcohol withdrawal follow a predictable timeline after the cessation of chronic heavy drinking. The "initial indication" and most common symptom is "tremors" (Option A), which typically begins 6 to 12 hours after the last drink. This is often accompanied by anxiety, insomnia, and autonomic hyperactivity. Hallucinations (Option C), specifically alcoholic hallucinosis, usually occur between 12 and 48 hours. Withdrawal "seizures" (Option D) are also common in the first 24 to 48 hours. "Delirium Tremens" (Option B) is the most advanced stage and typically develops much later, between 48 and 96 hours af--------------ter the last drink. Identifying tremors early is critical for clinicians because it serves as an early warning to begin prophylaxis with benzodiazepines to prevent the progression to life-threatening seizures or DT. Effective management requires monitoring with the CIWA-Ar scale to titrate medication doses based on the severity of the patient’s symptoms
questions.learning: The clinical stages of alcohol withdrawal follow a predictable timeline after the cessation of chronic heavy drinking. The "initial indication" and most common symptom is "tremors" (Option A), which typically begins 6 to 12 hours after the last drink.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a dietary fiber?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gums

Gum is the best answer among the given options. Even though all of the given options are dietary fibers, the consumption of gums through diet is very low and hence, it is the best answer.

Dietary fibers consist of both soluble and insoluble forms and include lignin, pectin, inulin, cellulose, hemicellulose, etc.

Advantages of fibers:

• Forms bulk of the stool and reduces stool transit time
• Reduces incidence of carcinoma colon, DM, CAD, diverticulitis
questions.learning: Gums Gum is the best answer among the given options. Even though all of the given options are dietary fibers, the consumption of gums through diet is very low and hence, it is the best answer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A gasless abdomen is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute pancreatitis

A gasless abdomen is an X-ray feature that can be seen in acute pancreatitis. Patients with acute pancreatitis can have significant vomiting and diarrhea that may produce a gasless abdomen.

Common causes of gasless abdomen include:

• High obstruction: gastric outlet obstruction, congenital atresia
• Small bowel obstruction
• Bowel ischemia
• Ascites
• Acute pancreatitis
• Gastroenteritis
• Large abdominal mass - due to displacement
• Post-surgery following total colectomy, esophagogastrectomy, gastrectomy, and low anterior resection
• A paucity of small bowel gas may be a normal finding in some adults

Note: In intussusception, an X-ray shows small bowel obstruction, a mass, and a paucity of gas in the right iliac fossa.
questions.learning: Acute pancreatitis — A gasless abdomen is an X-ray feature that can be seen in acute pancreatitis. Patients with acute pancreatitis can have significant vomiting and diarrhea that may produce a gasless abdomen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 2-month-old male infant presents with a scrotal swelling that has been present since birth and is exacerbated by crying. The swelling has suddenly become painful, red, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Strangulated inguinal hernia

The clinical scenario of a 2-month-old male infant with a reducible scrotal swelling that is exacerbated by crying present since birth (congenital) and has become suddenly painful, red, and irreducible is most suggestive of a strangulated inguinal hernia. Infants are at high risk for incarceration of an inguinal hernia because of the narrow inguinal ring.

An inguinal hernia represents a protrusion of abdominal contents through a patent processus vaginalis into the inguinal canal and sometimes into the scrotum. It is a common indication for surgical repair in children. When a hernia becomes incarcerated and is not reducible, it can lead to strangulation of its contents.

Management of a strangulated inguinal hernia requires emergency surgical repair. It is usually performed by open inguinal repair, and a contralateral side evaluation may be considered. Laparoscopic approaches can also be used in certain cases. The repair of a patent processus vaginalis is emphasized to prevent recurrence.

Other options:

Option A: Epididymitis occurring before 6 months of age is usually due to infected urine ascending through the vas deferens. In contrast, epididymo-orchitis typically develops after puberty in sexually active boys and presents with acute testicular pain, fever, dysuria, increased frequency of urination, and urethral discharge. Pain may subside on elevation of the testis (Prehn’s sign).

Option B: Testicular torsion presents with acute scrotal pain associated with vomiting and absent cremasteric reflex.

Option D: A hydrocele refers to the accumulation of fluid between the parietal and visceral layers of the tunica vaginalis, usually limited to the scrotum. They are generally asymptomatic, non-tender, and may fluctuate in size, often decreasing overnight; they can also occur bilaterally. In infants, hydroceles may sometimes be tense and cause discomfort.

questions.text: Excess ammonia reduces which of the following substrates of the Krebs cycle?

questions.text: A patient presents with complaints of tingling sensation in hands and feet, generalised weakness, easy fatiguability, pallor, and ataxia. Deficiency of which vitamin causes these symptoms?

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A couple presents with infertility, and the husband’s semen analysis is normal. The wife reports menorrhagia, and her hysterosalpingography reveals distal fallopian tube dilatation with a characteristic “tobacco pouch” appearance. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis affecting the wife?
questions.explanation: The “tobacco pouch” appearance on hysterosalpingography refers to irregular, dilated distal fallopian tubes with outpouchings, which is classically associated with endometriosis involving the tubes. In tubal endometriosis, ectopic endometrial tissue causes cyclical bleeding, inflammation, and fibrosis, leading to distorted tubal architecture and infertility. The associated menorrhagia further supports endometriosis, as it commonly presents with abnormal uterine bleeding along with infertility. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Tubal salpingitis usually causes hydrosalpinx with smooth, sausage-shaped dilatation, not the irregular “tobacco pouch” appearance. (C) Tubal polyp is a localized lesion and does not produce diffuse distal dilatation or characteristic radiological patterns. (D) Tubal spasm is temporary and functional, seen during imaging due to muscular contraction, and does not cause persistent structural changes or infertility
questions.learning: The “tobacco pouch” appearance on hysterosalpingography refers to irregular, dilated distal fallopian tubes with outpouchings, which is classically associated with endometriosis involving the tubes.

questions.text: All are seen in Cystic fibrosis except:

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by CFTR gene mutation leading to thick, viscous secretions affecting multiple organs.

• Gastrointestinal: meconium ileus in neonates, pancreatic insufficiency causing malabsorption
• Respiratory: recurrent infections, bronchiectasis, nasal polyps
• Hepatobiliary: can cause biliary cirrhosis but not biliary atresia
• Hematological: fat-soluble vitamin (vitamin K) deficiency → bleeding tendency

Why biliary atresia is not seen:

• Biliary atresia is a separate obstructive condition of the extrahepatic bile ducts, not related to CFTR dysfunction (bile duct obstruction is seen in CF, not atresia)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 34-year-old man presents with a painless right groin lump extending into the scrotum. On examination, a cough impulse is noted when pressing with the index finger on the swelling, and the swelling can be fully reduced through the deep inguinal ring with an audible gurgling sound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical findings of a groin lump extending into the scrotum that is reducible through the deep inguinal ring definitively identifies an Indirect Inguinal Hernia . Indirect hernias enter the inguinal canal through the internal (deep) ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, and often follow the path of the spermatic cord into the scrotum. The "gurgling sound" noted during reduction is a classic sign indicating that the hernia sac contains loops of bowel. Direct inguinal hernias (Option B) occur through a weakness in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal (Hesselbach’s triangle) and do not typically enter the scrotum or reduce through the deep ring. Femoral hernias (Option A) are found below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and are more common in females. Umbilical hernias (Option D) occur at the navel. Because the defect is specifically associated with the deep inguinal ring and reaches the scrotum, indirect inguinal hernia is the correct anatomical diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical findings of a groin lump extending into the scrotum that is reducible through the deep inguinal ring definitively identifies an Indirect Inguinal Hernia .

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient who is a teacher by profession presents to the clinic with hoarseness of voice. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vocal nodule

This clinical scenario is suggestive of a vocal nodule.

Vocal nodules are also known as singer’s or screamer's nodes. It occurs at the mid-membranous portion of the vocal cords at the free edge. It is the area of maximum vibration of the cord and thus is subjected to maximum trauma. It presents as bilateral swellings in the vocal cords.

Vocal nodules occur due to vocal trauma when a person speaks in a loud voice for prolonged periods. They mostly affect teachers, actors, vendors, or pop singers.

Symptoms of vocal nodules are hoarseness, vocal fatigue, and pain in the neck on prolonged phonation.

Treatment includes educating the patient on proper use of voice. Surgery is reserved for patients who remain symptomatic despite voice therapy.

Option A: Vocal polyp is caused by sudden shouting which results in hemorrhage and edema of the vocal cord.Affected individuals present with hoarseness of voice and diplophonia(double voice). Other factors associated with it are allergy and cigarette smoking. It presents as a benign swelling on the free edge of the vocal cord.

Option B: Vocal cysts are retention cysts due to blockage of seromucinous glands of the laryngeal mucosa. They occur in the false vocal cords.

Option D: Reinke's edema is the collection of fluid in Reinke's space. Affected individuals present with diffuse swelling of the vocal cords. Treatment involves the removal of gelatinous collection by a longitudinal incision on the vocal cord.

Pearl PF0616: Muscles of larynx

Remember 2 exceptions:

* All muscles are adductors, except PCA (an abductor)

* All muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, except cricothyroid (superior laryngeal nerve)

Safety muscle of larynx: Posterior cricoarytenoid

Safety muscle of tongue: Genioglossus

Vocalis is known as the modulator of larynx because, the anterior part of the vocalis muscle can tense the vocal cord, and its posterior part can relax the vocal cord.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions exhibit the given radiological findings?
questions.explanation: The Chest X-ray demonstrates multiple, large, discrete, and well-circumscribed bilateral nodules, a classic finding known as "cannon-ball metastasis". This pattern is highly characteristic of Lung metastasis, most commonly originating from primary tumors such as renal cell carcinoma, testicular seminoma, or choriocarcinoma. Miliary TB (Option A) presents with numerous tiny (1–2 mm), millet-seed-like nodules distributed evenly throughout the lungs. Aspergillosis (Option B) usually presents as a mass within a pre-existing cavity or as areas of consolidation. Consolidation (Option C) appears as a more confluent, ill-defined area of opacity, often within a single lobe, rather than multiple discrete round masses. Cannon-ball metastases typically signify an advanced, disseminated malignancy. Identifying this specific radiological pattern is a high-yield clinical clue that directs the search for a primary malignancy elsewhere in the body
questions.learning: The Chest X-ray demonstrates multiple, large, discrete, and well-circumscribed bilateral nodules, a classic finding known as "cannon-ball metastasis".

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is most likely to show the following finding on USG?
options: Metastasis to the breast from another primary site
questions.explanation: The ultrasound image displays a classic Fibroadenoma. Its key benign sonographic features include a well-circumscribed margin, an oval shape, and a characteristic "wider than tall" orientation (horizontal diameter is greater than the vertical height). A breast cyst (Option B) would be completely "anechoic" (black) with posterior acoustic enhancement. Breast carcinoma (Option C) characteristically appears as an irregular, ill-defined mass that is often "taller than wide" with posterior acoustic shadowing. Metastasis (Option D) usually presents as multiple, discrete solid masses but is much rarer than a primary fibroadenoma. The "wider than tall" sign is a very reliable indicator of a benign lesion in breast imaging. In a young woman, such a finding on USG often precludes the need for biopsy unless the lesion is growing or atypical. Standard management for a classic fibroadenoma is clinical observation and reassurance
questions.learning: The ultrasound image displays a classic Fibroadenoma. Its key benign sonographic features include a well-circumscribed margin, an oval shape, and a characteristic "wider than tall" orientation (horizontal diameter is greater than the vertical height).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following methods is used to measure fetal anemia?
options: Peak systolic velocity in the fetal middle cerebral artery (MCA)
questions.explanation: The measurement of Peak Systolic Velocity in the fetal Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA-PSV) is the non-invasive gold standard for detecting fetal anemia. In anemic states, blood viscosity decreases, which leads to a compensatory increase in the velocity of blood flow through the MCA. This is measured using Doppler ultrasonography and compared to normative values. Umbilical artery Doppler (Option A) is primarily used to assess placental insufficiency rather than anemia. While cord blood sampling (Option B) can directly measure hemoglobin levels, it is highly invasive and carries significant procedural risks. Chorionic villus sampling (Option C) is utilized for genetic testing in the first trimester, not for evaluating anemia. Therefore, MCA-PSV is the preferred first-line screening tool for monitoring pregnancies at risk of Rh isoimmunization or other causes of fetal red cell depletion

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The time required for preoxygenation before tracheal intubation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 min

Preoxygenation with tidal volume breathing of 3 mins is required before tracheal intubation.

Preoxygenation or denitrogenation is the process of replacing nitrogen in the lungs with oxygen.

This delays the onset of critical hypoxia during the period of apnea by 5-8 minutes.

This lengthened apnea time provides an improved margin of safety while the anesthesiologist secures the airway and resumes ventilation.
questions.learning: 3 min Preoxygenation with tidal volume breathing of 3 mins is required before tracheal intubation. Preoxygenation or denitrogenation is the process of replacing nitrogen in the lungs with oxygen.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The given image is of a patient in whom mastoidectomy is done. Identify the lateral semi-circular canal:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B

The structure marked as ‘B’ in the given image represents the lateral (horizontal) semi-circular canal. The tympanic (horizontal) segment of the facial nerve lies below the lateral horizontal semicircular canal.

Other markings represent:

A: Superior semicircular canal (SSC)

C: Posterior semicircular canal (PSC)

D: Incus

The semicircular canals are positioned in the superior part of the mastoid region. These canals are situated adjacent to the middle ear, with the lateral semicircular canal being the nearest to the middle ear. The superior and posterior canals share a common crescent-shaped space in between. The one that lies in close proximity to the lateral semicircular canal is the posterior semicircular canal.

The semicircular canals are part of the bony labyrinth. They house the semicircular ducts which are the end organs for angular momentum. They are 3 semicircular canals, lateral (horizontal), superior (anterior), and posterior. They lie in planes at right angles to one another.

Stimulation of semicircular canals produces nystagmus. The nystagmus is rotatory from the superior canal, horizontal from the horizontal canal, and vertical from the posterior canal.
questions.learning: B The structure marked as ‘B’ in the given image represents the lateral (horizontal) semi-circular canal. The tympanic (horizontal) segment of the facial nerve lies below the lateral horizontal semicircular canal.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents to the outpatient department with low-grade fever, headache, and mild upper respiratory symptoms for the past four days. On examination, an erythematous rash is noted on the cheeks, which, according to the parents, appeared on the face first and then spread to the trunk and limbs. The causative agent of this disease is a single-stranded DNA virus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a "slapped-cheek" erythematous rash that spreads to the trunk in a "lace-like" pattern, following a mild febrile prodrome, is diagnostic for Erythema infectiosum (Fifth disease). The question confirms this by mentioning the causative agent is a single-stranded DNA virus, which is Parvovirus B19. Hand, foot, and mouth disease (Option A) involves painful vesicles on the palms, soles, and mouth. Measles (Option B) presents with high fever, Koplik spots, and a confluent rash that starts behind the ears. Rubella (Option D) involves a rapid-spreading rash and significant retroauricular lymphadenopathy. Parvovirus B19 is unique as the only SS-DNA virus significant in human disease. In children, it is a benign, self-limiting illness. However, it is clinically critical in patients with sickle cell disease (where it can cause an aplastic crisis) and in pregnant women (where it can cause hydrops fetalis)
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a "slapped-cheek" erythematous rash that spreads to the trunk in a "lace-like" pattern, following a mild febrile prodrome, is diagnostic for Erythema infectiosum (Fifth disease).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child presents to the OPD with a mild cold. On examination, he is found to have adenoid facies. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenoidectomy with coblation

Adenoid facies is a characteristic look seen in chronic adenoiditis. The treatment of choice in chronic adenoiditis is adenoidectomy with coblation.

Clinical features:

* Nasal obstruction is the most common symptom. This leads to mouth breathing. Nasal obstruction also interferes with feeding or suckling in a child. As respiration and feeding cannot take place simultaneously, a child with adenoid enlargement fails to thrive.

* Nasal discharge, sinusitis, and epistaxis.

* Bilateral conductive hearing loss and serous otitis media due to eustachian tube obstruction.

* Rhinolalia clausa - hyponasal voice.

* Adenoid facies - elongated face with a dull expression, pinched up nose, absent nasolabial crease, open mouth, prominent and crowded upper teeth.

* Sleep apnoea - chronic cases lead to hypoxemia and pulmonary vasoconstriction. This consequently leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

* Aprosexia - lack of concentration.

Management:

Definitive management is adenoidectomy. The treatment of choice is coblation adenoidectomy because it removes the tissue and prevents hemorrhage via radiofrequency ablation while curettage and microdebridement needs further cauterisation to control bleeding points. Older methods of classical adenoidectomy via mouth has been replaced by these newer techniques as the older methods were blind procedure
questions.learning: Adenoidectomy with coblation Adenoid facies is a characteristic look seen in chronic adenoiditis. The treatment of choice in chronic adenoiditis is adenoidectomy with coblation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Voriconazole is not effective against which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mucormycosis

Voriconazole is not effective against mucormycosis.

Mucormycosis is treated by amphotericin B. Posaconazole can also be used. However, other azoles are not effective against this fungus.

Voriconazole is the drug of choice for the treatment of aspergillosis. It can also be used for Candida species (including glabrata and krusei), Scedosporium and Fusarium.
questions.learning: Mucormycosis Voriconazole is not effective against mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is treated by amphotericin B.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following demographic indicators is used to compare the life expectancy of two different countries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HDI

The demographic indicator used to compare the life expectancy of two different countries is Human Development Index(HDI).

Human Development Index (HDI) is a measure of a country's average achievements in three dimensions of human development. The components include:

* A long and healthy life, as measured by life expectancy at birth

* Knowledge (literacy), as measured by mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling, and

* A decent standard of living, as measured by GNI (gross national income) per capita.

HDI values range from 0 to 1, with 1 as the maximum value.

Life expectancy at 1 year, literacy and infant mortality rate are components of the Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI).
questions.learning: HDI — The demographic indicator used to compare the life expectancy of two different countries is Human Development Index(HDI). Human Development Index (HDI) is a measure of a country's average achievements in three dimensions of human development.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Arrange the following fibers of the internal capsule in order from posterior to anterior: 1. Frontopontine fibers 2. Corticonuclear tract 3. Corticospinal tract 4. Sublentiform fibres
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 4 → 3 → 2 → 1

The internal capsule is organized from anterior to posterior as follows:

• Anterior limb → Frontopontine fibers
• Genu → Corticonuclear fibers
• Posterior limb → Corticospinal fibers
• Retrolenticular part → Occipitopontine fibers

Reversing this order gives posterior → anterior:

Occipitopontine → Corticospinal → Corticonuclear → Frontopontine

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A trainee surgeon is performing his/her first cholecystectomy. The area marked with an asterisk in the diagram represents:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Calot’s triangle

The asterisk marks the Calot’s triangle (hepatocystic triangle), an important anatomical landmark during cholecystectomy.

It is bounded by:

• Cystic duct
• Common hepatic duct
• Inferior surface of the liver

The cystic artery is usually found within this triangle, making identification of the triangle crucial to avoid bile duct and vascular injuries during cholecystectomy.

Why not the other options?

• (a) Rouviere’s area: A landmark on the posterior aspect of the liver used to identify the plane of the common bile duct during laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
• (b) Bismuth’s triangle: Not the anatomical triangle shown here.
• (c) Calot’s triangle — Correct: Important surgical landmark containing the cystic artery.
• (d) Area of Lund: Another term associated with the region of the cystic artery/Calot’s triangle, but not the specific triangle indicated.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A chronic smoker presents with bilateral pitting pedal edema and abdominal distension. Examination reveals ascites and the presence of an S3 gallop on cardiac auscultation. What underlying abnormalities or defects are most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a chronic smoker with bilateral pitting pedal edema, abdominal distension, and ascites indicates significant "right-sided heart failure." In chronic smokers, this is often "cor pulmonale"—right heart failure secondary to chronic lung disease (like COPD). The presence of an S3 gallop reflects a volume-overloaded state in the ventricle. In the context of right heart failure and chronic lung disease, the most common valvular defect observed is Tricuspid Regurgitation (TR). As the right ventricle dilates from high pulmonary pressures, the tricuspid valve annulus also stretches, preventing the leaflets from closing properly. This backflow of blood into the right atrium and then the systemic venous system causes the elevated JVP, hepatomegaly (ascites), and peripheral edema seen here. Aortic (Option A, C) and Mitral (Option D) defects involve the "left" side of the heart and would more likely present with pulmonary edema (crackles) before systemic venous congestion. Thus, tricuspid regurgitation is the classic valvular association for this clinical picture

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman presents to you with fever, arthralgia, ulcers, fatigue for the past six months, and new-onset hematuria. Urine examination reveals RBC casts and proteinuria. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lupus nephritis

The above clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of lupus nephritis.

Lupus nephritis is a common complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). It results from immune complex deposition containing DNA and anti-DNA. Clinical features include proteinuria, hematuria, and hypertension. The disease is divided into 6 classes based on the severity. Patients with class V disease are at an increased risk of thrombotic complications. Lupus nephritis can result in end-stage disease warranting dialysis or transplantation.

SLE is an autoimmune condition more commonly seen in women. Antinuclear antibodies, anti-dsDNA, and anti-Sm are the autoantibodies implicated. Symptoms include maculopapular butterfly rash, photosensitivity, oral or nasal ulcers, fever, and intermittent polyarthritis. Pleuritis and pericarditis can also be associated. Systemic glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, or mycophenolate mofetil are used for management. Due to the possible teratogenic effects of these drugs, hydroxychloroquine is the mainstay in pregnancy.

Other options:

Option A - Acute interstitial nephritis is a type of acute kidney injury. It is marked by oliguria and raised creatinine. Various causes of interstitial injury include the use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), pyelonephritis, leukemia, and sepsis. White blood cell (WBC) casts and granular casts may be seen.

Option B - Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis usually affects male children between the age of 2-14. Skin or pharyngeal infection with M types of the organism is implicated. Symptoms include hematuria, pyuria, and hypertension. Flank pain and headache are also associated symptoms. Red blood cell (RBC) casts are seen in the urine.

Option D - IgA nephropathy arises due to mesangial IgA deposition. It is characterized by recurrent macroscopic hematuria after an upper respiratory infection associated with proteinuria. Mesangial proliferation is a distinctive feature. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and steroids can be used for management.
questions.learning: Lupus nephritis — The above clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of lupus nephritis. Lupus nephritis is a common complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with vertigo, tinnitus, and head tilt. He underwent myringoplasty for the safe type of chronic suppurative otitis media(CSOM) 6 months back. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Peri-lymphatic fistula

The presentation of vertigo, tinnitus, and head tilt following myringoplasty suggests a diagnosis of perilymphatic fistula.

A perilymphatic fistula is an abnormal connection between the inner ear and middle ear, resulting in leakage of perilymph from the cochlea or vestibule. This most commonly occurs through the round or oval window.

Causes of perilymphatic fistula include post-stapedectomy, ear surgery with dislocation of the stapes, head trauma, inner ear injury due to forceful Valsalva or barotrauma, raised intracranial pressure, and occasionally spontaneous or idiopathic.

Clinically, intermittent vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and a sense of fullness in the affected ear are present. The fistula test is positive, and high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the temporal bone is highly sensitive for detecting the fistula. A combination of CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can diagnose almost all cases. Audiometry and electrocochleography may be performed additionally.

Management of perilymphatic fistula can be conservative or surgical. Conservative measures involve avoiding activities that increase inner ear or intracranial pressure and using intra-tympanic steroids for acute decompensation.

Other options:

Option B: Labyrinthitis presents with unilateral vestibular symptoms like sudden onset of persistent vertigo with associated symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, sweating, and pallor. Symptoms may progress resulting in nystagmus and hearing loss. Tinnitus is not a common finding in labyrinthitis.

Option C: Paget's disease of bone usually presents with hearing loss as a prominent feature, when the skull is involved. It is not associated with a history of surgery, trauma, or vestibulocochlear symptoms.

Option D: Vestibular Schwannoma (acoustic neuroma), originates from Schwann cells in the vestibular division of the vestibulocochlear (VIIIth cranial) nerve within the internal auditory canal. The main symptoms are progressive unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus. Other cranial nerves (V, IX, X, XI) may also be involved.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the structure marked in the diagram showing the development of ovarian follicles.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Antral follicle

The structure marked in the image is of a secondary follicle, also called an antral follicle.

Development of ovarian follicles:

At birth, the ovarian cortex contains numerous primordial follicles which contain primary oocytes surrounded by a single layer of flat follicular cells. Most of these follicles degenerate in the prepubertal life and are called atretic follicles. At puberty, around 20 primordial follicles get activated in each menstrual cycle. Out of these 20 primordial follicles, only one follicle is dominant which reaches maturity and releases the oocyte during ovulation.

The different stages of development of the primordial follicle are:

a) Primary follicle:

* Follicle cells change from flattened cells to cuboidal and the stromal cells surrounding the follicle differentiate into spindle-shaped cells called 'theca externa'.

* The oocyte increases in size and secretes a proteoglycan material around it which forms the layer called 'Zona Pellucida' which is seen between the plasma membrane of the oocyte and the granulosa cells.

b)Secondary follicle(Antral follicle):

* The primary follicles continue to increase in size and the granulosa cells multiply.

* Numerous cavities coalesce to form a single fluid space called antrum.

* The granulosa cells envelop the oocyte to form a structure called Cumulus oophorus.

c) Tertiary follicle (Graffian follicle):

* Numerous secondary follicles are formed but only one tertiary follicle develops while others regress and become atretic follicles.

* As the antrum draws the fhe follicle increase in size and expands to a diameter of 2 cm to become Graffian follicle.

* The oocyte and the surrounding granulosa cells called corona radiata break away from the follicular wall and float in the follicular fluid.

* The primary oocyte completes its first meiotic division to form the secondary oocyte and a polar body.

* The secondary oocyte is arrested in the metaphase of the second meiotic division until fertilization takes place.

* The follicle ruptures to release the oocyte which is captured by for the fimbriae.

d) Corpus Luteum:

* The remainder of the follicle after ovulation is called the Corpus luteum. It synthesizes a carotenoid pigment called lutein which gives it a yellowish colour.

* If the oocyte is not fertilized then corpus luteum degenerates 12-14 days after ovulation to become corpus albicans.

* If fertilization occurs then the hCG produced by the trophoblast maintains the corpus luteum. It releases progesterone, estrogen, and relaxin, and regresses at around 8 weeks when the placenta takes over.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which intracellular organelle is mainly responsible for breaking down and eliminating bacteria and viruses within the cell?
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are the "digestive system" of the cell. They are specialized membrane-bound organelles containing a diverse array of over 40 acidic hydrolases (enzymes) capable of breaking down almost all types of biological polymers. Their primary role in host defense is the degradation and elimination of bacteria and viruses that have been internalized through phagocytosis or endocytosis. Peroxisomes (Option A) are involved in lipid metabolism and the neutralization of reactive oxygen species like hydrogen peroxide. The Golgi complex (Option C) is responsible for the modification and packaging of proteins. Ribosomes (Option D) are the sites of protein synthesis. Because lysosomes provide the acidic environment and potent enzymes necessary to dismantle and destroy foreign pathogens, they are the organelle definitively responsible for cellular waste elimination and microbial killing
questions.learning: Lysosomes are the "digestive system" of the cell. They are specialized membrane-bound organelles containing a diverse array of over 40 acidic hydrolases (enzymes) capable of breaking down almost all types of biological polymers.

questions.text:
Which of the following are vitamin-B12 dependent enzymes?

1. Methyl malonyl CoA isomerase
2. Homocysteine synthase
3. Folate reductase
4. Methionine synthase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 4 only

Among the given enzymes, methyl malonyl CoA isomerase and methionine synthase are vitamin B12 dependent enzymes.

There are two vitamin B12-dependent enzymes:

• Methionine synthase (homocysteine methyltransferase): Catalyzes the conversion of homocysteine to methionine
• Methylmalonyl CoA mutase: methylmalonyl CoA, formed as an intermediate in the catabolism of valine, isoleucine, and propionyl CoA is converted to succinyl CoA

The below figure shows B12 serving as a cofactor of methionine synthase. Its deficiency may cause a folate trap.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient exhibits an abnormal gait in which the legs cross over each other while walking, producing a characteristic scissoring pattern. This finding suggests increased muscle tone due to excessive neural activity. Hyperactivity of which nerve is most likely responsible for this scissoring gait?
questions.explanation: A "scissoring gait" is caused by excessive adduction of the thighs, leading to the legs crossing over each other during ambulation. This is primarily driven by hyperactivity or spasticity of the hip adductor muscles, which are innervated by the obturator nerve. This gait pattern is commonly seen in patients with upper motor neuron lesions, such as those with cerebral palsy. The superior gluteal nerve (Option A) innervates the gluteus medius and minimus; its weakness causes a Trendelenburg gait. The inferior gluteal nerve (Option B) supplies the gluteus maximus, and its dysfunction leads to difficulty in standing up or climbing stairs. The femoral nerve (Option D) supplies the quadriceps, primarily facilitating knee extension. Because the scissoring movement is a direct result of overactive adduction, the obturator nerve's role in supplying the adductor longus, brevis, and magnus makes it the correct choice

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Match the following conditions :

1) Glycogen accumulation in liver and renal cells and lactic acidemia, associated with hypoglycemia
a)Cori disease

2) Glycogen accumulation in lysosomes
b)McArdle disease

3) Exercise intolerance
c)Von Gierk disease

4) Accumulation of branched structures
d)Pompe disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 -c, 2 -d, 3 -b, 4 -a

The correct answer is option B: 1 -c, 2 -d, 3 -b, 4 -a

1) Glycogen accumulation in liver and renal cells and lactic acidemia, associated with hypoglycemia
c) Von Gierk disease

2) Glycogen accumulation in lysosomes
d)Pompe disease

3) Exercise intolerance
b)McArdle disease

4) Accumulation of branched structures
a)Cori disease

Von Gierke disease (type I glycogen storage disorder) occurs due to the deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase enzyme in the liver, kidney, and intestinal mucosa. Patients present commonly by 3-4 months of age with hypoglycemia (leading to seizures), lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly. Affected children often have a doll-like face with fat cheeks, relatively thin extremities, short stature, and a protuberant abdomen due to massive hepatomegaly. The kidneys are also enlarged, whereas spleen and heart are not involved. Laboratory findings include hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia.

Pompe's disease (type II glycogen storage disorder) occurs due to a mutation in alpha-1,4-glucosidase (also known as acid maltase), a lysosomal enzyme. A defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of glycogen in the lysosomes of peripheral, voluntary muscles and progresses to involve the cardiac muscle and diaphragm. Clinical features include hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome), cardiomyopathy, hepatomegaly, and failure to thrive. Myozyme can prevent worsening or can reverse cardiac and skeletal abnormalities.

Cori disease (type III glycogen storage disorder) occurs due to a deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme. The features of Cori disease include hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and hyperlipidemia but with normal blood lactate and uric acid levels. Muscle weakness and atrophy can also occur in these patients. Liver biopsy shows the accumulation of glycogen in the form of limit-dextrins (branched structures).

McArdle disease (type V glycogen storage disorder) typically presents during late childhood or in the second decade of life. The muscle glycogen phosphorylase enzyme deficiency interferes with ATP generation by glycogenolysis in the muscles. This causes muscle glycogen accumulation. Symptoms are exercise intolerance associated with muscle cramps. This leads to severe muscle damage resulting in a massive release of myoglobin in the blood.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is seen in methanol intoxication?
options: Metabolic alkalosis with high anion gap
Metabolic acidosis with high anion gap
Metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap
Metabolic alkalosis with normal anion gap
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Metabolic acidosis with high anion gap

Methanol intoxication is characterized by metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap.

Methanol is metabolized in the body as follows:

Methanol -Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH)→ Formaldehyde -Aldehyde Dehydrogenase→ Formic acid

Formic acid is an unmeasured anion causing a high-anion gap and metabolic acidosis. It accumulates in the CNS and retina and causes blurring vision/loss of vision.

Other causes of high-anion gap metabolic acidosis:

• Lactic acidosis
• Ketoacidosis: alcohol, starvation, diabetes
• Toxins: Ethylene glycol, methanol, salicylate
• Renal failure (acute and chronic)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient is brought to the emergency department with clinical features suggestive of opioid poisoning. What is the antidote of choice in this situation?
questions.explanation: Opioid poisoning classically presents with a triad of unconsciousness, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils (miosis). The definitive antidote of choice is Naloxone. Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist that rapidly displaces opioids from their receptors, reversing the life-threatening respiratory depression within minutes of intravenous administration. Flumazenil (Option A) is the specific antagonist for benzodiazepine overdose, not opioids. Atropine (Option B) is an anticholinergic used for organophosphate poisoning or bradycardia. Physostigmine (Option D) is used for reversing anticholinergic toxicity, such as an atropine overdose. Because Naloxone specifically and rapidly targets the opioid pathway, it is the mandated intervention in any suspected narcotic overdose emergency

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Macula densa is formed by which part of the nephron?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DCT

Macula densa is formed by specialized tubular epithelial cells of the distal convoluted tubule.

The juxtaglomerular apparatus consists of the following parts:

• Macula densa: At the end of the thick ascending limb of Henle, and at the beginning of the distal tubule, the tubular epithelial cells are specialized to form the macula densa. They detect sodium concentration of the fluid in the tubule (chemoreceptor). In response to elevated sodium, the macula densa cells trigger the contraction of the afferent arteriole, reducing the flow of blood to the glomerulus and the glomerular filtration rate. This happens as follows: When there is increased sodium, there is increased sodium-potassium ATPase activity which leads to increased ATP hydrolysis causing more adenosine formation. The adenosine receptors on the macula densa cells stimulate it to release more calcium, so that there is vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole, thereby decreasing the GFR.
• Lacis cells: Extraglomerular mesangial cells situated between afferent and efferent arteriole.
• Granular cells/JG cells: Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole, they secrete renin. Fall in pressure in afferent arteriole stimulates renin release (mechanoreceptor), which, in turn, increases blood pressure.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Mrs. M is a poor, migrant worker who has recently moved into a village along with her husband to work in the local brick kiln. The ASHA of that particular village visits her and comes to know that she has missed her last period. The last menstrual period (LMP) was on 6th January, while the ASHA visited her on 4th March of the same year. The lady has never delivered a child or had an abortion earlier. The ASHA talks to her and finds out that her age is 28 years, and measures that her height is 144 cm and weight is 52 kg. A blood test was performed and her haemoglobin was found to be 11.6 g/dL. From the data given in the case scenario, consider if the lady’s pregnancy would fall under a “high-risk” pregnancy on account of: 1. Her age 2. Her height and parity 3. Her haemoglobin level Mrs. M’s pregnancy qualifies as a “high-risk” pregnancy under which of the above parameters?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

Consider the risk factors given in the case:

1. Age: Not a high-risk factor

• She is 28 years old.
• High-risk age groups are generally <18 years or ≥35 years.

2. Height and parity: High-risk → Correct

• Her height is 144 cm, which is below the commonly used high-risk cutoff of 145 cm.
• She is primigravida (G1P0). In this programme-based context, her short stature is the relevant high-risk criterion.

3. Hemoglobin: Not a high-risk factor in this case

• Hb = 11.6 g/dL, which is not anemia by the pregnancy cutoff of <11 g/dL.

Therefore, the pregnancy qualifies as high risk under parameter 2 → B.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Chloride level in sweat is used in the diagnosis of which disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystic fibrosis

The chloride level of sweat, known as the sweat test, is used to diagnose cystic fibrosis (CF). A sweat chloride level of >60 mmol/L is diagnostic of CF.

CF is an autosomal recessive disorder with a mutation in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (CFTR) gene on chromosome 7q.

The below image depicts the organs affected by CF:

Diagnostic tests include:
1. Immunoreactive trypsinogen for newborn screening of cystic fibrosis.
2. Sweat chloride test: Increased chloride concentration >60 mmol/L is diagnostic.
3. Genetic testing for CFTR gene mutations is the gold standard and should be done for all cases.
4. Nasal transepithelial potential difference can be estimated in equivocal cases.

Diagnostic criteria:
Presence of

• Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or
• Positive newborn screening or
• A sibling with cystic fibrosis.

Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by

• Two positive sweat chloride test results obtained on separate days or
• Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or
• An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference.

Other options:

Option A: Phenylketonuria occurs due to the deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, leading to elevated phenylalanine levels. Diagnosis is confirmed by measuring plasma phenylalanine concentration.

Option C: Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency of β-glucosidase. Diagnosis is confirmed by fibroblast/leukocyte β-glucosidase activity and gene mutations.

Option D: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a genetic connective tissue disorder due to defective type-1 collagen. DNA sequencing is the first diagnostic test.
questions.learning: Cystic fibrosis — The chloride level of sweat, known as the sweat test, is used to diagnose cystic fibrosis (CF). A sweat chloride level of >60 mmol/L is diagnostic of CF.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old man who was accused of murder was taken into police custody. As a part of the interrogation, the prisoner was kept in a prone position with both his wrists and ankles bound behind his back and secured with a rope. What is this method known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hog tie

This type of physical restraint in which a person is placed in prone position with his wrists and ankles bound behind his back and secured by a rope is known as hog-tying or total appendage restraint procedure. This can cause breathing difficulty and the person can become unresponsive. Rarely, death may occur due to asphyxia, soon following the physical restraint.

Carotid hold also known as choke hold or bar arm involves placing the forearm straight across the front of the neck. The free hand grips the wrist and pulls it back causing obstruction of the airway and carotids resulting in immediate unconsciousness. Fracture of the hyoid or larynx can occur with greater force. Pressure on the carotid bodies can cause sudden cardiac arrest.

In carotid sleeper hold, also known as lateral vascular neck restraint, the arm is placed about the neck with the antecubital fossa centered at the midline of the neck. The free hand grips the wrist and the arm is pulled backward, compressing carotid arteries and jugular veins but not vertebral arteries or trachea. The person loses consciousness in 10 to 15 seconds and regains consciousness within 10 to 20 seconds upon releasing the pressure. Here, the neck structures are not damaged. Death may rarely occur due to catecholamine release or hypoxia which can trigger myocardial infarction or dysrhythmias in patients with ischemic heart disease.
questions.learning: Hog tie — This type of physical restraint in which a person is placed in prone position with his wrists and ankles bound behind his back and secured by a rope is known as hog-tying or total appendage restraint procedure.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The railway police has brought a person with suspected poisoning. On examination, he was confused with slurred speech, hot skin, dry mouth, and dilated pupils. What is the probable poisoning?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Datura

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Datura poisoning.

Datura has two main types: Datura alba with white flowers and Datura nigra with purple flowers. The fruit is spiny and contains many small, yellowish-brown seeds. All parts of the plant are toxic, especially the seeds and fruits. Datura contains alkaloids like atropine, hyoscyamine, and scopolamine, which are potent anticholinergic agents. They block muscarinic receptors both peripherally and centrally, resulting in the classical anticholinergic toxidrome.

This typical presentation is seen in children who accidentally ingest datura seeds, especially from roadside or railway plants, where datura often grows wild—hence known as "railway poison". Signs of poisoning include 8 D's:

* Dryness of mouth

* Dysphagia

* Dilated pupils

* Drunken gait

* Delirium

* Dry-hot skin

* Drowsiness

* Death due to respiratory failure.

Gastric emptying is often delayed, and the small, plentiful seeds can become trapped among the gastrointestinal folds after ingestion. Thus gastric decontamination can be an important therapy.

Physostigmine, a reversible acetylcholine esterase antagonist, is an effective treatment for severe anticholinergic poisoning.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the respiratory burst in neutrophils?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NADPH oxidase

The deficiency of NADPH oxidase is responsible for the respiratory burst in neutrophils.

NADPH + 2O2 → NADP+ + 2·O2− + 2H+

NADPH oxidase in the inflammatory cells (neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes, and macrophages) produces superoxide anion by reducing oxygen by a process of respiratory burst during phagocytosis.

There are multiple sources of oxygen radicals in the body:

* Ionizing radiation (x-rays and UV) causes lysis of water, leading to the formation of hydroxyl radicals.

* Transition metal ions (Cu+, Co2+, Ni2+, and Fe2+) can react nonenzymatically with oxygen or hydrogen peroxide to form hydroxyl radicals.

* Nitric oxide can react with superoxide to yield peroxynitrite, which decays to form hydroxyl radicals.

* NADPH oxidase in the inflammatory cells produces superoxide radicals.

Other options:

Options A: Catalase is involved in protecting cells from oxidative damage by removing hydrogen peroxide, it is not involved in the generation of reactive oxygen species during the respiratory burst.

Option C: Defensin is an anti-bacterial compound that plays a role in the defense mechanism of the cell.

Option D: Myeloperoxidase is an enzyme found in the granules of neutrophils that uses hydrogen peroxide to produce more potent antimicrobial agents.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents with jaundice characterized by conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and intrahepatic cholestasis. Liver biopsy reveals eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The laboratory finding of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is never physiological (Option D) and always requires investigation. The definitive diagnostic clue in this case is the liver biopsy finding: eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules. These granules are characteristic of Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (A1AT) Deficiency, which is a leading cause of genetic neonatal hepatitis (Option B). The granules represent misfolded A1AT protein accumulated within hepatocytes. Hypoplasia of the biliary tract (Option A) and Choledochal cysts (Option C) are structural causes of cholestasis but would not show these specific intracellular PAS-positive granules. Neonatal hepatitis can eventually lead to cirrhosis and liver failure. Diagnosis is confirmed by serum A1AT levels and protease inhibitor (Pi) phenotyping. Therefore, given the pathognomonic histological evidence of A1AT protein accumulation, neonatal hepatitis is the correct clinical diagnosis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following minerals help with stabilization of insulin secretion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zinc

Among the options provided, Zinc is best known for its role in the stabilization of insulin secretion.

Zinc is an essential trace element that plays a crucial role in various physiological processes, including insulin metabolism and secretion.

It is involved in the synthesis, storage, and secretion of insulin by pancreatic beta cells. Zinc acts as a cofactor for enzymes involved in insulin processing and storage within the beta cells.

Deficiency of zinc can lead to impaired insulin synthesis and secretion, which may contribute to metabolic disturbances seen in conditions like diabetes.

Other options:

* Copper is involved in the formation of enzymes called cuproenzymes, including ceruloplasmin, which plays a role in iron metabolism and antioxidant defense.

* Cadmium is a toxic heavy metal and is not known to have any beneficial role in the body, including insulin regulation.

* Iron is crucial for the formation of hemoglobin, which is responsible for transporting oxygen in the blood. It plays a role in overall metabolic processes and energy production within the body. Excess iron levels in the body can be harmful and are associated with various health conditions, including insulin resistance.

questions.text: A man met with a road traffic accident, which resulted in paralysis of both his upper and lower limbs. He has not passed urine and tenderness is elicited in the cervical region. What will you advise regarding radiography?

Management in a trauma patient with a suspected cervical fracture involves the following steps:

1. Spinal immobilization with a rigid cervical collar and a long spine board is the immediate step in the management of blunt/penetrating cervical trauma cases.
2. It is followed by a gross assessment of spinal cord function by eliciting extremity movement. Tenderness over the injured vertebrae or the presence of a deformity is indicative of an associated fracture.
3. Imaging is done by X-ray or CT. Portable X-ray machines are preferred to avoid further injury while mobilizing the patient. They are useful in visualizing thoracic and lumbar vertebrae but not the cervicothoracic junction. Cervical CT has been made the modality of choice in most emergency departments owing to the high quality of images that can be obtained.

questions.text: Which of the following is false about the given condition?
options: Repeated radical surgery every 24 hours may be required to adequately manage this condition

The condition is caused by beta hemolytic streptococcus and may sometimes be polymicrobial

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hyperbaric oxygen has no role in the treatment of this condition

The given image is likely that of Meleney's gangrene. Hyperbaric oxygen has been shown to reduce mortality in patients with Meleney's gangrene and therefore plays a significant role in the management of this condition.

Necrotizing fasciitis of the abdominal wall is known as Meleney's gangrene. It presents with extensive necrosis of the abdominal wall, thrombosis of the microvasculature, and an acute inflammatory infiltrate. Bullae develop on the abdominal wall, which progress to overt cutaneous gangrene. The affected area is often painful, erythematous, and edematous, with possible systemic signs of infection such as fever and malaise. Early recognition and aggressive treatment are essential for a favorable outcome.

Management includes prompt surgical debridement of the necrotic tissue, broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover the polymicrobial nature of the infection, and supportive measures such as fluid resuscitation and correction of electrolyte imbalances. In some cases, hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be utilized as an adjunctive treatment to improve tissue oxygenation and enhance the healing process.

Other options:

Option A: Surgical excision of necrotic tissue is often required daily as the infection tends to spread beyond the borders of the debridement wound.

Option C: Meleney's gangrene is caused by beta-hemolytic streptococci or Staphylococcus aureus and may also be polymicrobial.
