questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which statement correctly characterizes a single-exposure point-source epidemic?
options: Has more than one incubation period
questions.explanation: A single exposure point source epidemic occurs when a large group of susceptible individuals is exposed to a single common source (like contaminated food at a party) at a specific point in time. The characteristic feature of this type of epidemic is that it is explosive in nature, meaning there is a rapid rise in the number of cases followed by a relatively quick decline. All cases typically occur within a single incubation period (making Option A incorrect). The resulting epidemic curve characteristically has a single peak (Option B is incorrect). A slow rise and fall (Option D) is characteristic of a propagated epidemic, where the disease spreads slowly from person to person. Identifying an epidemic as "point source" is vital for outbreak investigations, as it directs health officials to search for a localized, time-limited source of contamination. The explosive nature of such outbreaks often overwhelms local healthcare facilities rapidly, requiring an immediate and intensive public health response
questions.learning: A single exposure point source epidemic occurs when a large group of susceptible individuals is exposed to a single common source (like contaminated food at a party) at a specific point in time.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Calculate the percentage of burns in a preschool child shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 25-30%

From the given image, the percentage of burns in the child is 25-30% calculated based on Lund and Browder chart.

In the given image, the right arm, chest, abdomen, and both thighs are involved in burns. According to Lund and Browder chart, 2% is for the right arm, 13% for chest and abdomen involvement, and 4% for each thigh. Hence, the total involvement is 2+13+4+4 = 23%. The closest value to 23% among the given options is 25-30% (option B).

Lund and Browder chart is an accurate method to measure burns if it is used correctly. In this, different proportions of body surface areas in children are taken into consideration. This chart compensates for the changes in the shape of the body with age and can accurately assess the burns area in children.

The below image shows the Lund and Browder chart.

Note: Wallace's rule of nines is used in estimating medium to large burns in adults. It helps in the quick estimation of the burns. In this, the total burn is calculated by dividing the body into areas of 9%. It is not accurate in children.
questions.learning: 25-30% From the given image, the percentage of burns in the child is 25-30% calculated based on Lund and Browder chart. In the given image, the right arm, chest, abdomen, and both thighs are involved in burns.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which is the most potent naturally occurring estrogen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Estradiol

Estradiol is the most potent naturally occurring estrogen.

Classic estrogens are C18 steroid compounds containing a phenolic ring. Only three estrogens are present in significant quantities in the plasma of the human female—β-estradiol, estrone, and estriol.

The principal estrogen secreted by the ovaries is β-estradiol.

Small amounts of estrone are also secreted, but most of this is formed in peripheral tissues from androgens secreted by the adrenal cortices and by ovarian thecal cells.

Estriol is a weak estrogen; it is an oxidative product derived from both estradiol and estrone, with the conversion occurring mainly in the liver.

The estrogenic potency of β-estradiol is 12 times that of estrone and 80 times that of estriol. Hence, estradiol is the most potent natural form of estrogen.

In the liver, estradiol, estrone, and estriol are converted to inactive glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. All these compounds, along with other metabolites, are excreted in the urine.
questions.learning: Estradiol Estradiol is the most potent naturally occurring estrogen. Classic estrogens are C18 steroid compounds containing a phenolic ring.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: All of the following are features of fragile X syndrome except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Micro-orchidism

Macro-orchidism (large testicles) are seen in fragile X syndrome, not micro-orchidism.

Fragile X syndrome is the second most common genetic cause of mental retardation (Down syndrome being the most common). It is caused by a trinucleotide mutation, characterised by multiple tandem repeats of the CGG sequence in the familial mental retardation-1 (FMR1) gene. It is associated with the phenomenon of anticipation, where the disease phenotype worsens over generations within a family.

The affected males are mentally retarded, with an IQ in the range of 20 to 60.

The characteristic phenotypic features include the following:

• Long face with a large mandible
• Large everted ears
• Macro-orchidism
• Hyperextensible joints
• High arched palate
• Mitral valve prolapse

The given image shows a child suffering from fragile X syndrome.
questions.learning: Micro-orchidism Macro-orchidism (large testicles) are seen in fragile X syndrome, not micro-orchidism. Fragile X syndrome is the second most common genetic cause of mental retardation (Down syndrome being the most common).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
As per the verbal autopsy report 2010-2013, arrange the most common cause of death among 1-4-year-old children in descending order:

1. Diarrhea
2. Pneumonia
3. Malaria
4. Injuries
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 > 1 > 4 > 3

According to the verbal autopsy report of 2010-2013, the most common cause of death among 1-4 year old children in descending order is Pneumonia > Diarrhea > Injuries > Malaria.

According to the Verbal autopsy report 2010-2013, the top 5 causes of death among children aged 1-4 years are:

1. Pneumonia
2. Diarrheal diseases
3. Injuries
4. Other non-communicable diseases
5. Malaria

1-4 year mortality rate also known as the child death rate is the number of deaths of children aged 1-4 years per 1000 children in the same age group in a given year. It thus excludes infant mortality. It is given by the formula,

1-4 year mortality rate (child death rate) = (no. of deaths of children aged 1-4 years during a year x 1000) / Total no. of children aged 1-4 years at the middle of the year.

It is a more refined indicator of the social situation than the infant mortality rate as it reflects adverse environmental health hazards like malnutrition, poor hygiene, infections, and accidents. It is not affected by perinatal hazards. In the 1-4 year group, second year is the period with the highest risk of death (mainly due to childhood infections like measles, whooping cough, diphtheria, diarrhea, and ARI), after which the rates decline progressively.
questions.learning: 2 > 1 > 4 > 3 According to the verbal autopsy report of 2010-2013, the most common cause of death among 1-4 year old children in descending order is Pneumonia > Diarrhea > Injuries > Malaria.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the ions A and B based on conductance graph of a neuron shown below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Na, K

Channel A: Na+, Channel B: K+

Na+ channels are fast activating and are responsible for depolarization phase of action potential.

K+ channels are slow activating and open for prolonged duration than the sodium channels. They are responsible for repolarization phase of action potential. Also, the postassium channels return slowly to their closed state, which is responsible for after-hyperpolarization.

The sequence of events during the action potential occur in 7 steps as described below.

1. Resting state - Both channels are closed

2. Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus. Sodium enters into the cell. The membrane reaches threshold potential.

3. The sodium influx causes opening of more sodium channels through positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs.

4. Sodium conductance decreases.

5. Na+ channels close and K+ channels open. Repolarization occurs.

6. Sodium channels are reset, and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus (relative refractory period). During this phase, the potassium channels remain open and slowly return to closed state causing after-hyperpolarization.

7. Both channels are closed. The membrane returns to RMP.
questions.learning: Na, K Channel A: Na+, Channel B: K+ Na+ channels are fast activating and are responsible for depolarization phase of action potential. K+ channels are slow activating and open for prolonged duration than the sodium channels.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old man presents to the emergency department with respiratory distress and hypotension following a trauma. He has subcutaneous emphysema and there is an absence of air entry into the right side of the lungs. What is the next best step?
options: Start IV fluids with large bore cannula
Needle decompression into the 5th intercostal space anterior to the midaxillary line
Take the patient to the ICU and intubate him
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Needle decompression into the 5th intercostal space anterior to the midaxillary line

The given clinical scenario of a young male developing respiratory distress with hypotension, subcutaneous emphysema, and unilaterally absent air entry is suggestive of tension pneumothorax. The immediate next step, in this case, would be needle decompression at the fifth intercostal space anterior to the mid-axillary line (as the patient is an adult).

In children, the second intercostal space in the midclavicular line is chosen as the site for needle decompression.

Needle decompression turns a tension pneumothorax into an open pneumothorax. It has to be followed by tube thoracostomy. An intercostal chest drain (ICD) tube is inserted in the triangle of safety, just anterior to the midaxillary line on the side of the lung injury. The site of insertion is the same in both children and adults.

The triangle of safety is bounded by the lateral border of the pectoralis major anteriorly, the anterior border of the latissimus dorsi posteriorly, and the fifth intercostal space inferiorly, with the apex below the axilla. This provides a safe landmark for the insertion of an ICD with minimal risk of tissue injury.

Tension pneumothorax is a condition where air accumulates in the pleural space due to a one-way valve air leak, leading to the collapse of the affected lung. This can cause a mediastinal shift, compression of the opposite lung, and decreased venous return, resulting in obstructive shock. It commonly occurs during positive-pressure mechanical ventilation, but can also happen after chest trauma, subclavian/internal jugular venous catheter insertion, or chest wall defects. The diagnosis is clinical, and immediate treatment is necessary without waiting for radiological confirmation.

Tension pneumothorax is characterized by chest pain, tachypnoea, tachycardia, hypotension, tracheal deviation away from the side of injury, absent breath sounds on the affected side, cyanosis, and neck vein distention. Patients can also develop subcutaneous emphysema as a complication secondary to the pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: During pregnancy, ABO incompatibility does not occur due to which antibody?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IgM

IgM antibodies cannot cross the placenta from the maternal to the fetal circulation. Therefore, they do not have a significant role in causing hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) or ABO incompatibility during pregnancy.

ABO incompatibility is the most common cause of hemolytic disease in newborns and affects the firstborn. It is usually mild and subclinical. This incompatibility between the mother and fetus generally results in milder disease than Rh incompatibility does.

It arises when a mother with blood group type O becomes pregnant with a fetus of a different blood type (A/B). The mother's serum contains naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B, which can cross the placenta and cause hemolysis of fetal RBCs.

Although antibodies against A and B factors occur without previous immunisation (natural antibodies), they are usually IgM, which does not cross the placenta. However, IgG antibodies to A antigen may be present, which cross the placenta, resulting in A-O iso-immune hemolytic disease in the firstborn infant (A-O is more common than B-O).
questions.learning: IgM IgM antibodies cannot cross the placenta from the maternal to the fetal circulation. Therefore, they do not have a significant role in causing hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) or ABO incompatibility during pregnancy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: For a 40-year-old patient undergoing a minor surgical procedure, which type of intravenous fluid is considered most appropriate for use during the surgery?
questions.explanation: For a standard or minor surgical intervention in a healthy adult, Crystalloids (such as Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate) are the most appropriate and commonly used intraoperative fluids. Crystalloids are effective for replacing insensible losses and maintaining hemodynamic stability during the procedure. They are safe, inexpensive, and readily available. Colloids (Option B), such as albumin or starch solutions, are reserved for cases with significant blood loss or severe capillary leak, as they remain in the intravascular space longer but carry risks of allergic reactions and renal issues. Isolyte P (Option A) is a maintenance fluid typically used in pediatric populations due to its lower sodium content; using it in an adult could lead to hyponatremia. Option D is a medical condition, not a fluid. Standard surgical management focuses on "goal-directed" fluid therapy to avoid both dehydration and fluid overload, both of which can impair postoperative recovery and wound healing. Crystalloids remain the foundational choice for routine volume maintenance
questions.learning: For a standard or minor surgical intervention in a healthy adult, Crystalloids (such as Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate) are the most appropriate and commonly used intraoperative fluids.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a history of lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) presents with her fetus in the occiput posterior (OP) position. What is the most appropriate management strategy in this case?
questions.explanation: A woman with a previous lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) can be offered a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC) if there are no contraindications. The presence of a fetus in the occiput posterior (OP) position is not an absolute indication for cesarean section. OP position is relatively common during labor, and in many cases, the fetal head rotates spontaneously to occiput anterior, allowing successful vaginal delivery. Although OP position may be associated with prolonged labor, back pain, and increased need for assistance, it does not preclude a trial of vaginal birth. Continuous fetal monitoring and careful observation for scar integrity are essential due to the history of LSCS. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Cesarean section: Reserved for complications like fetal distress, failed labor, or scar dehiscence, not just OP position. (C) External cephalic version: Used for breech presentation, not for OP position. (D) Vacuum-assisted delivery: Considered only in the second stage of labor if descent is inadequate, not as an initial approach. Thus, trial of normal vaginal delivery is the most appropriate management
questions.learning: A woman with a previous lower segment cesarean section (LSCS) can be offered a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC) if there are no contraindications.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the labels marked as 1, 2 and 3.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 – Pepsin, 2 – Papain, 3 – Mercaptoethanol

This question refers to the enzymatic and chemical cleavage of immunoglobulin G (IgG).

• 1. Pepsin

• Cleaves below the hinge region.
• Produces one F(ab')₂ fragment (contains both antigen-binding sites joined together).
• The Fc portion is degraded into small peptides.

• 2. Papain

• Cleaves above the hinge region.
• Produces two Fab fragments and one intact Fc fragment.
• Each Fab fragment contains a single antigen-binding site.

• 3. Mercaptoethanol (β-mercaptoethanol)

• A reducing agent that breaks disulfide bonds between immunoglobulin chains.
• Separates heavy and light chains and can split F(ab')₂ into individual Fab fragments.

High-Yield Comparison

| Agent | Site of Action | Products Formed

| ----- | -------------- | ---------------

| Pepsin | Below hinge region | F(ab')₂ + degraded Fc

| Papain | Above hinge region | 2 Fab + 1 Fc

| Mercaptoethanol | Reduces disulfide bonds | Separates heavy and light chains; splits F(ab')₂ into Fab fragments

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Name the drug that acts on both the marked areas.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Omapatrilat

The drug that acts on both the marked areas is omapatrilat.

Omapatrilat is a dual inhibitor of neutral endopeptidase and Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). It decreases angiotensin II and increases atrial and brain natriuretic peptide, promoting vasodilation, diuresis, and anti-hypertrophic effect.

Other options:

Option A - Sacubitril is a neprilysin inhibitor. It reduces the breakdown of natriuretic peptides such as ANP, BNP, and CNP, thereby increasing their levels. Sacubitril combined with valsartan reduces mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).

Option C - Losartan is the angiotensin receptor blocker used in the treatment of hypertension. Hyperkalemia is an important side effect of ARBs. It appears to be a safe and efficacious agent to lower serum uric acid levels in patients with hyperuricemia.

Option D - Nesiritide is a recombinant human brain natriuretic peptide (BNP). It causes vasodilatation and natriuresis. It is administered intravenously and used in acute decompensated heart failure.
questions.learning: Omapatrilat — The drug that acts on both the marked areas is omapatrilat. Omapatrilat is a dual inhibitor of neutral endopeptidase and Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient develops hypotension and cardiac arrhythmias after receiving a supraclavicular brachial plexus block using 0.5% bupivacaine. What is the first-line management for this complication?
questions.explanation: The development of hypotension and arrhythmias shortly after a regional nerve block with a local anesthetic (like bupivacaine) is diagnostic for Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST). Bupivacaine is particularly cardiotoxic as it binds tightly to cardiac sodium channels. The specific first-line treatment and antidote for LAST is the rapid administration of a 20% intravenous lipid emulsion (Intralipid). The "lipid sink" theory suggests the emulsion absorbs the lipophilic anesthetic molecules from the blood and tissues, reducing their toxic effects on the heart and brain. While Invasive ventilation (Option A) and Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (Option D) may be required in severe cases of cardiac arrest, Intralipid is the targeted pharmacological intervention to reverse the toxicity itself. Sodium bicarbonate (Option C) is not the primary treatment for LAST. All settings where regional anesthesia is performed must have a "lipid rescue kit" readily available. Early recognition of the prodromal signs of toxicity, such as metallic taste or perioral numbness, is essential to prevent cardiovascular collapse
questions.learning: The development of hypotension and arrhythmias shortly after a regional nerve block with a local anesthetic (like bupivacaine) is diagnostic for Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient with progressive painless loss of vision presents to the ophthalmology OPD. The fundus image of the patient is given below. What could be the probable finding and the cause of it?
options: Soft exudate, central retinal vein occlusion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hard exudate, diabetes mellitus

The given image shows small, discrete yellowish, waxy areas with crenated margins that are suggestive of hard exudates, seen in diabetes mellitus.

In diabetic retinopathy, hard exudates occur due to chronic localized edema and are composed of leaked lipoproteins and lipid-filled macrophages.

Other common causes of hard exudates include hypertensive retinopathy, Coats’ disease, and circinate retinopathy.

Cotton wool spots (soft exudates) appear as whitish fluffy spots with indistinct margins that represent areas of infarcts in nerve fiber layer. Common causes are hypertensive retinopathy, toxemic retinopathy of pregnancy, diabetic retinopathy, anemias, and collagen disorders like discoid lupus erythematosus, polyarteritis nodosa, and scleroderma.

The image shows cotton wool spots

Flame-shaped hemorrhages are superficial retinal hemorrhages that occur due to disruption of the capillaries in the retinal nerve fiber layer. Common causes are diabetic retinopathy, non-ischemic central retinal vein occlusion, traumatic retinopathy, Eale's disease, hypertensive retinopathy, and anemic retinopathy.

Fundus examination of central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) reveals massive engorgement, congestion, and tortuosity of retinal veins. Ischemic CRVO has massive retinal hemorrhages giving a splashed tomato appearance involving the whole fundus.
questions.learning: Hard exudate, diabetes mellitus — The given image shows small, discrete yellowish, waxy areas with crenated margins that are suggestive of hard exudates, seen in diabetes mellitus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with a pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasma presents with visual field loss. Which specific visual field defect is most likely to be observed in this patient?
questions.explanation: The optic chiasm contains the crossing fibers originating from the nasal retina of both eyes. These nasal retinal fibers are responsible for detecting the temporal (outer) fields of vision. A pituitary adenoma typically enlarges and compresses the central portion of the chiasm from below. This pressure disrupts the crossing nasal fibers, leading to a loss of the temporal visual fields in both eyes, a condition known as bitemporal hemianopia. Homonymous hemianopia (Option C) and homonymous anopia (Option B) result from lesions in the optic tract or radiations, where corresponding halves of the visual field are lost (e.g., both right fields). Quadrantanopia (Option D) occurs with partial lesions of the optic radiations in the temporal or parietal lobes. Thus, bitemporal field loss is the classic sign of a chiasmal lesion
questions.learning: The optic chiasm contains the crossing fibers originating from the nasal retina of both eyes. These nasal retinal fibers are responsible for detecting the temporal (outer) fields of vision.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 2-week-old infant presents with fever and poor feeding. Lumbar puncture reveals cloudy CSF with predominantly neutrophilic pleocytosis, and CSF culture shows bacitracin resistance. Which organism is the most likely cause of this neonatal meningitis?
questions.explanation: In a two-week-old neonate, the most common cause of bacterial meningitis is Streptococcus agalactiae, also known as Group B Streptococcus (GBS). The CSF findings of high neutrophils and low glucose confirm acute bacterial meningitis. The critical microbiological clue is bacitracin resistance; while Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A) is bacitracin-sensitive, GBS is characteristically resistant. Pneumococcus (Option A) and Meningococci (Option D) are common causes of meningitis in older children and adults but are less frequent in the immediate neonatal period compared to GBS and E. coli. GBS is typically acquired from the maternal birth canal during delivery. Management involves emergency intravenous antibiotics, usually a combination of ampicillin and an aminoglycoside or cefotaxime. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis given to GBS-colonized mothers has significantly reduced the incidence of early-onset neonatal GBS disease. Recognizing the combination of neonatal age and bacitracin resistance is essential for rapid etiological identification on medical board examinations
questions.learning: In a two-week-old neonate, the most common cause of bacterial meningitis is Streptococcus agalactiae, also known as Group B Streptococcus (GBS). The CSF findings of high neutrophils and low glucose confirm acute bacterial meningitis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: School health program is under
questions.explanation: The implementation of the School Health Program is a primary responsibility of the Primary Health Center (PHC). The PHC medical officer and staff are tasked with conducting periodic health screenings of school children in their service area. This includes immunization, treatment of minor ailments, and identification of the "4 Ds" (Defects, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Developmental delays) as part of the RBSK initiative. Community Health Centers (CHC) (Option B) and District Hospitals (DH) (Option C) serve as referral levels for cases identified at the PHC or school level. While Health and Wellness Centres (Option D) play an increasing role in community outreach, the administrative and clinical leadership for school health services historically and structurally remains with the PHC. The program aims to ensure early detection of vision or hearing problems and provide nutritional support. Effective school health programs are essential for ensuring that children are healthy enough to participate fully in education and reach their maximum developmental potential
questions.learning: The implementation of the School Health Program is a primary responsibility of the Primary Health Center (PHC). The PHC medical officer and staff are tasked with conducting periodic health screenings of school children in their service area.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 1-year-old child is brought to the healthcare unit that you are working on. His mother mentions that he had received the first dose of DPT vaccine at 6 weeks of age but has missed vaccination since then. What would you advise the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Give second dose of DPT

The advice for the patient is to give the second dose of DPT (Diphtheria-pertussis-tetanus).

DPT is a combined vaccine given for immunization against the three diseases diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus. It is given to infants as early as 6 weeks following birth. The pertussis component of the vaccine is not recommended beyond 6 years due to the decrease in the severity of pertussis infection with age. 7 years of age onwards, only Td combinations are used.

It is given in 3 doses with an interval of 4 weeks followed by booster doses at 18-24 months and at 5 years of age. The dosage is 0.5 mL and is given in the anterolateral aspect of the thigh intramuscularly. The immunization can be resumed without repeating the previous dose in case of any delayed or interrupted immunization.

Adverse effects include fever, and neurological complications such as encephalitis, convulsions, infantile spasms and Reye's syndrome.

Anaphylaxis is a contraindication for subsequent vaccination with diphtheria, pertussis, or tetanus vaccine. Encephalopathy following vaccination is a contraindication for pertussis vaccine. DT is given for successive doses.

Events such as inconsolable cry, fever more than 40.5°C, seizures with or without fever are considered as precautions, and not contraindications for DTwP.

Note: IAP guidelines state that "temperature more than >40.5°C is a precaution and not contraindication". Park's 27th Ed states that "temperature above 40°C is a contraindication to DPT". This topic is controversial, however, IAP guidelines are commonly followed by practitioners.
questions.learning: Give second dose of DPT — The advice for the patient is to give the second dose of DPT (Diphtheria-pertussis-tetanus). DPT is a combined vaccine given for immunization against the three diseases diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In skeletal muscle, dihydropyridine and ryanodine receptors are coupled by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mechanically

In skeletal muscle, dihydropyridine and ryanodine receptors show mechanical coupling involving structural interaction between the two.

Dihydropyridine receptors (DHPRs) are voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the T tubule membrane.

The ryanodine receptor (RyR) is a ligand-gated Ca2+ channel with Ca2+ as its natural ligand.

Skeletal muscle excitation-contraction (E-C) coupling is thought to occur by a "mechanical coupling" mechanism involving protein-protein interactions that lead to activation of the sarcoplasmic reticulum ryanodine receptor by the voltage-sensing transverse (T-) tubule dihydropyridine receptor.
questions.learning: Mechanically — In skeletal muscle, dihydropyridine and ryanodine receptors show mechanical coupling involving structural interaction between the two. Dihydropyridine receptors (DHPRs) are voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the T tubule membrane.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve is affected when there is referred pain from ureteric colic felt in the groin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Genitofemoral

Pain from ureteric colic is transmitted via sympathetic afferent fibers accompanying T11–L2 spinal segments. As the stone descends in the ureter, pain is referred along dermatomes supplied by these nerves.

Referred pain pattern:

• Upper ureter → flank (T11–T12)
• Mid ureter → lower abdomen
• Lower ureter → groin, scrotum, or labia majora

This groin pain occurs because the genitofemoral nerve (L1–L2) supplies the skin of the upper anterior thigh and genital region, producing referred pain in the groin during ureteric colic.

• Origin: L1–L2 lumbar plexus
• Divides into:

o    Genital branch → scrotum/labia majora, cremaster muscle

o    Femoral branch → skin of upper anterior thigh
questions.learning: Genitofemoral Pain from ureteric colic is transmitted via sympathetic afferent fibers accompanying T11–L2 spinal segments. As the stone descends in the ureter, pain is referred along dermatomes supplied by these nerves.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man living in Nellore, Andhra Pradesh presents with the following lesions on his teeth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fluorosis

The above image along with the endemic area of Andhra Pradesh is diagnostic of Dental fluorosis.

Dental fluorosis (also termed mottled enamel) is an extremely common disorder, characterized by hypomineralization of tooth enamel caused by ingestion of excessive fluoride during enamel formation.

Fluorosis occurs when drinking water contains excess amounts of fluorine, in the range of 3-5mg/L. It is endemic in parts of India- Andhra Pradesh (Nellore, Nalgonda, Prakasam), Punjab, Haryana, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu.

Mechanism:

* In the extra-cellular environment of maturing enamel, an excess of fluoride ions alters the rate at which enamel matrix proteins (amelogenin) are enzymatically broken down and the rate at which the subsequent breakdown products are removed.

* Fluoride may also indirectly alter the action of protease via a decrease in the availability of free calcium ions in the mineralization environment.

* This results in the formation of enamel with less mineralization.

* This hypomineralized enamel has altered optical properties and appears opaque and lustreless relative to normal enamel.

Classification:

The two main classification systems which are used in the grading of severity of dental fluorosis are Dean’s system and TF system.

Symptoms correspond to levels of fluoride intake:

* Dental fluorosis: (1.5mg/L) Occurs if excess fluoride is ingested during the period of tooth calcification, i.e. in the first 7 years of life. Best seen on the upper incisors and almost exclusively affects only permanent teeth. It causes mottling on dental enamel, the appearance of chalky-white patches on the teeth, and loss of shine in the early stages. The white spots progressively turn yellow and can even become brown-black. The loss of enamel gives a corroded appearance.

* Skeletal fluorosis: (3-6mg/L) Occurs due to the heavy deposition of fluoride in the skeleton. Fluorosis stimulates osteoblastic activity, fluorapatite crystals are laid down in bone and these are usually resistant to secondary osteoclastic resorption. This leads to calcium retention, osteosclerosis, and osteophytosis. Ossification of ligaments and fascial attachments is characteristic.

* Crippling fluorosis: (>10mg/L) Can lead to permanent disability.

Genu valgum and osteoporosis of the lower limb are seen in a newer form of fluorosis in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. It is seen in people consuming jawar (sorghum), as it promotes greater retention of ingested fluoride.

Interventions for Fluorosis

* Change the drinking water source with a lower fluoride content (0.5 to 0.8 mg/L). Running surface water contains lower quantities of fluorides than groundwater sources.

* Chemical treatment in a water treatment plant can be moderately expensive. The National Environmental Engineering Research Institute, Nagpur developed a technique for removing fluoride by a chemical treatment called the Nalgonda technique.

* Fluoride supplements should not be prescribed for children who drink fluoridated water.

* The use of fluoride toothpaste in areas of endemic fluorosis is not recommended for children up to 6 years of age
questions.learning: Fluorosis — The above image along with the endemic area of Andhra Pradesh is diagnostic of Dental fluorosis. Dental fluorosis (also termed mottled enamel) is an extremely common disorder, characterized by hypomineralization of tooth enamel caused by…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The parents notice that their child is tired and that he has shortness of breath on climbing stairs and while lying down. What is the first investigation that you would do?
options: MRI to rule out enlarged heart
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chest x-ray

The first investigation to be done for a child who feels shortness of breath on climbing stairs and in the supine position is a chest x-ray.

The child having shortness of breath on climbing stairs is known as dyspnea on exertion. The most common cause is congestive heart failure. The child feeling shortness of breath in the supine position is orthopnea. It is relieved on sitting or standing.

Respiratory causes include asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD), pneumonia, and pulmonary embolism. Cardiovascular causes include congestive heart failure(CHF), pulmonary edema, valvular heart defect, and pulmonary hypertension.

Evaluation begins with assessing the airway, breathing, and circulation of the patient. Oxygen saturation can appear normal at rest, and hence oxygen saturation during physical activity should be obtained. A chest x-ray is the first diagnostic test which can show pulmonary pathology or pumonary edema and other signs of CHF that could help in identifying the cause and further evaluation.

Other options:

Option A: An echocardiogram can be done if the chest X-ray is abnormal. It is done to evaluate cardiac function, valvular function, and pericardial space.

Option C: Spirometry is done when the chest x-ray is normal. It is done to determine lung function. Abnormal spirometry can indicate either an obstructive pathology such as asthma, or COPD or a restrictive disease such as interstitial fibrosis.

Option D: Cardiac MRI (Magnetic resonance imaging) is an emerging modality done to look for cardiomegaly. It is for the accurate evaluation of left and right ventricular mass, size, and function. It is also used for localizing ischemic and non-ischemic causes such as myocarditis.
questions.learning: Chest x-ray — The first investigation to be done for a child who feels shortness of breath on climbing stairs and in the supine position is a chest x-ray.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The image shows a femur bone. Which muscles are attached at point “A”?
questions.explanation: The anatomical landmark labeled "A" on the proximal femur is the lesser trochanter. This bony prominence serves as the primary insertion site for the iliopsoas muscle. The iliopsoas is the strongest flexor of the hip and is formed by the fusion of the psoas major and iliacus muscles. The gluteus maximus (Option A) inserts into the gluteal tuberosity and the iliotibial tract. The quadriceps femoris (Option C) consists of four muscles that primarily insert into the patella and tibial tuberosity. The adductor magnus (Option D) inserts along the linea aspera and the adductor tubercle. Clinically, avulsion fractures of the lesser trochanter are rare and often seen in adolescent athletes or as a sign of metastatic disease in older adults. Understanding these specific insertion points is fundamental for diagnosing musculoskeletal injuries and planning surgical interventions involving the hip and thigh
questions.learning: The anatomical landmark labeled "A" on the proximal femur is the lesser trochanter. This bony prominence serves as the primary insertion site for the iliopsoas muscle.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Where is Ovoid and tandem radiotherapy used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cervical cancer

Ovoid and tandem radiotherapy is used for cervical cancer.

Ovoid and tandem brachytherapy is a combination technique where a tandem applicator and ovoid applicators are used for radiation treatment.
A tandem is a narrow tube, that is inserted through the cervix into the uterus, while the ovoids are placed in the upper part of the vagina. Once in place, a radioactive source is introduced into both the tandem and ovoids, ensuring precise radiation delivery to the cancerous tissues.

Both ovoid and tandem brachytherapy are designed to deliver targeted radiation therapy, maximising the dose to the tumor while minimizing side effects to adjacent healthy structures.

Brachytherapy is a form of radiation therapy in which the radiation source is placed close to the tumour. It can be either a low-dose or high-dose rate system. High-dose brachytherapy is safe and effective.
Dosage is calculated with respect to the amount of radiation received at two arbitrary points A and B (Image below).

Different techniques of brachytherapy:

Techniques
Device
No. of application
Duration

Stockholm

Intrauterine tandem

One vaginal plaque

Three
24 hours each week

Paris

Intrauterine tandem

Three vaginal ovoids

One
120 hours

Manchester

Intrauterine tandem

Two vaginal ovoids

Two
72 hours each weekly

Radiation dose in surrounding normal tissue is less due to inverse square law (Inverse square law - the intensity of radiation is inversely proportional to squared distance from the source of radiation). This method is unsuitable for large tumours and has potential risks of radiation exposure to medical staff.

Note: After loading technique by remote control is the recent development of brachytherapy. It protects the staff from radiation exposure.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organism is intrinsically resistant to the given drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Candida krusei: Fluconazole

Candida krusei is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole due to altered ergosterol pathway enzymes and reduced drug affinity. This resistance is predictable and clinically important. Other listed organisms are generally susceptible to their respective drugs. Fluconazole resistance is a classic hallmark of C. krusei.

| Drug | Mechanism

| ---- | ---------

| Fluconazole | ↓ Ergosterol synthesis

| Amphotericin B | Pore formation

| Micafungin | ↓ β-glucan (cell wall)

| Voriconazole | Ergosterol inhibition

Candida krusei = resistant to fluconazole

Candida glabrata = dose-dependent sensitivity

Voriconazole = DOC for Aspergillus

Amphotericin B = broad-spectrum

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A man with multiple myeloma who has undergone several cycles of chemotherapy presents with progressive fatigue, recurrent upper respiratory tract infections, and easy bruising. CBC reveals severe pancytopenia. Which of the following is the most important dose-limiting toxicity of melphalan?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bone marrow suppression

Melphalan is an alkylating agent (nitrogen mustard) commonly used in the treatment of multiple myeloma. Its dose-limiting toxicity is bone marrow suppression (myelosuppression), which manifests as anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and pancytopenia, leading to fatigue, recurrent infections, and bleeding tendencies. The patient has:

• Multiple myeloma receiving melphalan
• Progressive fatigue
• Recurrent infections
• Easy bruising
• Severe pancytopenia

These findings are characteristic of melphalan-induced bone marrow suppression, the principal dose-limiting toxicity.

Why not the other options?

• B. Hemorrhagic cystitis: Characteristic adverse effect of cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide due to the metabolite acrolein; prevented with MESNA.
• C. Pulmonary fibrosis: Classically associated with bleomycin and busulfan, not melphalan.
• D. Peripheral neuropathy: Most commonly caused by vincristine, bortezomib, and taxanes, not melphalan.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following radiopharmaceutical is most commonly used in PET imaging to detect metabolically active tissues?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fluorodeoxyglucose (¹⁸F-FDG)

¹⁸F-Fluorodeoxyglucose (¹⁸F-FDG) is the most commonly used radiopharmaceutical in Positron Emission Tomography (PET). It is a glucose analogue that accumulates in metabolically active tissues, making it highly useful for detecting malignancy, infection, and inflammation.

After entering the cell via glucose transporters, FDG is phosphorylated but cannot undergo further metabolism, leading to intracellular trapping. Areas with increased glucose metabolism therefore show increased FDG uptake (“hot spots”) on PET imaging.

Why not the other options?

• A. Technetium-99m: Used in SPECT, bone scans, renal scans, hepatobiliary scans, and thyroid imaging; not PET.
• B. Iodine-131: Used for radioiodine therapy and thyroid imaging; emits β and γ radiation, not routinely used for PET.
• D. Gallium-67: Used for imaging infection, inflammation, and lymphoma, but with planar scintigraphy/SPECT, not PET.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A child presents with a fever and continuing seizures for the past 30 minutes. The relatives say that there had been no seizure-free intervals in the past 30 minutes. What is the next best step to manage this patient?
options: Manage the fever and wait for seizure to subside
Manage the airway and wait for seizure to subside
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Give midazolam immediately

This scenario described above is of status epilepticus. The first line drug used is IM midazolam or IV diazepam/lorazepam.

Status epilepticus refers to continuous or repetitive, discrete seizures with impaired consciousness which lasts for more than 5 minutes.

The duration of seizure activity to meet the definition of status epilepticus has traditionally been specified as 15–30 min. However, a more practical definition is to consider status epilepticus as a situation in which the duration of seizures prompts the acute use of anticonvulsant therapy, i.e., more than 5 minutes.

Management of status epilepticus:

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A nurse sustained a needle stick injury while sampling the blood of a patient who is HIV-positive. Which of the following is incorrect?
options: Washing hands with soap and water
Measure baseline viral markers of health care worker immediately
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Administration of tenofovir monotherapy

Triple therapy (tenofovir 300mg + lamivudine 300mg + dolutegravir 50mg) is recommended for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), not monotherapy.

Steps to be undertaken after a needlestick injury are:

• Wash the wound and skin with water and soap. Do not scrub and avoid antiseptics.
• Assess exposed individual:

• Check baseline viral markers
• Monitor for acute seroconversion illness within 3-6 weeks after exposure
• If testing is positive, refer to ART center

• Assess exposure source and determine the risk of transmission
• Counseling and support
• Initiate PEP at the earliest - preferably < 2 hours and ideally < 72 hours
• 28-day prescription with drug information
• HIV test at 3 months after exposure
questions.learning: Administration of tenofovir monotherapy Triple therapy (tenofovir 300mg + lamivudine 300mg + dolutegravir 50mg) is recommended for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), not monotherapy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In India, which organization is responsible for promoting health awareness?
questions.explanation: The Central Health Education Bureau (CHEB) is the apex national body in India responsible for health promotion and health education. Established under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), its primary mission is to create health awareness through various media, community outreach, and the development of educational materials. Option A (CBHI) is primarily responsible for health data, statistics, and information management. Option B (ICMR) is the premier body for the formulation and coordination of biomedical research. Option D (National Health Library) serves as a repository for medical literature and information resources. CHEB focuses on behavioral change communication (BCC), which is vital for the success of national health programs targeting diseases like tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, and maternal health issues. By promoting preventive health behaviors and public awareness, CHEB helps reduce the overall disease burden on the Indian healthcare system and improves community health outcomes

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Tracheal deviation is given on the chest X-ray. Which is difficult?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tracheostomy

Tracheal deviation indicates mediastinal shift due to underlying pathology (e.g., mass, collapse, pleural effusion), which can distort normal neck anatomy and make tracheostomy difficult.

• Tracheostomy requires midline tracheal access
• In deviation → trachea is shifted laterally → difficult to locate and cannulate
• Risk of false passage, bleeding, or injury to adjacent structures

Why not other options:

• Laryngeal airway: Inserted blindly via mouth → not affected by tracheal position
• Endotracheal intubation: Done via larynx → tracheal deviation usually doesn’t prevent tube placement
• Cricothyroidotomy: Landmark-based at cricothyroid membrane → less affected by tracheal shift

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the Motivation model of health education, there are three stages for the adoption of new ideas. What is the third one other than awareness & motivation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Action

The third stage in the Motivation model of health education, following awareness and motivation, is action.

In the process of adopting new ideas or behaviours, individuals progress through distinct stages. The first stage, awareness, involves gaining general information about health needs and issues, which serves as the foundation for further exploration. Without awareness, individuals may not recognize the importance of making changes to their health behaviours.

The second stage, motivation, encompasses interest, evaluation, and decision-making. Here, individuals express curiosity about the information presented, seek out additional details, and weigh the pros and cons of adopting the new behaviour. This stage often requires interpersonal communication and support from peers and family, as individuals contemplate the implications of their choices.

Finally, in the action stage, individuals actively adopt and implement the new behaviour or idea into their lives. This involves not just the decision to change but also taking concrete steps to integrate the new practice into their daily routine. It is during this stage that the new behaviour becomes part of an individual's values and lifestyle, leading to sustained change. Effective communication strategies are essential to support individuals as they navigate through these stages, ensuring a successful transition to healthier behaviours.

Note:  The three models of health education:

• Medical model: Transfer of proven medical information into education
• Motivational model: Awareness → Motivation → Action or Internalization
• Social intervention model: Changing of a social environment
questions.learning: Action — The third stage in the Motivation model of health education, following awareness and motivation, is action. In the process of adopting new ideas or behaviours, individuals progress through distinct stages.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are risk factors for Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)? 1. Use of contraceptive pills 2. IUD use 3. Genetic predisposition 4. Sexually active teenagers Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 3 and 4

Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an ascending polymicrobial infection of the upper female genital tract. It is most commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Several behavioral and gynecological factors increase the risk of acquiring PID.

• 1. Use of contraceptive pills ✗

• Combined oral contraceptive pills are not a risk factor for PID. They may even reduce the risk of ascending infection by thickening cervical mucus.

• 2. IUD use ✓

• There is a slightly increased risk of PID during the first 3 weeks after IUCD insertion. Long-term IUCD use itself does not significantly increase the risk if no STI is present, but for examination purposes it is considered a risk factor.

• 3. Genetic predisposition ✓

• Host genetic factors affecting immune response may increase susceptibility to PID and its complications.

• 4. Sexually active teenagers ✓

• Adolescents are at increased risk because of:

• Higher prevalence of STIs
• Cervical ectopy, facilitating infection
• High-risk sexual behavior
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an ascending polymicrobial infection of the upper female genital tract. It is most commonly caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person was brought dead and an autopsy was performed to find the cause of death. The following findings were noted on examination. What is the probable cause of death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Throttling

The given autposy images are suggestive of throttling.

In throttling, the following mechanisms may lead to death:

• Occlusion of blood supply to the blood to the brain - carotid arteries
• Occlusion of the airway - minor role
• Carotid sinus pressure may result in vagus nerve stimulation resulting in cardiac arrest (vasovagal shock)

Other signs in deaths due to asphyxia:

• Petechial hemorrhages in the face, eyebrows, eyelids, forehead, ears, conjunctiva, sclera

• When they occur in the visceral pleura, they are called Tardieu’s spots

• Congested larynx with slight oozing
• Marked venous congestion of internal organs
• Emphysematous, congested  lungs with serosanguinous fluid exudates in alveoli
• Dark-coloured blood due to accumulation of CO2

Option B: Strangulation is a very generalised term used to describe deaths due to violent asphyxia. Eg- ligature strangulation, throttling etc

Option C:  In the case of hanging, there will be a ligature mark, injury to the cervical spine etc.

Option D: In case of mugging the neck is compressed or squeezed by holding it between the crook of the elbow or knee. The attack is usually made from behind. Though a victim killed by this method shows signs of asphyxia and other struggle marks, the examination neck will not show any evidence of violence, as the compression was affected by the soft muscles of the arm or leg.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A chronic tobacco chewer presented with an ulcerative-nodular lesion of 4x5 cm over the lip, as shown below. Which investigation would most likely confirm his diagnosis?
options: Superficial incisional biopsy along with normal tissue
Deep incisional biopsy of Ulcer along with normal tissue
Excisional biopsy along with normal tissue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Deep incisional biopsy of Ulcer along with normal tissue

The given clinical scenario along with the image showing ulcero-proliferative mass is suggestive of lip cancer which is a type of oral carcinoma. Histopathological diagnosis in the form of a deep incisional biopsy of an ulcer along with normal tissue is the gold standard for diagnosis.

Incisional biopsy is taken from the edge of the ulcer along with normal tissue as the centre of the ulcer is usually necrotic. A narrow deep biopsy is better than a shallow broad biopsy. (Option A)

Excisional biopsy is done for smaller benign lesions. It is not done in oral cancers as they are usually bigger in size. An excisional biopsy may increase the spread of cancer or cause functional impairment. (Option C)

Techniques like brush biopsy and exfoliative biopsy are less sensitive. Hence, they are not used for diagnosis. (Option D)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with a long-standing history of chronic liver disease and alcohol dependence presents to the emergency department after suddenly vomiting a large amount of blood. Considering his clinical background, what is the most likely cause of this episode of massive hematemesis?
questions.explanation: In a patient with known chronic liver disease and portal hypertension, the most likely cause of sudden, life-threatening hematemesis is bleeding esophageal varices. These varices are dilated collateral veins formed due to high pressure in the portal system. A Mallory-Weiss tear (Option A) involves bleeding from a mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction, typically after repeated forceful vomiting, rather than the primary massive event seen here. Boerhaave's syndrome (Option C) is a full-thickness esophageal rupture that presents with severe chest pain and sepsis, rather than primary massive hematemesis. A perforated ulcer (Option D) typically presents with sudden, intense abdominal pain and "air under the diaphragm" on imaging, rather than isolated massive vomiting of blood. For a "chronic liver disease" patient with "large quantity" bleeding, variceal rupture is the highest-probability diagnosis, requiring urgent endoscopy and stabilization
questions.learning: In a patient with known chronic liver disease and portal hypertension, the most likely cause of sudden, life-threatening hematemesis is bleeding esophageal varices.

questions.text: Which of the following proteins connects the lines marked in the following image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Titin

Titin is the largest protein in the human body and acts as a molecular spring within the sarcomere. It extends from the Z line to the M line, anchoring the thick (myosin) filament and maintaining its central position during muscle contraction and relaxation.

• The marked lines represent the Z discs and M line of the sarcomere.
• Titin spans from the Z disc to the M line, connecting these structures and providing passive elasticity.
• It prevents overstretching and helps the sarcomere return to its resting length after contraction.

| Protein | Function

| ------- | --------

| Titin | Connects Z line to M line; molecular spring

| α-Actinin | Anchors actin filaments at the Z disc

| Desmin | Intermediate filament linking adjacent Z discs of neighboring myofibrils

| Myosin | Major thick filament responsible for force generation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient, a known case of left inguinal hernia presents to the emergency with an acute onset of pain abdomen associated with nausea, vomiting and abdominal distension. His pulse rate is 102/min, BP is 100/70 mmHg and respiratory rate is 24/min. On local examination, the skin overlying the swelling is tense and erythematous. There is localized tenderness over the swelling; the swelling is irreducible with absence of cough impulse. The most probable clinical diagnosis in this patient is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Strangulated hernia

A strangulated hernia occurs when the blood supply to the herniated bowel is compromised, leading to ischemia. It presents with features of intestinal obstruction along with local signs of inflammation. Features include pain, irreducibility, absent cough impulse, localized tenderness, tense erythematous skin, and signs of intestinal obstruction.

Why not the other options?

• A. Obstructed hernia: Causes intestinal obstruction but blood supply is intact; skin is usually not erythematous or tense.
• C. Incarcerated hernia: Irreducible but without obstruction or vascular compromise.
• D. Irreducible hernia: Simply cannot be reduced; no features of obstruction or strangulation.
questions.learning: Strangulated hernia — A strangulated hernia occurs when the blood supply to the herniated bowel is compromised, leading to ischemia. It presents with features of intestinal obstruction along with local signs of inflammation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Assertion (A): The pH of stored whole blood gradually decreases with increasing duration of storage. Reason (R): Even during storage, red blood cells continue anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactic acid, which accumulates and lowers the pH of the blood.
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion
Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
Assertion is false, but the Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion

Stored blood undergoes storage lesions, a series of biochemical and structural changes that occur over time.

One important change is the progressive fall in pH, primarily because:

• Red blood cells remain metabolically active during storage.
• They continue anaerobic glycolysis, even at refrigerated temperatures.
• This leads to lactic acid accumulation, causing gradual acidification of the stored blood.

Other important storage lesions

• ↓ ATP
• ↓ 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG)
• ↑ Potassium (K⁺) in plasma
• ↓ pH
• Reduced RBC deformability
• Progressive depletion of coagulation factors (especially Factors V and VIII)
questions.learning: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion Stored blood undergoes storage lesions, a series of biochemical and structural changes that occur over time.

questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A neurophysiology question states that the extracellular concentration of potassium is 5 mmol/L and the intracellular concentration is 50 mmol/L. Using a Nernst slope of 61 mV (at 37°C, monovalent ion, log10 form), what is the approximate equilibrium potential for potassium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. -61 mV

The Nernst equation for a monovalent ion at 37°C is:

E = 61 log ([Ion]out / [Ion]in)

For potassium:

Eₖ = 61 log (5/50)

Eₖ = 61 log (0.1)

Eₖ = 61 × (−1)

Eₖ = −61 mV

A 10-fold higher intracellular K⁺ concentration gives a potassium equilibrium potential of approximately −61 mV.

Why not the others?

• A. +61 mV: Concentrations reversed (50 outside, 5 inside)
• C. +6.1 mV / D. −6.1 mV: Would result from a much smaller concentration gradient

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: According to neonatal resuscitation guidelines, chest compressions are initiated when the heart rate falls below what value?
questions.explanation: According to the universal Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) guidelines, chest compressions must be initiated if the infant’s heart rate remains below 60 beats per minute despite at least 30 seconds of effective positive-pressure ventilation (PPV). This threshold indicates that ventilation alone is insufficient to maintain circulatory function. Options A, C, and D are incorrect based on standard algorithms; 100 bpm is the threshold for stopping PPV if the baby is breathing spontaneously. Chest compressions in neonates are performed using the two-thumb technique at a ratio of 3 compressions to 1 breath (90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute). The clinician should also increase the oxygen concentration to 100% when compressions begin. Therefore, 60 bpm is the critical clinical decision point for escalating resuscitation from airway management to active circulatory support
questions.learning: According to the universal Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) guidelines, chest compressions must be initiated if the infant’s heart rate remains below 60 beats per minute despite at least 30 seconds of effective positive-pressure ventilation (PPV).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with oral cavity findings are seen in the image below. He is a smoker. What would you choose as your next step in the management of this patient?
options: Cessation of smoking and do biopsy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cessation of smoking and do biopsy

The patient, who is a chronic smoker, presenting with a wrinkled white patch on the ventral surface of his tongue is likely to have leukoplakia.  Confirmation of this diagnosis will require a biopsy of the lesion. Leukoplakia is a premalignant lesion, with a malignant potential of 1 - 17.5%, hence it is imperative that the patient is advised on cessation of smoking.

Leukoplakia is a premalignant condition of the oral cavity characterized by whitish patches or plaques that cannot be rubbed off.  They appear as small, well-circumscribed lesions and can extensively involve a large area of the oral mucosa.

Variants of leukoplakia are:

• Homogenous variant: Smooth white patch. Less asociation with malignancy.
•  Non-homogenous variants:

• Speckled leukoplakia is whitish lesions on an erythematous base. They have the highest risk of malignant transformation.
• Proliferative verrucous leukoplakia is rare and has a high risk for malignant transformation.
• Erosive (erythroleukoplakia) is when it is interspersed with erythroplakia and has erosions and fissures. This also has malignant potential.

Management includes smoking cessation and reduction in alcohol consumption. A biopsy should be done. A CO2 laser is often used for ablation.

A photographic record of the lesion is useful for long-term follow-up in cases of conservative treatment.

Given below is a list of premalignant lesions of the oral cavity with their risk of malignancy:

High-risk lesions
Medium risk lesions
Low-risk lesions

• Erythroplakia (homogenous/speckled)

•  Seen as red velvety lesions
•  Speckled type is the most  aggressive
•  The treatment of choice is surgical ablation

• Oral submucous fibrosis

• Hypersensitive reaction to betel nut product.
• Other risk factors are - tobacco, chili, vitamin deficiency
• Clinical features - trismus, ankyloglossia, soreness, and burning sensation in the mouth.
• Management includes antioxidants, intralesional triamcinolone, and surgical excision.

• Oral lichen planus

• Reticulate fine lace-like pattern.
• Management is topical corticosteroids.

• Proliferative verrucous leucoplakia

• A white patchy lesion that cannot be rubbed off.
• Speckled leucoplakia has an erythematous base
• The treatment of choice is excision

• Syphilitic glossitis

• Associated with tertiary syphilis

• Discoid lupus erythematosus

• Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis
•

• White patches that can be rubbed off with a hyperaemic border.
• Management includes prolonged treatment with topical antifungals or systemic antifungal therapy. If no improvement or if there are any signs of dysplasia, surgical excision is done.

• Dyskeratosis Congenita

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding UTI? 1. Urine is an excellent culture medium for bacteria. 2. Atrophic urethritis in postmenopausal women is a risk factor. 3. Antibiotics are recommended in all cases of asymptomatic bacteriuria. 4. Certain strains of E. coli have a particular propensity to invade the urinary tract. Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 4

Urinary tract infection (UTI) occurs when uropathogens, most commonly uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC), colonize and invade the urinary tract. Risk factors include female sex, urinary stasis, catheterization, sexual activity, and postmenopausal atrophic urethritis/vaginitis due to estrogen deficiency.

Why not statement 3?

• Asymptomatic bacteriuria should not be treated routinely. Antibiotics are recommended only in pregnancy and before invasive urological procedures associated with mucosal bleeding (and selected recent renal transplant patients), not in all cases.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Urinary tract infection (UTI) occurs when uropathogens, most commonly uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC), colonize and invade the urinary tract.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What dose of folic acid is recommended for a woman who wants to become pregnant but has a history of pregnancy complicated with a neural tube defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4 mg/day

In a pregnancy complicated with a history of neural tube defect, 4 mg/day of folic acid is recommended.

Supplementation with folic acid is standard practice before and during pregnancy to reduce the incidence of neural tube defects and for as long as a woman is breastfeeding.

Option A: In a normal pregnancy, folic acid is given at a dose of 400-500 mcg/day.

Options B and C: In adults with conditions having a high cell turnover like hemolytic anemia, supplementation of folic acid at a dose of 1-2 mg/day is recommended.

In hyperhomocysteinemia, folic acid is given at a dose of 1 mg/day.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 28-year-old patient presents with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections and chronic pain in the left flank. Further evaluation with a CT scan of the abdomen reveals characteristic findings pointing toward a renal structural abnormality. Based on these clinical features and imaging results, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The CT scan demonstrates a Horseshoe kidney, which is the most common renal fusion anomaly. It is characterized by the fusion of the lower poles of both kidneys across the midline by an isthmus of either functioning renal tissue or fibrous band. This fusion usually occurs anterior to the aorta and the inferior vena cava. Polycystic kidney disease (Option B) would show numerous, fluid-filled cysts within normal-shaped but enlarged kidneys. Renal ectopia (Option C) refers to a kidney located in an abnormal position (e.g., pelvic kidney) but not fused to the other. Hydronephrosis (Option D) is the dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces. Patients with horseshoe kidneys are at a higher risk for frequent UTIs and stone formation due to the abnormal orientation of the ureters, which often leads to urinary stasis. The isthmus is characteristically trapped by the inferior mesenteric artery during embryonic ascent. Recognition of this anomaly is vital for surgical planning in the retroperitoneum
questions.learning: The CT scan demonstrates a Horseshoe kidney, which is the most common renal fusion anomaly. It is characterized by the fusion of the lower poles of both kidneys across the midline by an isthmus of either functioning renal tissue or fibrous band.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents with cyclical pelvic pain every month. She has not achieved menarche yet. On examination, a suprapubic bulge can be seen in the lower abdomen. PR examination reveals a bulging swelling in the anterior aspect. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Transverse vaginal septum above the vagina
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Imperforate hymen

The given case scenario is suggestive of cryptomenorrhea due to an imperforate hymen.

Cryptomenorrhea is a condition where menstruation occurs but is not visible due to an obstruction of the outflow tract. The menstrual fluid gets collected in the reproductive tract.

Imperforate hymen is a urogenital anomaly. Imperforate hymen results due to failure of canalization of the inferior end of the vaginal plate. This anomaly usually remains unrecognized until puberty. It can lead to mucocolpos in early infancy. Patients present with amenorrhea, cyclic abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, and a hypogastric lump on abdominal examination. A bluish bulging membrane at the vaginal opening is noted on genital examination and the Valsalva maneuver.

Ultrasound of the pelvis reveals normal internal genitalia and hematocolpos. Laparoscopy should be performed along with hymenectomy to exclude endometriosis.

Most common causes of cryptomenorrhea:

• Intact/imperforate hymen - a bluish convex bulge is seen
• Transverse vaginal septum - a pinkish concave covering is seen

Ultrasound pelvis confirms the diagnosis. A simple cruciate incision of the hymen allows the free drainage of the collected menstrual blood and restores the reproductive capacity in most cases.

Other options:

Option A: Transverse vaginal septum occurs due to the failure of Müllerian duct fusion or failure of vaginal plate canalization. On examination, the vagina may appear shortened and the cervix may not be identifiable. Secondary sexual characteristics appear normal. The diagnosis can be confirmed with ultrasound or MRI.

Option B: Vaginal atresia is characterized by the absence of the lower portion of the vagina with well-differentiated superior structures like the uterus. On examination, the hymenal ring is normal, proximal to which only a vaginal dimple or small pouch is found.

Option D: Cervical agenesis is the congenital absence of the cervix typically with a normal uterus. These patients also lack the upper vagina in most cases. They present with primary amenorrhea and cyclic pelvic pain. If a functional endometrium is present, a patient may have a distended uterus, and endometriosis may develop. The absence of a cervix is seen on examination.
questions.learning: Imperforate hymen — The given case scenario is suggestive of cryptomenorrhea due to an imperforate hymen. Cryptomenorrhea is a condition where menstruation occurs but is not visible due to an obstruction of the outflow tract.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with hypertension remains poorly controlled despite treatment with antihypertensive medications, including a diuretic. Laboratory evaluation reveals hypokalemia. What should be the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: Hypertension that remains resistant to standard therapy (including diuretics) and is accompanied by spontaneous hypokalemia is highly suggestive of primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome). In this condition, an adrenal adenoma or hyperplasia secretes excess aldosterone, which forces the kidneys to reabsorb sodium (raising blood pressure) and excrete potassium (causing hypokalemia). The most appropriate treatment is Spironolactone, which is an aldosterone receptor antagonist. It directly blocks the action of excess aldosterone, helping to both lower blood pressure and correct the low potassium levels. KCl (Option A) would only temporarily fix the potassium levels without addressing the underlying hypertensive cause. Torasemide (Option C) and Hydrochlorothiazide (Option D) are diuretics that increase potassium loss and would significantly worsen the patient's hypokalemia
questions.learning: Hypertension that remains resistant to standard therapy (including diuretics) and is accompanied by spontaneous hypokalemia is highly suggestive of primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A cystic lesion in the suprasellar region with calcification is seen on the MRI. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Craniopharyngioma

A cystic lesion in the suprasellar region with calcification is suggestive of craniopharyngioma. It is derived from Rathke’s pouch and arises near the pituitary stalk, commonly extending into the suprasellar cistern.

Other options:

Option B: Pituitary adenomas are seen in the sellar region. Microadenomas are best shown on contrast-enhanced images. Macroadenomas are seen as snowman or figure of eight appearance.

Option C: Meningioma is a supratentorial tumor, mainly in the parasagittal region. A classical dural tail may be seen in intracranial meningiomas but is not pathognomic. The MRI image below shows a well-defined, hyper-intense, and homogeneously enhanced mass close to the midline suggestive of meningioma.

Option D: Oligodendroglioma is exclusively found in the cerebral hemispheres, most commonly in the frontal lobes. Upto 90% of oligodendrogliomas contain visible calcification on CT. The CT image below shows a calcified cortical mass that suggests oligodendroglioma.
questions.learning: Craniopharyngioma — A cystic lesion in the suprasellar region with calcification is suggestive of craniopharyngioma. It is derived from Rathke’s pouch and arises near the pituitary stalk, commonly extending into the suprasellar cistern.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 32-year-old man presents with history of recurrent jaundice over the previous decade. Family gives history of the patient having episodes of facial grimacing. Which one of the following is a clinical clue to the diagnosis?
options: Adenoma sebaceum in the mid face
Osler’s nodes at the finger tips
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kayser-Fleisher rings in the cornea

The combination of recurrent jaundice and facial grimacing (orofacial dystonia) in a young adult is highly suggestive of Wilson’s disease (hepatolenticular degeneration). A key clinical clue is the presence of Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings, which are brownish-green deposits of copper in Descemet’s membrane of the cornea, best detected by slit-lamp examination.

Why not the other options?

• A. Adenoma sebaceum in the mid face: Seen in Tuberous sclerosis.
• B. Erythema nodosum on the skin: Associated with sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis, and streptococcal infections.
• D. Osler’s nodes at the fingertips: Painful nodules seen in infective endocarditis.
questions.learning: Kayser-Fleisher rings in the cornea — The combination of recurrent jaundice and facial grimacing (orofacial dystonia) in a young adult is highly suggestive of Wilson’s disease (hepatolenticular degeneration).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The template DNA strand is 5'CATTCAATATCGATC3'. The resulting mRNA sequence after transcription is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5'GAUCGAUAUUGAAUG3'

5'GAUCGAUAUUGAAUG3' will be the sequence of mRNA produced from this fragment of template DNA.

The non-template strand or coding strand or sense/plus strand in the DNA will have the same sequence of the RNA that is produced, except that the non-template or coding strand has T is in place of U.

As all sequences are written in the 5′ to 3′ direction, unless otherwise specified, an RNA sequence of GAUCGAUAUUGAAUG would correspond to a DNA sequence, on the non-template strand, of CATTCAATATCGATC. Both the non-template strand and RNA produced will be a complementary sequence to the template strand.

Note:

Template strand - known as minus or antisense or non-coding strand.

Coding strand- known as plus or sense or non-template strand.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The maneuver shown in the image is being performed during delivery. What is the primary purpose of this maneuver?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prevent perineal trauma

The image demonstrates the Ritgen maneuver (also called the modified Ritgen maneuver), which is a delivery technique specifically performed to prevent perineal trauma during the second stage of labor. The Ritgen maneuver involves controlled extension of the fetal head during delivery to prevent perineal trauma by allowing gradual tissue distension and controlled emergence of the head. It is performed during the second stage of labor when the fetal head is crowning.

Principle of Ritgen Maneuver

The obstetrician:

• Applies upward pressure on the fetal chin through the perineum
• Controls the speed of head extension

This allows gradual delivery of the fetal head.

Controlled extension of fetal head

↓

Reduced strain on perineum

↓

Prevention of perineal tear

The maneuver is done:

• During crowning
• When the largest diameter of fetal head stretches the perineum

This is the stage where perineal injury risk is highest.

| Benefit | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Prevents perineal tears | Controlled head delivery

| Protects pelvic floor | Reduces overstretching

| Smooth delivery | Gradual extension

Other Measures to Prevent Perineal Trauma

| Method | Purpose

| ------ | -------

| Perineal support | Reduce tearing

| Warm compress | Improve elasticity

| Controlled delivery | Slow head extension

| Episiotomy (selective) | Prevent severe tears
