questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient who is a known case of hypertension on multiple anti-hypertensive medications came to OPD. His ECG finding is given below. Which of the following drugs is responsible for the ECG finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Spironolactone

Based on the ECG findings (tall T waves), the most likely diagnosis is hyperkalemia, and among the given drugs, spironolactone is the drug that is most likely to cause hyperkalemia.

Spironolactone is a potasium-sparing diuretic. It is a competitive inhibitor of the mineralocorticoid receptor in the late distal tubule and collecting duct of the kidneys. It causes a decrease in sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the distal tubule. As a result, spironolactone promotes sodium diuresis but maintains body potassium levels.

Hyperkalemia is defined as a serum potassium level of more than 5.5 mEq/L.

Hyperkalemia can cause drastic conduction changes. It can be diagnosed by a sequence of changes affecting the ST-T segments and QRS complex. ST-T segment changes reflect a change in repolarization while QRS complex changes reflect a change in depolarization.

The ECG changes that can be seen in hyperkalemia depend on the extent of hyperkalemia.

•

Drugs that cause hyperkalemia include:

• Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors
• Angiotensin receptor blockers eg. Losartan
• Mineralocorticoid receptor blockers like spironolactone, eplerenone, drospirenone
• Epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) blockers like amiloride and triamterene
• Others: Trimethoprim, pentamidine, nafamostat

Treatment of hyperkalemia involves the following:

1. Administer intravenous calcium gluconate, which raises the threshold and reduces excitability. It is cardioprotective
2. Administer regular insulin with dextrose. The insulin will reduce the serum potassium concentration by causing an intracellular shift. The dextrose will counteract the hypoglycemic effects of insulin.
3. Salbutamol nebulization will also shift potassium inside the cell.
4. Remove potassium with calcium-based resins, diuretics, or hemodialysis.

Other options:

Option A: The major potential side effect of prazosin is postural hypotension and syncope.

Option B: Metoprolol is a cardioselective beta blocker. Cardioselective beta blockers are less likely to cause hyperkalemia as an adverse effect. The risk of metoprolol-induced hyperkalemia is increased if the patient is also diabetic.

Option C: Hydrochlorothiazides increase the renal excretion of potassium and thus cause hypokalemia if the dietary intake of potassium is less.
questions.learning: Spironolactone — Based on the ECG findings (tall T waves), the most likely diagnosis is hyperkalemia, and among the given drugs, spironolactone is the drug that is most likely to cause hyperkalemia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Split thickness skin graft for wound closure on thigh includes:
options: Epidermis and variable parts of dermis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epidermis and variable parts of dermis

Split-thickness skin graft for wound closure on the thigh includes epidermis and variable parts of the dermis.

Split-thickness skin graft (Thiersch graft ) consists of the whole of the epidermis and only a portion of the dermis.

Full-thickness skin grafts (Wolfe graft): include the epidermis and entire dermis, with portions of the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles.

Advantages of split skin graft over full-thickness skin graft:

* Large grafts can be harvested.

* In the case of thinner split-thickness grafts, the donor site heals more rapidly and can be reused in severe cases such as burns.

* Uptake is good. Meshing can be done, i.e. small splits are made in graft and any exudates collected can come out through this and this improves graft take-up.

* Meshing also allows the graft to expand.

Advantages of a full-thickness skin graft over split skin graft:

* It has a lesser degree of post-graft contraction

* Best cosmetic appearance as they include the highest number of skin appendage elements.

The most preferable donor site is buttocks in cosmetically sensitive individuals and children. The most commonly used donor site is the thigh.

* The graft is taken from the donor site with a handheld Humby knife or electric dermatome.

* Grafts are perforated to allow exudates to escape and improve ‘take’. It can further be meshed to allow expansion.

* Grafts will take up only on the beds which are vascularized, hence preparation of wound bed is an essential step.

* Skin grafts are completely dependent on nutrition on the tissue over which they are placed and can heal well over muscle, perichondrium, and periosteum. They do not take well over bone or cartilage or on tissue that has been irradiated or infected or is hypovascular.

* A clean healthy wound bed with a meshed graft tied in place to stop movement will encourage take.

* The presence of group A beta-hemolytic streptococci is a contraindication in grafting as it can destroy split grafts completely and also convert donors to full-thickness defects.

* The donor area is dressed appropriately and the dressing is opened after 10 days and not earlier.

The given image shows Humby's knife. The average thickness of the graft obtained from a Humbys knife is 0.3 mm.

Pearl PF1917: Skin graft : phases of uptake of the graft

The take of skin graft occurs in three phases:

* Imbibition (Plasmatic circulation): during the first 48 hours, the graft is nourished with plasma exudate from host bed capillaries.

* Inosculation, in which cut vessels from the host bed line up with the cut ends of the vessels of the graft to form anastomoses

* Neovascularization, in which blood vessels grow from the recipient bed into the graft

Sensibility returns to the graft over time, with reinnervation beginning at approximately 4 to 5 weeks and being completed by 12 to 24 months. Pain returns first, with light touch and temperature returning later.

Note: some books give that the 3 phases are imbibition,revascularisation (inosculation+neovascularisation) and organisation (fibrin layer holds the graft in place and this is replaced by postgraft day 7 with fibroblasts)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: True statement for oxytocin?
options: It can be given by oral route
It is secreted by anterior pituitary
In higher doses, it exerts diuretic like action
questions.explanation: Oxytocin is a posterior pituitary hormone with several critical reproductive functions. The only true statement provided is that it is responsible for galactokinesis (Option A), which is the "milk let-down" or milk ejection reflex. It causes the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the mammary alveoli. It is NOT given by the oral route (Option B) because it is a peptide and would be digested; it is given parenterally or intranasally. It is synthesized in the hypothalamus and stored/secreted by the posterior pituitary, not the anterior (Option C). Crucially, in high doses, oxytocin has an anti-diuretic effect (similar to ADH) due to cross-reactivity with V2 receptors, which can lead to water intoxication (Option D is the opposite). Therefore, its role in milk ejection is its definitive physiological hallmark
questions.learning: Oxytocin is a posterior pituitary hormone with several critical reproductive functions. The only true statement provided is that it is responsible for galactokinesis (Option A), which is the "milk let-down" or milk ejection reflex.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Hypertriglyceridemia is seen in all of the following conditions except:
options: High intake of fructose in diet
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Abetalipoproteinemia

Hypertriglyceridemia results from increased hepatic VLDL production or reduced triglyceride clearance. It is commonly seen in diabetes mellitus, high-fructose diets, and nephrotic syndrome. In contrast, abetalipoproteinemia is characterized by an inability to form apoB-containing lipoproteins (chylomicrons, VLDL, and LDL), resulting in very low plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels.

• Abetalipoproteinemia (microsomal triglyceride transfer protein deficiency) → absent chylomicrons, VLDL, and LDL → low triglycerides, not hypertriglyceridemia.

Why not the other options?

• A. Diabetes mellitus: insulin deficiency/resistance increases lipolysis and hepatic VLDL synthesis, causing hypertriglyceridemia.
• C. High intake of fructose: promotes hepatic de novo lipogenesis and VLDL production, increasing triglycerides.
• D. Nephrotic syndrome: increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis and reduced lipid clearance lead to hypertriglyceridemia.
questions.learning: Abetalipoproteinemia Hypertriglyceridemia results from increased hepatic VLDL production or reduced triglyceride clearance. It is commonly seen in diabetes mellitus, high-fructose diets, and nephrotic syndrome.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the other name for an outlet forceps?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wrigley's forceps

Wrigley's forceps is an outlet forceps. It is used to provide traction force and can also be used in cesarean sections.

It is shown in the image below.

Pearl PF1918: Obstetrics forceps

Commonly used forceps:

1) Simpson forceps

* The most commonly used types of forceps in outlet delivery.

* Has elongated cephalic curve.

* These are used when there is substantial molding of the fetal head.

2) Elliot forceps

* Has an adjustable pin for regulating the lateral pressure on the handles.

* They are used most often when there is minimal molding.

* More suitable for outlet delivery.

3) Kielland forceps

* Has small pelvic curve and a sliding lock.

* Suitable for head with little molding.

* The most common forceps used for rotational delivery.

* Helps correct asynclitism.

4) Piper forceps

* Distinct perineal curve.

* Allows for application to the after-coming head in breech delivery.

5) Tucker-McLane forceps

* Suitable for fetal head with little molding.

* Used in rotational delivery.

6) Barton forceps and traction handle

* Used in rotational delivery.

* Most importantly used for delivery of occipitotransverse positions in a platypelloid pelvis.

* It is an obsolete procedure.
questions.learning: Wrigley's forceps Wrigley's forceps is an outlet forceps. It is used to provide traction force and can also be used in cesarean sections.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient diagnosed with diabetes has high increased LDL and VLDL because of ?
options: Hormone sensitive lipase and lipoprotein lipase both increased
Hormone sensitive lipase increased & lipoprotein lipase decreased
Lipoprotein lipase increased & hormone sensitive lipase decreased
Lipoprotein lipase and hormone sensitive lipase both decreased
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hormone sensitive lipase increased & lipoprotein lipase decreased

In diabetes mellitus (especially uncontrolled diabetes), insulin deficiency or resistance alters lipid metabolism, leading to hypertriglyceridemia and increased VLDL and LDL levels.

1. Effect on Hormone-Sensitive Lipase (HSL)

• Insulin normally inhibits HSL in adipose tissue.
• When insulin is deficient → HSL activity increases.
• This causes enhanced lipolysis in adipose tissue, releasing large amounts of free fatty acids (FFA) into the circulation.
• The liver takes up these FFAs and converts them into triglycerides, which are packaged as VLDL → increased VLDL production.

2. Effect on Lipoprotein Lipase (LPL)

• Insulin normally stimulates LPL, which hydrolyzes triglycerides in VLDL and chylomicrons to allow uptake into tissues.
• In diabetes → LPL activity decreases due to lack of insulin.
• This results in reduced clearance of VLDL and chylomicrons, further increasing plasma triglycerides.
questions.learning: Hormone sensitive lipase increased & lipoprotein lipase decreased In diabetes mellitus (especially uncontrolled diabetes), insulin deficiency or resistance alters lipid metabolism, leading to hypertriglyceridemia and increased VLDL and LDL levels.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A middle-aged man working in sandblasting developed hemoptysis, and a productive cough. Chest X-ray is suggestive of tuberculosis. Which of the following is associated with the same?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicosis

Silicosis is associated with tuberculosis.

Silicosis occurs in industries such as sandblasting, pottery and ceramics, mining, and construction. Silicosis patients are prone to developing tuberculosis, in a condition called silico-tuberculosis.

Silica causes pulmonary alveolar macrophage dysfunction and hence, patients with silicosis have a higher risk of developing lung infections from organisms like M. Tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, and fungi.

Radiographic imaging of silicotuberculosis shows cavitation.

In silicotuberculosis: it is still unclear whether silico-tuberculotics are really tubercular or purely silicosis, because

* Sputum is rarely AFB+ve

* Children and women of silicotuberculosis patients do not develop tuberculosis

* The post-mortem on silicotuberculosis fail to prove the existence of tuberculosis disease

* Radiological evidence of both the condition is similar

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following autoantibody isotype is involved in the pathogenesis of Acute inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IgG

IgG isotype of autoantibody is involved in the pathogenesis of Acute inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP), which is a type of Guillian Barre syndrome (GBS).

Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute autoimmune disease that causes fulminant polyradiculoneuropathy. It is a T-cell-mediated immune response.

GBS is usually associated with a history of upper respiratory infection (URI) or acute gastroenteritis (AGE) 1-3 weeks prior. The causative organisms may be Campylobacter jejuni, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

It presents with the following features:

* Ascending motor paralysis (lower limbs > upper limbs)

* Sensory deficits may or may not be seen

* Deep tendon reflexes—absent

* Transient bladder dysfunction—severe cases

* Autonomic manifestations—loss of vasomotor control, postural hypotension, and cardiac dysrhythmias.

Histological examination shows inflammation of peripheral nerves, manifested as perivenular and endoneurial infiltration by lymphocytes, macrophages, and a few plasma cells. On electron microscopy, an early effect on myelin sheaths is seen. There is segmental demyelination induced by the actions of activated macrophages.

There are several types of Guillain–Barré syndrome:

* Demyelinating

* Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP)—most common

* Axonal

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient is asked to copy the face of a clock, and the resulting drawing is shown below. What is the correct term used to describe this finding?
questions.explanation: The image displays a classic result of the "Clock Drawing Test" where the patient has crowded all the numbers onto the right side of the clock face, completely ignoring the left side. This is the hallmark of Hemispatial Neglect (Option B) (also known as unilateral neglect). This condition usually results from a lesion in the right parietal lobe (often after a stroke), causing the patient to lose awareness of the left half of their environment. Confabulation (Option A) is the fabrication of memories seen in Korsakoff syndrome. Kinetic apraxia (Option C) is the loss of ability to perform fine, skilled movements despite normal strength. Asterixis (Option D) is a "flapping tremor" of the hands seen in hepatic or metabolic encephalopathy . Because the patient has completely failed to represent one side of the spatial layout, hemispatial neglect is the only accurate neurological term. This test is a simple and effective bedside screening tool for parietal dysfunction
questions.learning: The image displays a classic result of the "Clock Drawing Test" where the patient has crowded all the numbers onto the right side of the clock face, completely ignoring the left side.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the condition given in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Placenta previa

The given image shows placenta previa.

The grades of placenta previa are:

* Type I (Low-lying): The major part of the placenta is attached to the upper segment and only the
lower margin encroaches onto the lower segment but not up to the os.

* Type II (Marginal): The placenta reaches the margin of the internal os but does not cover it.

* Type III (Incomplete or partial central): The placenta covers the internal os partially (covers the
internal os when closed but does not entirely do so when fully dilated).

* Type IV (Central or total): The placenta completely covers the internal os even after it is fully dilated.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A probe is inserted into the duct from which the nipple discharge is emerging. A tennis racquet incision is made and the flap is dissected to reach the duct. The duct is then excised. This procedure is known as?
options: Wide excision of the lactiferous duct.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Microdochectomy

Microdochectomy is the excision of the entire lactiferous duct (single duct disease). It is done for duct papilloma.

Microdochectomy:

• In a duct papilloma where no palpable mass is present, the duct is expressed to observe the discharge.
• A fine probe or stiff nylon suture is gently inserted into the duct, and the probe is secured to the nipple skin using silk sutures to prevent displacement during the procedure.
• A tennis racquet shaped incision is made to elevate the skin flaps, and the duct with the probe is excised along with the skin flap for 5 cm until the papilloma is identified (The papilloma will always be located within 5 cm from the duct orifice).
• The wound is closed without a drain, and a compression bandage is applied.

It is ideal to rule out DCIS by frozen section biopsy.

Cone excision and wide excision are done under major duct excision (Adair-Haldfield operation). It is done for duct ectasias with multiple duct involvement and multiple papillomas.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents to the emergency department with a burn on his upper thigh extending to his leg. On examination, there is soddening of the skin. There is erythema, vesicles, and a line of demarcation. What type of burn is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Moist heat burn

Moist heat burns (scalds) are caused by hot liquids or steam

Characterised by : sodden (water-soaked) skin, erythema, vesicle (blister) formation, and well-defined margins.

Mechanism: Heat transfer via liquid → greater penetration → superficial to partial-thickness burns

• Skin appears soft, moist, and sodden (not dry or charred)
• Common sites: thighs, legs, trunk (due to accidental spillage)

Why this diagnosis:

• Sodden skin is the most distinguishing feature
• Presence of vesicles and erythema indicates partial-thickness injury
• Clear line of demarcation seen in scald injuries

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the instrument shown below in image?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a Veress needle, a specialized instrument used in laparoscopic surgery to create a pneumoperitoneum (insufflating the abdomen with gas). It features a spring-loaded, blunt inner stylet that retracts when it meets resistance (like the fascia or peritoneum) and pops forward once it enters the empty abdominal cavity to protect the underlying viscera from injury. A Hasson cannula (Option B) is used for "open" laparoscopy, which involves a direct incision rather than a needle. Small and large bore cannulas (Options A and C) are more general surgical tools for drainage or access. The Veress needle is the cornerstone of the "closed" technique for gaining laparoscopic access. Proper technique, including checking for a "negative" aspiration and observing low initial insufflation pressures, is mandatory to ensure safe entry and avoid major vascular or bowel injuries. Correct identification of this instrument is a high-yield clinical task in surgical board exams

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient comes with repeated infections of trichomonas vaginitis, her physician advises for a Pap smear. She asks you regarding the purpose of this test. What would be your appropriate response?
options: It is a screening test for cervical cancer
It is a diagnostic test for trichomonas infection
It helps to diagnose cancer in her genital tract
It helps to diagnose other associated genital infections in her
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is a screening test for cervical cancer

A pap smear is a screening test for cervical cancer. It is not a diagnostic test (option C). The presence of abnormal cells/ a positive test requires further evaluation by colposcopy, cervical biopsy, or fractional curettage.

If trichomonas is reported from Pap testing, it should be confirmed by saline microscopic preparation (option B).

Cervical cancer screening should start at age 21. Women aged 21-29 should have a Pap smear every 3 years, while women aged 30-65 should have both HPV and Pap co-test every 5 years. Women should stop having cervical cancer screening after the age of 65 years. If suspicious PAP, screening till 75 years. HIV+ women should have annual checkups until three consecutive negative tests followed by testing every 3 years for life.

Pap testing should be done prior to vaginal examination. Lubricants should not be used and the patient should not be menstruating during the pap test. The patient should not have intercourse 24hrs prior to the test. The ideal time is around ovulation.

Procedure:

• The patient is put in a dorsal position, and the labia are parted
• Cusco’s self-retaining speculum is introduced
• The squamocolumnar junction is scraped with Ayer’s spatula:

• Bifid end - ectocervical sample
• Blunt end - vaginal cytology

• Endocervix is scraped with a cytobrush
• The sample is spread on a glass slide
• The slide is immediately fixed using 95% ethyl alcohol
• Stained with Papanicolau stain or short-duration Papanicolau stain (SPS).
questions.learning: It is a screening test for cervical cancer — A pap smear is a screening test for cervical cancer. It is not a diagnostic test (option C).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Regarding development of ocular structures, consider the following statements: 1. The eye begins to develop by the third week of intrauterine life. 2. The macula develops fully by around 4 years of postnatal life. 3. The cornea attains adult diameter by approximately 2 years of age. 4. The lens continues to grow throughout life. Which of the above statements are true?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

• The eye starts developing in the 3rd week of intrauterine life with formation of the optic pit.
• The cornea reaches near-adult diameter by about 2 years, earlier than many other ocular structures.
• The lens continues to grow throughout life due to continuous addition of lens fibers.
• The macula is not fully developed at birth. Foveal differentiation — centrifugal displacement of the inner retinal layers away from the foveola and centripetal migration/elongation of cones — completes by roughly 4 months of postnatal life. This is why:

• Fixation and following become steady by \~3 months
• Visual acuity is only \~6/200 at birth, reaching near-adult levels only after foveal maturation

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A female suffered a head injury from a road traffic accident. On examination, there is elevated intracranial pressure. Which diuretic among the following can be used in her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mannitol

In this patient with raised intracranial pressure after a road traffic accident, mannitol is the diuretic of choice in her management to reduce intracranial pressure.

Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that draws fluid out of the brain tissue and into the bloodstream as it forms a hypertonic solution when it reaches the bloodstream, thereby reducing intracranial pressure (ICP). It is commonly used in cases of traumatic brain injury or other conditions that cause elevated ICP. This effect helps to relieve pressure on the brain, preventing further damage.

Other options:

The other diuretics listed Hydrochlorothiazide, Spironolactone, and Acetazolamide are not typically used for managing elevated ICP. They are not hypertonic solutes and thus do not lead to a rapid reduction of the ICP as mannitol does.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following does not suggest a medical cause of mental illness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Auditory hallucination

Auditory hallucination is not suggestive of a medical cause of mental illness.

Hallucinations are perceptions in the absence of stimuli to account for them.

Auditory hallucinations are the hallucinations most commonly seen in the psychiatric setting. Nonauditory hallucinations often suggest that there is a neurologic, medical, or substance withdrawal issue rather than a primary psychiatric issue.

Features of the medical cause of mental illness:

* Acute onset (within hours or minutes, with prevailing symptoms) First episode

* Older age

* Current medical illness or injury

* Significant substance abuse

* Nonauditory disturbances of perception

* Neurologic symptoms—loss of consciousness, seizures, head injury, change in headache pattern, change in vision

* Classic mental status signs—diminished alertness, disorientation, memory impairment, impairment in concentration and attention, dyscalculia, concreteness

* Other mental status signs—speech, movement, or gait disorders

* Constructional apraxia—difficulties in drawing clocks, cubes, intersecting pentagons, Bender–Gestalt test
questions.learning: Auditory hallucination Auditory hallucination is not suggestive of a medical cause of mental illness. Hallucinations are perceptions in the absence of stimuli to account for them.

questions.text:
Identify the correct pair
i- Mummification, ii- Adipocere, iii- Marbling, iv- Lividity of death

i
Mummification

ii
Adipocere

iii
Marbling

iv
Lividity of death
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. i-3, ii-4, iii-1, iv-2

Image 1. Marbling: It is the discoloration of superficial veins due to the formation of sulphmethemoglobin, which starts in 24 hours and becomes prominent in 36-48 hours.

Image 2. Lividity of death: Postmortem lividity (suggillation, postmortem hypostasis/postmortem staining/livor mortis/suggillation/vibices) develops in the dependent portions of the body due to engorged vessels showing through the skin.

Image 3. Mummification: It occurs in the absence of moisture in the air and continuous action of dry or warmed air.

Image 4. Adipocere: It forms under warm and humid weather due to hydrolysis of lipids.

questions.text: All of the following structures are derived from the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Linea semilunaris

Linea semilunaris is derived from the aponeurosis of the internal oblique muscle.

Pectineal ligament, inguinal ligament and lacunar ligament are derived from the external oblique aponeurosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: If an individual has visual acuity worse than 3/60 but better than 1/60 in the better eye, along with a visual field restricted to less than 10° around the central fixation, how should this level of visual impairment be classified?
questions.explanation: Visual impairment is classified based on visual acuity in the better eye with best possible correction and visual field. According to standard public health definitions used in India and by the WHO, social blindness refers to a level of vision where a person has visual acuity worse than 6/60 but equal to or better than 1/60, or a visual field restricted to less than 10° around central fixation. In the given case, the individual has: 1. Visual acuity worse than 3/60 but better than 1/60, and 2. Visual field < 10° These findings clearly fall within the category of social blindness, as both the acuity and field criteria match this classification. Other options are incorrect: (B) Economic blindness is not a standard WHO classification. (C) Curable blindness refers to cause, not severity. (D) Manifest blindness is not a recognized classification term

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Bindi Leukoderma is caused by which chemical? (NEET PG 2019)
options: Crocein Scarlet MOO and Solvent Yellow 3
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Para Tertiary butylphenol (PTBP)

Bindi leukoderma is a form of chemical leukoderma (contact depigmentation) caused by repeated exposure to para-tertiary butylphenol (PTBP), a phenolic compound commonly present in the adhesive used to fix decorative bindis on the forehead.

Pathogenesis

• PTBP is selectively toxic to melanocytes.
• Repeated contact causes destruction of melanocytes, leading to localized depigmented patches at the site of application.
• Lesions may resemble vitiligo but are induced by chemical exposure.

Clinical Features

• Well-defined depigmented macules or patches on the forehead
• Corresponds to the site of bindi application
• May spread beyond the area of contact in susceptible individuals
• More common in women using adhesive bindis regularly

| Chemical | Association

| -------- | -----------

| Para-tertiary butylphenol (PTBP) | Bindi leukoderma, adhesive-related depigmentation

| Monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone (MBEH) | Occupational leukoderma; potent melanocytotoxic agent

| Paraphenylenediamine (PPD) | Hair dye dermatitis and pigmentation disorders

| Phenols/Catechols | Industrial chemical leukoderma
